maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: House proceeded to the consideration of amendments made by the Senate to Bill (No. 112) to amend the Immigration Act - The Minister of the Interior.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: That the said amendments be agreed to except the amendment whereby the words' [DOT] or for any other cause whatsoever ' are inserted in the eleventh line thereof, and, as to said last mentioned amendment, the same be disagreed to because such amendment confers upon the Governor in Council power to forbid the landing of any person whatever in Canada in the discretion of the Governor in Council which is an altogether excessive and improper power to rest in the executive authority.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifiton) moved :

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Where are the Senate amendments to be found ?

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
I presume they are in the original Bill. 1 will read them so that they can be followed. The Bill was pretty fully discussed in the House, and I need not go over what was said in connection with the general subject. But in the Senate some amendments have been made. The second section has been amended by adding after the word ' necessary ' the words :-
And every owner or master of a vessel who violates the provisions of this Act ; or who aids or abets an immigrant of passenger in acting in contravention of such order or proclamation ; or who refuses or neglects to take back on board the vessel any such immigrant or passenger, shall incur a penalty not exceeding ten hundred dollars and not less than one hundred dollars in the case of each and every immigrant or passenger.
I have no objection to that amendment. It seems to me, perhaps, effective in amplifying the origtinal intention of the Bill. Then, the first section, which enacts a section to follow section 24 of the Act, has been amended by inserting after the word 1 any ' in the tenth line, the word ' loathsome.' This would make it read
The Governor General may, by a proclamation or order, whichever he considers most expedient and whenever he deems it necessary prohibit the landing in Canada of any immigrant or any other passenger who is suffering from any loathsome, dangerous or infectious disease or malady

-And so on. I see no particular objection to that amendment, but there lias been inserted after the word ' malady,' the words ' for any other cause whatsoever.' Now, that would make the section read in this way.
The Governor General may, by proclamation or order, whichever he considers most expedient, and whenever he deems it necessary, prohibit the landing in Canada of any immigrant or other passenger who is suffering from any dangerous or infectious disease or malady, or for any other cause whatsoever.
So that, as the Act is amended by the Senate, the Governor in Council may, in the arbitrary exercise of his discretion, prevent any passenger for any cause from coming into Canada. I need only point out that if my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax), should go across to see the Coronation and the government, not desiring hi-s presence here next session thought it desirable to prevent his landing, under this Act they could legally prevent him from coming into the country again. The persons we may stop, are not classified or restricted in any way. I do not know whether the attention of the Senate was called to the extremely remarkable powers which they desire to confer upon the government, but, certainly, the government does not consider that the executive authority should have such unlimited powers for the exclusion of people coming into Canada. No such principle has been adopted by parliament before, and we think that parliament would like at least to have a full discussion of the matter toefore adopting such a principle. I agree with the other amendments, tout I think this one had better go back.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: 1 think it would be better not to include these words. They seem to confer very wide power which is hardly necessary at the present time. As to the object of it, possibly some members of the government who are to remain here during the Coronation would like to keep out of the country some of those who are going. However, I would not like to see an unfair advantage taken of any of them in this way and I agree with my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior in this motion.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
While this amendment seems to go too far, I think there should be a wider range of specified ailments and conditions that would be legal ground for excluding a party, so that those who are undesirable immigrants for other causes than such as are here given might be prevented from landing in the country. Notwithstanding this Act, people who are mentally



unsound and physically unfit may come in if they are not the victims of some loathsome, dangerous or infectious disease.
Motion agreed to.

speechtext: This seems to be a pretty serious kind of Bill to put through at this stage of the session. I did not suppose, on account of the delay in bringing it before the House, that there was any inten-

speechtext: tion on the part of the government to pass it this session.

maintopic: INCORPORATION OF JOINT STOCK COMPANIES.
speechtext:
This Bill has been carefully gone into in the Senate. The object is merely to simplify the method whereby letters patent are now granted. They are now granted by Governor in Council, and there is a good deal of red tape in the procedure. The gist of the Bill is in the first clause. I do not think my hon. friend will find it very formidable. Letters patent are to be issued by the Secretary of State.
Mr. BORDEN Halifax). If it were merely a Bill regulating the issue of letters patent, that would be comparatively simple. It is desirable that the formation of companies should be free as much as possible from any red tape. But this is a great deal more than that, because it deals with the constitution of these companies, with their powers, the liabilities of the directors, the shareholders ; in fact, it is a Joint Stock Companies Act to all intents and purposes- a very important Bill indeed.

maintopic: INCORPORATION OF JOINT STOCK COMPANIES.

maintopic: INCORPORATION OF JOINT STOCK COMPANIES.

We are to sit here and listen to the clauses being read, and accept the assurances of the right hon. gentleman and of the Minister of Justice, that all these clauses are perfectly right-they are the existing clauses, and there is no use of any further amendment. Well, I do not regard that as a desirable way of dealing with legislation of this kind. I certainly did not expect this legislation would be pressed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Before you leave the chair, Mr. Speaker, i *wish to call the attention of the House and of the government to a grievance which has arisen among the produce merchants of Montreal, and which probably exists throughout the Dominion. I wrote to the Minister of Agriculture last night, whose department that matter particularly concerns. He was here this morning, and I suppose I may state the facts. In the early part of the spring the Canadian commission merchants and those employed by them who had business in England, when calling upon their clients there, were surprised to find that in many instances they had been forestalled by the visit of a gentleman named Bull. Mr. Bull had presented himself

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is his name John ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
It is not John Bull but Charles Bull. He presented the card which I hold in my hand and by which card he purported to represent ' The Chas. A. Bull, Produce Company, cable address, ' Chasab,' 850,000 subscribed capital,' and gave his address as Montreal, Canada. In presenting himself to the people in the commission business and those interested in the importation of produce from Canada he had a letter which, according to the testimony of one commission merchant of the city of Montreal, who was in England at that time -I speak of February, March and the early part of April-from the Secretary of the High Commissioner in England. Fifteen of these letters had been distributed among the commission merchants there and these . letters, of which I have one here, were letters introducing Mr. Bull, written by Mr. Golmer, Secretary to the High Commissioner in England and written upon paper of the High Commissioner's office. I shall read this letter, which was addressed to the merchants and produce importers witli whom Mr. Bull desired to establish business relations :
Dear Sir,-I am desired by the High Commissioner to give to the bearer, Mr. Charles A. Bull, this note of introduction to you, in the hope that you will be able to spare a few minutes conversation with him on a matter in which he is interested.
Mr. Bull, who is engaged in the export trade in Canadian produce, brought a letter of introduction to Lord Strathcona from Mr. Fisher, Dominion Minister of Agriculture, with whom he is acquainted.

I am, dear sir,
Yours faithfully,

Secretary.
The Canadian merchants having dealings with English merchants, as a rule, found themselves in some embarrassment, being confronted by this letter in most of the places where they went to. One of them took one of these letters and brought it to this country together with the card issued by Mr. Bull. It was represented to these gentlemen that Mr. Bull, although soliciting business for this new company and although having a letter from the High Commissioner's office upon the recommendation of the Dominion Minister of Agriculture, had very little experience in that line of business, and probably on this account the commission merchants lost less than they would have otherwise, because lion, members of this House know very well to what extent a gentleman going from Canada and holding a letter of recommendation in his hand from the High Commissioner, issued at the special request of the Minister of Agriculture-might be placed in a position of advantage. Those who are acquainted with the customs of the trade in England will easily imagine what amount of influence such a document would have given Mr. Bull. At that time Mr. Bull had no legally incorporated company, but there was a project on foot in this -country for the formation of a company in which company I find that the brother of the lion. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), and I think, one of the employees of the Department of Agriculture were the principal promoters. I wrote the hon. Minister of Agriculture last night before I left the House a letter addressed to his department in which I told him) I would bring this matter up. I do not know whether or not he Received the letter.

At that time it is claimed that Mr. Bull represented, not a company, because there was no company then formed, but some parties interested in the export trade of Canadian produce, and that principal among these parties were the brother of the hon. Minister of Agriculture and an employee in the Department of Agriculture. I will quote to the House from the Quebec Official ' Gazette,' of the 10th of May, the present month, a notice to the parties seeking incorporation. At page 1,014 there is a notice of an application of some parties for incorporation under the name of the Charles A. Bull Produce Company, and in the sixth paragraph are given the names of the promoters of this produce company applying for incorporation.
Sixth. The names in full and the address and callings of the applicants are as follows :
Charles Irving Knight, of East Hatley, province of Quebec, general merchant ; Aaron Bull, of East Farnham, in the province of Quebec, gentleman ; Charles Albert Bull, of the city of Montreal, produce merchant ; Miss Annie Allison Horrigan, of the city of Portland, England, spinster ; Roswell Corse Fisher, of the city of Montreal, gentleman ; Horace H. Bailey, of the City of Ottawa, in the province of Ontario, clerk ; of which the first three are to be the first directors of the said company. All the said directors reside in Canada. and are subjects of His Majesty.
Now, it is claimed that of all these parties whose names I have given and who were on the 10th of May applying for incorporation, but wiho had not then obtained incorporation, the only responsible parties are Mr. MONK.
Mr. Aaron Bull, who, I understand, is one of the chief supporters of my hon. friend in his constituency, Mr. Roswell Corse Fisher of Montreal, a brother of the hon. gentleman, and Mr. Horace Bailey, who. 1 am informed, is an employee in the Department of Agriculture. What the merchants of Montreal complain of is that the hon. Minister of Agriculture should have given this letter of introduction to Mr. Bui) which enabled him to obtain from tbe High Commissioner in England a letter of introduction to each one of the importers, and which consequently placed the exporters of Montreal, who have been engaged in business for a long time and who have built up their business, in a handicapped position in regard to the promotion of their interests in England. It is claimed that.in so acting the Minister of Agriculture went beyond the duties of his office : that if he issued a letter in that way in favour of any one engaged in that line of business-which is a difficult business to build up and in which business some people have been engaged for many years-he should have given that letter, having an official character, to each one of those gentlemen or not given it to any one of them. One of these gentleman found letters of this kind in England in fifteen places where he was in the habit of doing business. They found that in the face of this letter of an official character coming from the High Commissioner upon the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture, they were handicapped in obtaining orders. That is the complaint which they have made to me. It seems to me that it is a complaint well founded, and in pursuance of their desire I thought it my duty to bring it to the notice of the House.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
(Hon. Sydney Fisher.) I regret that I did not receive the letter of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) beforehand, so that I could have had with me a copy of the letter of introduction to the High Commissioner which I gave to Mr. Bull. I may say that it is quite a frequent occurrence that all persons engaged in Canadian business who are going to England ask for letters of introduction to the High Commissioner. Mr. Charles A. Bull asked me through a letter which I will show to the hon. gentleman for a letter of introduction to the High Commissioner. Having known Mr. Bull for a long time personally, although not connected with him in any business way, I gave him that letter of introduction. Mr. Bull appears to have presented the letter to the High Commissioner's office and to have received a letter from Mr. Colmer, secretary to the High Commissioner, introducing him to certain people with whom he wished to open business relations. Personally, I have always understood that it was one of the functions of our High Commissioner's office in London, to enable Canadians going to the old country to be introduced, when

they were known, or when they had proper references, to people In England for business purposes. I have myself on frequent occasions given letters of Introduction to the High Commissioner to people from different parts of Canada with whom I was personally acquainted, and I know that others who are acquainted with the High Commissioner have done the same thing. As far as the company which Mr. Bull represents is concerned, what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) has just read to the House is the first which I have ever heard of it. I do not know that Mr. Bull is forming such a company ; I did not know that my brother, Mr. Roswell C. Fisher, was concerned with it, nor do I know who else was concerned.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Might I ask if it is true that Mr. Horace Bailey is employed in the department ?

speechtext:

I now nothing more about that than I do about the incorporation of that company of which I have never heard in my life until the hon. gentleman read the notice of incorporation. Mr. Charles A. Bull is a young man who came from my own county a good many years ago and entered business in Montreal. He has been a produce dealer there, and has done a good deal of buying and selling of butter and cheese in Montreal. He informed me that he wished to open direct communication with the old country and it was for that purpose that lie asked from me a letter of introduction to the High Commissioner, so that when lie went to England he might have somebody to whom to refer. Mr. Aaron Bull, whose name is mentioned there, is one of the most respectable and substantial farmer of my county, a gentleman whom I could trust and rely on in every shape and way ; an old Quaker, if I may use the term, whose name is noted for integrity and substantial standing in the community in which he lives. Mr. Charles A. Bull is his son, and he is a young man who, as I say, went to Montreal' some years ago to enter business, and who, as far as I know, lias conducted himself in a proper and trustworthy way. He has been concerned in a business which has not met with the approval of all the produce dealers in Montreal, because he has been a rival of theirs, and has been working up a trade on somewhat different lines from the established lines of the butter and cheese associations of the city of Montretal. In that way he has incurred, if not the enmity, at
all events the dislike, of those who have been long established in the trade. I do not know, however, that there is anything in his methods which are objectionable or to which exception can be taken. If there is I know not of it. I do not know, that because his business happens not to have been on the lines of the established houses there, that therefore it is necessarily bad or improper in any way. Not having received notice of this matter being brought up, I have not got with me a copy of the letter which I gave to Mr. Bull, nor a copy of his letter to me asking for that introduction. I believe that the letter which I gave him will not show in any way any improper relations between him and me, or any relations except those of courtesy to one whom I knew and who asked for a letter of introduction in going to England, which I was quite willing to give him.

We have been accustomed during the past four or five years to a somewhat different nomenclature with regard to expenditure in this country, from that which prevailed during the years when the gentlemen on the treasury benches were in opposition. In those days, notably the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright), the present Postmaster General (Hon. Mr. Muloek), the premier himself

and the Minister of Customs (Hon. Mr. Paterson), was not far behind then-they preached throughout this country to the people of Canada that there was a reckless and extravagant expenditure on the part of the Conservative administration; an expenditure which it was said at that time reached the sum of about ?36,000,000 a year on consolidated account.

Why, in days gone by the hon. gentleman would have shuddered at such on expenditure as he shuddered at the nepotism of days gone by. But these things do not shock him now at all. Well, I do not really know with how many tails the hon. gentleman himself is now connected. You have noticed that from listening to the debates in this House and from noticing the comments of the Diberal press in the country. Another curious circumstance has taken place. speechtext:
sary inquiry into these expenditures. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance is supposed to be the watch dog of the treasury. He reminds me very much of a watchdog spoken of by an American humorist. The burglars seemed frequent in the neighbourhood of this gentleman, and he procured a dog for the purpose of preventing any undue abstraction of Ills goods and chattels. A burglar did arrive while the watch dog was there. The faithful and intelligent animal fraternized with the burglar and immediately seized by the throat a policeman who arrived shortly afterwards to arrest the burglar. The attitude of the Minister of Finance, when we were pursuing our inquiries in the Public Accounts Committee into the expenditure, seemed to me very much like that of this watch dog. He fraternized witli the gentlemen who were making raids on the treasury benches, but was hot and eager to seize by the throat any gentleman who was prepared to make any criticism or inquiry.
Look at the moneys which were voted by this parliament for public buildings in the Yukon and at the mode in which some of those moneys was expended. Officials were provided in that country, not only with a salary but a very ample living allowance as well, in some cases ranging to $3,000, and possibly more, and we found, when we went into the public accounts, that money voted for public buildings in the Yukon had been applied in paying the living expenses of these gentlemen in addition to the salary and living allowance voted them by parliament. When we inquired into this extraordinary condition, the hon. Minister of Public Works simply shrugged his shoulders and washed his hands of the whole business. He said that he was ordered to pay the money by the Minister of Justice, and when we inquired about it from the Minister of Justice that hon. gentleman also disclaimed responsibility by saying that at the time he was not in office. There was not one member of the administration who could give us the slightest information or justification for this expenditure of public money.
Look at the expenditure on the Gallops Rapids. The hon. Minister of Railways and Canals has an item of $50,000 in his estimates for expenditure on these rapids. Consider the position of affairs there. We are told that the Auditor General, or some official of this government who had a due regard for the public service, gave notice to certain contractors that the vote had lapsed on the 30th June last. Notwithstanding .that, we have the Minister of Railways and Canals admitting, as he was forced to admit by cross-examination by hon. members on this side, that the work has been going on there to the extent of a great many thousands of dollars during the past year. We were not able to ascertain by whose direction or to what extent that work had gone on. T'he only information we were able

to get from the Minister of Railways and Canals was that he and his department knew nothing about it, but that the contractors came down here during the present year and presented their bill for a good many thousands of dollars, which they desired this government to pay. It was said that if the government had not ordered this work it would not be paid for. But it transpired a little later on that officers of the government had been in charge of the work, and yet we could not fasten responsibility for the expenditure of this money upon any member of the government. That is the information we have up to the present time. Perhaps we shall have further information before the prorogation of this House. And not only that, but we were assured by an bon. gentleman on this side who professed to know whereof he spoke that the work was not only useless but detrimental because it impeded the course of steamships up and down that canal. Then look at the Intercolonial Railway-contracts let without tender to the extent of twenty or thirty miles of road on the ground that ten miles of the same line had been let at the same figure after public call for tender. Rook at the expenditure of public money in the county of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance- and I am not referring to this specially because it is in his own county, but as an illustration of the methods of hon. gentlemen opposite. Consider the matter that I brought to the attention of the House this year, where a carnal was cut from the sea to a lake, for the ostensible purpose of creating a harbour for fishermen. But when the canal was cut, it was found that the bottom of the lake was higher than the sea-level, and the only result of the work was that the lake was drained into the sea.

The point in all this, however, is not who gave me the information ; the real point in the interest of this country is whether the information given to me Is correct or incorrect.
Further than that, I point out that the expenditure of public money, in many respects. does not proceed upon systematic lines or upon any principle whatever. We have brought down to us in the closing days of this session supplementary estimates of large volume. At two or three in the morning, with twenty or twenty-five men in this House, with three cabinet ministers, two of them asleep and the other putting through his estimates, we have been voting here hundreds and thousands, and hundreds of thousands-aye. "even millions of dollars for expenditures as to which we could not pretend at this stage of the session without undue waste of time to get any information Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
from the government. We have no less than 258 items in the supplementary estimates relating to rivers and harbours alone, items covering thousands of miles of this country, items concerning which it is utterly impossible for us at this time to gain accurate and necessary information. We have been obliged to allow these items to go through without the information which we should have. And we throw upon this government, as we have a right to do, the responsibility for the expenditure of this money without giving anv further information here than that which is afforded.
Criticism has been offered as to the duty of the opposition with regard to items of this kind. It has been said by hon. gentlemen on the other side, and also by the press which supports them, that the opposition, if they object to this enormous expenditure should move to strike out items that they do not approve of.
Well, the record of hon. gentlemen opposite with regard to that indicates that in making this assertion they are departing as far from the principles which they professed in the past as they have in a great many other respects. In 1879. the present Minister of Trade and Commerce proposed to make a reduction of $70,000 in the expenditure for civil government. In 1881, they moved no resolution against the expenditure. In 1882 they moved for a reduction of $8,000; in 1883, no resolution was moved; in 1884, no resolution; in 1885, no resolution; in 1886, no resolution; in 1887, no resolution; in 1888, no resolution. The House will bear in mind that during all these years my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce was going through this country clamouring against what he called the extravagant expenditure of the Conservative administration of that time. In 1S89 the present Minister of Trade and Commerce moved that the vote for Manitoba penitentiaries lie reduced by $10,526. In the same year Mr. McMullen, the present Senator McMullen, moved that the vote for East Pictou river improvements be reduced by $500. In the same year Sir Eouis Davies, a late member of this government, moved that the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway be reduced by $200,000, and gave as his reason the fact that coal was being carried from Springhill mine at less than cost. In the same year the present Minister of Trade and Commerce moved that a vote for the Department of the Interior be reduced by $95,748. In the same year- this was a very active year witli regard to motions for reduction of expenditure-Mr. Somerville moved that a vote of $195,135 be reduced by $50,000, because Mr. Henry Smith, who was formerly a member of the House, and Mr. W. A. Webster, who was immigration agent, had not furnished correct dates for their services. Iu the same year Mr. McMullen moved that the salary of C. C. Chipman be reduced by $2,300. or left out. In 1890 no resolution was moved,

nor was any moved in 1891, 1892, 1893, 1894, 1895 and 1890. During every one of these years the cry went up from hon. gentlemen opposite, and particularly from the hon. gentlemen to whom I have previously referred, that the expenditure of this country was scandalous and extravagant.
Now, where an opposition are not able to get, within a reasonable time, and without unduly protracting the session, information which would enable them to discriminate between hundreds of items brought down to this House, when they are unable to get information which would put them in the same position for forming an opinion that the government are in. the proper duty for an opposition is to protest against excessive expenditure, to throw upon the government the responsibility of making it, knowing as they do that the government have within their power the means of reducing that expenditure by eliminating from it items which are less worthy of public appropriation than those which are necessary to be made. That is the view which has been put forward in the English House of Commons as a sound principle, that an opposition in protesting, as we have protested, against undue expenditure, have discharged their duty without dealing in detail with the particular items of the expenditure brought down by the government.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not desire to go over these facts in greater detail, as they have been discussed, not only in the country but in this House for a long time. I say we must bear in mind in this country that we are passing through an era of great prosperity, which the Minister of Finance himself has, on more than one occasion, admitted cannot be expected to last indefinitely. I say that in that period of prosperity we are setting a measure of expenditure which we will find it hard to reduce when the. lean years come in the future. I say that in doing that we are not acting wisely. To expend every dollar of the public revenue during the abundant years, to go into debt in the extravagant manner in which this government has proceeded to lay burdens upon the country, is not a wise or judicious course. We should look to the future, we should measure our expenditure by the fact that the abundant revenues we now possess cannot always be expected to continue. Mr. Speaker, before offering the few observations which I think may be called for upon the general question of the expenditure of the country, permit me to say a word or two regarding what I cannot help characterizing as a most extraordinary action of tlie bon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) in reference to certain public works in my own constituency. If I refer to them particularly it is because he has referred to them particularly, and there is the further reason that the manner in which he has treated these expenditures made by the government may be taken, I suppose, as a good indication of the degree of fairness and of consideration which he applies to public questions of that character. At a comparatively early stage of the session my hon. friend read a list of a number of works in the counties of Shelburne and Queen's which I have the honour to 'represent and he charged in general, vague and indefinite terms, but still charged very emphatically, that there had been wrong-doing in some way. It was charged that the works were badly constructed, that they were extravagantly constructed or corruptly managed. The precise meaning of what the hon. gentleman wished to convey was not easy to determine, hut that he did desire to convey the impression that there had been corrup-

tion, mismanagement and extravagance in connection with these different public works is beyond all question. What are the circumstances under which the hon. gentleman brought these matters to the attention of the House ? He began by saying, and that was to his credit, that he knew nothing about them. If the hon. gentleman had stopped at that, and, knowing nothing about them, had said nothing about them, he would have pursued a course far more creditable to himself and far more in keeping with the good order of our discussions in this House. I grant that an hon. gentleman at times may be obliged to refer to some things of which he knows nothing himself, but if he knows nothing himself he is obliged in all fairness to give the authority of the man who says he does know ; but here the hon. gentleman, on the strength of an anonymous letter, undertakes at the end of the session to make statements that are as slanderous as they possibly can be about these works, without the shadow of an attempt to prove the statements he has made. It was the hon. gentleman's duty, if he believed the statements which he made on the strength of an anonymous letter, to go before the Public Accounts Committee, to call the officials concerned, to bring up the public accounts, to call the Auditor General, to call the engineer who had to do with these things, and to have an intelligent and fair investigation into this matter. Not one of these things has the hon. gentleman done, but be hopes some one may believe, precisely what it is difficult to determine, but at all events that there is some wrong in connection with these works. The hon. gentleman will see that he has pursued a course that is in the highest degree discreditable to himself and unfair to every man connected with these works. It is unfair in a sense to myself, but that is a small part of the matter, because the hon. gentleman does not imagine, I suppose, that I actually did the work down there ; but it is unfair to the people connected with the work, it is unfair to the engineers, it is unfair to the faithful servants of the government for an hon. gentleman, and especially for one occupying the high position of this hon. gentleman as leader of a party, to stand up, and, on the faith of an anonymous letter, make these statements, as he has made them, and then leave the matter there and fail to pursue any inquiry before the Public Accounts Committee or some other tribunal. I say that he is chargeable from his own point of view and that his party has a right to charge him with a great wrong in this matter. If he had information that there was wrongdoing then, it was his duty to probe the matter to the bottom. I will give the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for South Leeds (Mr. Taylor) the credit of saying that in several Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
matters in regard to which they have wished more information, and in which they have thought there was some wrong-doing, they went to the Public Accounts Committee, they called up the Auditor General, they brought the public accounts, they summoned witnesses, they made some attempt to get information upon the point, and the men who were accused had a chance of appearing before the Public Accounts Committee. But, the hon. gentleman has not pursued that course. He has made these statements on the strength of an anonymous letter, he has not gone before the Public Accounts Committee, he has not asked for the Auditor General, he has not asked for a copy of the accounts, he has not summoned a witness, he has been content to make these statements, unjust, ungenerous, untrue; I characterize them as such. He has been content to repeat these statements, admitting that he knows nothing himself and shrinking from giving us the name of any man who will verify these statements, and now, having been content to make these statements, he is about to go away and leave the matter in that condition. I think I have a right to complain and I do. The House has a right to complain, the public have a right to complain, because, if the hon. gentleman knew that there was wrong-doing, or believed that there was wrong-doing, it was his duty to probe the matter and in failing to do that, he has failed to discharge one of his duties ns leader of the opposition.
As to the general question, my hon. friend will probably admit that he has not added very much which is new to the subject in the debate to-day. He has travelled over the same ground that he travelled a year ago, over the same ground that his predecessor travelled for several years, and over precisely the same ground that the former Minister of Finance on the'eve of the last general elections travelled. He has made a number of general charges of extravagance and I am inclined to think that the country will take about as much stock in the hon. gentleman's assertions in that line as the country has taken on previous occasions, of which the constitution and membership of the House are the best evidence. But the hon. gentleman, if we were to take his criticisms as being serious, would have us understand that the conditions of Canada are the same to-day as the conditions were in 1896. He would have us understand that it is a fair thing to make comparisons between the expenditure of that day and the expenditure of this day, utterly ignoring the fact that a great change has come over the condition of the country. To use a common phrase it has been a growing time. It is not only a growing time in the affairs of the government but it is a growing time in the affairs of every great enterprise in Canada as well. Every railway, every great corporation, nay, every business

firm in Canada which is carrying on more business is spending more money than in 1896, and according to my hon. friend's logic, because it is spending more money than in 1896 it is therefore on the verge of financial ruin. In government affairs and in individual affairs as well a large expenditure may not be an indication of extravagance, it may be an indication of wise administration, it may be an indication of far seeing ability, it may be an indication of the ability of the merchant, or the ability of the government. By providing for a larger expenditure it may be that you are providing means whereby the individual or the government will be more prosperous than they were with a lower expenditure. The conditions of Canada have changed. The hon. gentleman takes our aggregate expenditure and he makes no explanation as to what that expenditure represents. Take for instance the expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway. We have spent a great deal of money on the operation of the railway-I will leave out of consideration for a moment the capital account. We have spent a great deal more on the operation of the Intercolonial Railway than our predecessors spent. Therefore, the hon. gentleman says that we are extravagant. But on the other hand the Intercolonial Railway receipts are much larger than they were. Before we took office they were $3,000,000 and to-day the Intercolonial Railway receipts are $5,500,000. Yet, the hon. gentleman would have us understand that the increasing expenditure is an evidence of extravagance. Take if you will the Post Office Department. We are spending a great deal more money on the postal service of the country than we spent before, but what do the returns show ? In 1896 the net revenue of the Post Office Department was $3,200,000, and the revenue for the current year is estimated at $3,800,000. In both these cases the increased expenditure does not represent an increase of one cent on the burdens of the country, but it does represent greater facilities for carrying on the business of the country. The increased expenditure in the Railway Department and in the Post Office Department is something which the government need not be ashamed of, because it marks the growth of the progress and business of the country and the increased facilities which are provided for the people. Take the. Yukon. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden) gives us the total expenditure of the year, and he compares with the expenditures of 1896, but he forgot to tell us that there was practically no Yukon in 1896. We know that one or two officers of the government had gone in there in the earlier years, but up to the time that this government came into power the Yukon was practically an undiscovered country. It was only under the administration of the present government that the great development of that territory took place. Hon. gentlemen opposite tell us of the total expenditure but they fail to tell that for every dollar that has been spent in the Yukon we have got a dollar back, and more. Therefore, the increased expenditure in that direction is not an indication of extravagance, but it is one of the indications of the development of the country which has come to this Dominion during the past few years.

I have not the figures at hand, but it is only in the year 1897 that the great discoveries were made in the Yukon, and that the Yukon began to be known. It is only since this present government came into power that there was a rush of people from all parts of the world into that country, and that this government had to assume the administration of the Yukon. We had to administer that country far away from railways and telegraph lines, and in the race of all that has been said, I say that my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior has reason to be proud of the splendid development of that country under his administration. So far as the working expenses on the Intercolonial Railway are concerned, that road is at least in a better position to-day than it was before. It is less of a burden to the country-if it is a burden at all-than It was before. Its receipts are increasing so rapidly that it will practically pay for itself. I will refer to the capital expenditure later. Then the Post Office Department; that is not only not a greater burden, but it is a greater blessing to the people of Canada than it was ever before. Under a lower rate of postage we are getting a larger revenue, and for a less rate of taxation the people of Canada are getting greater accommodation than ever in the history of Canada. If you deduct from the total expenditures, the expenditure on the Post Office, on the Intercolonial Railway, on the Yukon ; these three revenue producing departments, you will find that in all that remains the increase in the expenditure of the country has been very moderate indeed, and that there is nothing like the increase that the hon. gentleman ((Mr. Borden, Halifax) represents. He can only make out his case by adding the increase on the Yukon and the increase on the Intercolonial Railway, which perhaps during the current year will pay its own way and even though

there was a loss last year it was in a better position than in the time of the Conservative government. However, if you take out these items of expenditure, as I say, the aggregate increase remaining will be found to be a very moderate amount indeed. X have already said that it has been a growing time; a time of great progress and advance in Canada. Let us take a rough indication to prove that. I repeat what X said on a former ocacsion, that if one wants a rough illustration of the progress of the country it would be a fair thing to compare the expenditures with the total trade of the country. Roughly, the total trade of the country is a measure of the development of the country, and if you take for a rough calculation your expenditure in comparison with the total trade you get some reasonable measure-I do not claim that it is exact-but you get some fair proportion; certainly a much fairer statement of the accounts than was presented by my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax). Now, what do I find V I find that in 1895 the consolidated fund expenditure of Canada- leaving out the capital-represented within a fraction of 17 per cent of the value of our total trade; while last year the consolidated fund expenditure of Canada represented only 12 per cent of the total trade of the country. Now, let us add both capital and income together, and take the total disbursements of Canada. In the year 1895 the total disbursements of Canada of all kinds-capital, revenue, &e.-represented 19* per cent of the total trade of the country, while last year it represented 14-9 per cent, or a fraction under 15 per cent as compared with 19* per cent in 1895. I do not present these figures as giving any exact measurement of the expenditure of the country, but roughly stated the total trade of the country is a fair indication of the general development of the business of the country, and when we show that the increased expenditure has only kept pace, or less than kept pace, with the development of the trade in the country, then I think we have a very fair and very satisfactory answer to make to the statement of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Bordon, Halifax).
My hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) talks of the public debt. He says we have increased the debt. Again, I say that we must have regard to the increasing population, and to the increasing business of the country, and taking these into account we need not fear a comparison on this question of the debt. I have on another occasion given a statement showing the increase of the net debt from the year 1896 to the year 1901.' It includes the statements as shown In the public accounts. If you assume a debt of a province, and have to pay interest on it, your expenditure is increased by so much; and what difference does it make ? I am not going into a discussion of what this increase of debt was for. A great deal of it wras for the graving docks of Quebec. A considerable portion of it was for that interesting bridge at Montreal. A great deal of it was for purposes which, if I desired to investigate them to-day, might make a

very interesting chapter in the history of our predecessors. But I am not dealing wiih that phase of the question at all. There are the figures; I need not discuss the purposes of the expenditures, whether they were good or bad. It is the increase of the debt we are discussing, and the public accounts show that during the 18 years of hon. gentlemen opposite they increased the net debt of this country to the extent of $6,500,000 per annum, while during the 5 years of our administration, up to the 30th of June last, our increase of the debt was $1,900,000 per annum.
Let us view the matter in another way. My hon. friends like to make calculations per head in some cases, but you will observe that they have not done so in this case. We find that our increase of the debt has not exceeded the rate of increase in the population of the country. This is a fair mode of comparison. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs alluded to it some time ago, and I am only repeating his argument. In 1806, the last year of the late government, the net debt of the country was equal to $50.96 per head of the population, whereas the net debt last year, the debt which the hon. gentleman grieves about as so alarming to the country, which he holds up as such a bugaboo, was equal to $49.18 per head. In this we have but another evidence that, just as the expenditure of the country is only keeping pace with the reasonable growth and development of the country, so the moderate increase of the debt which we are showing is only keeping pace with the increased development and the increasing obligations and burdens which we have to undertake.
So we might go on through all the statements of the hon. gentleman and show that he is comparing conditions of former days with utterly unlike conditions which exist to-day. Will you tell me that the conditions in 1896, when our predecessors had a revenue on the Intercolonial Railway of $3,000,000, are the same as the conditions of to-day, when we have a revenue of $5,500,000 ?

My hon. friend was perfectly satisfied to have a deficit of three quarters of a million dollars under the Conservative administration, and to go and vote the old ticket, and say that the Conservative party was a party of economy; but when he finds us giving a better railway service, one of which the country may be proud, and he discovers that in one year there is a deficit in the operating of the road, the hon. gentleman suddenly discovers that the whole thing is wrong. My hon.
friend is a most amiable and respected citizen of Toronto, but in the matter of politics he is about the blindest man in the House.
Well, Mr. Speaker, if perchance we admit for the sake of argument that this is an extravagant government, and that the country needs a government of economy, where are we going to find one ? From hon. gentlemen opposite ? What is the evidence of their economy ? What evidence have they given of it in past years ? Where is the evidence of it to-day ? Why, Sir, again and again we have been asked in this House by hon. gentlemen opposite to do what ? To spend less money ? No, to spend more money. Last year, when my hon. friend moved a resolution similar to this one, I was able to point across the House to an hon, gentleman who complained that we did not double track the Intercolonial Railway for a long distance. I could point to another hon. gentleman who complained that we did not go into larger expenditures in the North-west. I could point to another hon. gentleman, no less than the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who but a few days before had led a deputation to the government to demand that we should spend millions more on the improvement of the St. Lawrence. So I could go along the whole line and show that hon. gentlemen opposite, who talk about economy and who are going to vote for this resolution, have been urging on the government a more lavish expenditure. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier not only wanted greater expenditure on these things, but he complained because we had not appropriated a large sum to send a man to search for the North Pole. I will say in fairness to the hon. member for Jacques Cartier that he has been away lately in Ontario busily engaged in making speeches, not of the same kind that he made in the province of Quebec, and he perhaps did not know all that was going on in the House in his absence; and last night, the first time he got a chance, he demanded- what ? Economy ? No; but he called on the Minister of Public Works to spend more liberally on the approaches to the canal at Sault Ste. Marie.

And my hon. friend the Minister of Railways reminds me that on a previous occasion the hon. gentleman reproached him because he had not spent a large amount of money in establishing locomotive works at Moncton. My hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Mac-Laren) is now in his seat, and I am glad to be able to remind him, as he is going to vote for this amendment, that only three days ago, in a very able address, to which all listened with great pleasure as coming from a gentleman familiar with our commercial

affairs, lie pointed to the fact that the United States government were spending hundreds of millions for the improvement of their waterways, and he declared that it was time that we set to work and did likewise.
I think I have said enough to show that if perchance this is an extravagant government, which I am not disposed to admit, then heaven help the country if it has to look to hon. gentlemen opposite for economy, when not one of them throughout this session has ever offered a proposal for economy unless the saving of a cent a gallon on a few gallons of oil. I venture to say that these things are understood in the country. The people understand that the conditions of Canada are not the same to-day as they were in 1896. The world has moved since then. Canada, as an hon. gentleman once _ said, before 1890, was living in a back street, and doing business in a back street; but in 1896, she moved up to the front, and since then she has been doing better business, she has plate glass windows, she has her sign up, and under the administration of this government the name of Canada is becoming known and honoured throughout the world. The country generally recognizes this fact. From east to west the story is told of how Canada has prospered under this administration. Go down to the sea, and you will find a great industrial development in the island of Cape Breton. But, say these gentlemen, it is our policy did that.
No, Sir, it is not. They fiddled and faduied with their iron and steel bounties for ten years but never succeeded in building an industry which attracted much notice. It was only when this government took up the matter that the great development down there began, and that the great development in the steel industry began in Sault Ste. Marie. It was when we took steps to give a contract to that factory at Sault Ste. Marie to encourage them in turning out steel rails, that the towering buildings went up, and then these hon. gentlemen opposite quarreled with us because we gave that help. It was only under this government that the locomotive works at Kingston were restored to their old energy and activity. That was due to the aid given by this government, and hon. gentlemen opposite found fault: with us for having given that aid. Go to the great west and what do you find ? These gentlemen, who pride themselves so much on what they did for the North-west, managed to produce a condition of affairs there which culminated at one period in a great rebellion and which, in 1896, produced a high class stagnation. AVhat has happened since ? Under the administration of this government, which has not been disposed to shrink from expenditure when such expenditure was needed, every great industry in Canada has been spurred into activity, and out in the far west, instead of finding people hopeless and despondent, we find that not only are the people who were there be-Kcn. for prosperous, contented and happy, but thousands are coming from all parts of the world, even from that favoured land to me south, and now we have a stream of immigration into that country such as has not been known for many years. East and west north and south, we see the indications that under the hand of this government, aye, the extravagant hand if you choose to call it so-but it is not extravagant because wise expenditure is the truest economy-east and west north and south you will find that, under the hand of this government, all the industries of Canada have been spurred into activity, Canada has prospered, and is filled to-day with the hope and belief that we have many years of prosperity still before us.

I have listened with much interest to the statements of my hon. friend and leader (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and the answer of the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding). The hon. Minister of Finance commenced with a very fierce personal attack upon the leader of the opposition, an attack Which was quite undeserved. The leader of the opposition spoke of certain works carried on in Nova Scotia, notably in Shelburne county. One of these works, he said, had been washed away, another was of no public utility, while another, designed to afford a harbour of refuge for fishing boats involved such bad engineering that the canal dug from the sea into a lake only served to drain the lake, as the bottom of it was higher than the sea level. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) did not make these statements upon his own authority, but upon the authority of reports in the neighbourhood and of what the hon. Minister of Finance is pleased to call anonymous letters. These statements were made in Committee of Supply, and the hon. member for Halifax had the right to give any authority he pleased and, the right, if he pleased, to withhold the names of this correspondents. Are the facts true ? That is what the country is interested in knowing. The facts are known to the Department of the Minister of Public Works and the hon. Minister of Finance had only to ask the engineer to learn the truth or falsity of the statements made by the hon. leader of the opposition. But, the hon. Minister of Finance does not even take the trouble to deny these statements. Does he dare to say that the faots with regard to this ditch are not ns given by the hon. leader of the opposition ? He was challenged on this subject a couple of months ago; why, then, does not he produce the evidence ? If the facts which are In possession of the department were made known to this House, and if they proved that the statements made were incorrect, no ihon. gentleman would be more

ready to acknowledge bis mistake and make the amende honorable both to the House and to the Finance Minister than the leader of the opposition.
The Finance Minister gives a glowing account of the prosperity of this country, due, as he would have us infer, to the statesmanship of hon. gentlemen who are now in power. Can these bon. gentlemen point to one thing they have done, to one Act which they have put upon the statute-book that has contributed to the advancement or development of the country ? That development is due to the legislation of the predecessors of these hon. gentlemen, to the national policy, to the building of the Canadian Pacific Railway, to the building of the canals, to the bonus'ing of steel and iron works, and other Conservative measures. The hon. Minister of Finance takes credit for the opening of the locomotive works at Kingston and also for the development at Sault Ste. Marie. Why, I had an idea that I was the person who gave the first contract to Mr. Clergue at Sault Ste. Marie ; that it was I who leased to Mm the water power when 1 was Minister of Railways and Canals; that I was the means of having that gentleman build up his enterprises there after he had been induced by the national policy to come to this country. X had some idea that if there was development in iron and steel works in the Dominion, it was due to the policy which was adopted by the Conservative government and was over and over again condemned by hon. gentlemen opposite. And what has become of the promises of these hon. gentlemen to establish a rule of economy '! The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir Richard Cartwright) has been taunted with having accused the Conservative government of extravagance and of over burdening the people with taxation and increasing enormously the public debt. Ob, but these are different times, these are the growing times; and that is the one poor justification that these hon. gentlemen ban offer for increasing the total expenditure of the country-the capital expenditure on current revenue combined- from $42,000,000, as it was in the last year of our term of office, to $65,000,000 which the Minister of Finance proposes for next year. The bon. Minister of Finance makes a comparison to show that the amount of increase is not so very large after all. He asks us to deduct from the $65,000,000 of expenditure, the difference between the $3,500,000 which we estimated for the working of ithe Intercolonial Railway and the $5,000,000, which it) costs now. That is perfectly right. That amount should be deducted-$1,500,000. And I will admit also that w<e should deduct the difference between the amount of revenue which we received from the post office in 1890, and the amount which they receive at the present day-$500,000.	And I will admit further
that the expenditure on the Yukon would also be deducted from this account. But 152
make all these deductions, and you find that next year's expenditure will be nearly $20,000,000 greater than the expenditure during the last year of our term of office. What are we to think of public men, of statesmen, seeking the suffrages of the people with the promises of reduction in expenditure and in taxes, and, When they attain power falsifying every pledge they made, out-heroding Herod in their extravagance and corruption-even taking their own description of what used to exist-and also adopting the policy of their predecessors on every great public question ? The hon. Minister of Finance makes a comparison between the debt of the country now and as it was when the Conservative government 'went out of power. The public debt has increased $10,000,000 since in 1896, and the Minister of Finance says he will have to increase it by $6,000,000 next year. This makes a total of $16,000,000 of increase. To make a comparison of the results of our policy and theirs in respect to public debt, the hon. minister takes the increase of indebtedness during the last eighteen years of Conservative administration. Does he think that is fair ? He tells us he takes these figures from the public accounts. Yes; but would lie charge to the Conservative government the $77,000,000 of provincial debts which were assumed by the Dominion at confederation 7 If not, then, why should he hold the Conservative government responsible for the $20,000,000 of provincial debts taken over by the Dominion under the Conservatives ? Does not he know also that in his calculation he took in $10,000,000 expended for the purchase from the Canadian Pacific Railway of lands which had been given to them in consideration of their constructing the road, and that these lands were a quid pro quo for that increase of indebtedness V And does not he know that $62,000,000 of that debt represented an entirely abnormal expenditure, that upon the great work of the Canadian Pacific Railway? Leave out these three items of assumed provincial debt, expenditure in the repurchase of Canadian Pacific Railway lands, and expenditure on the Canadian Pacific Railway itself and the comparison will be favourable to us. He says that he took the accounts as he found them iu the public accounts. Does he take the accounts as he found them in 1897 when he came into power, when, for the purpose of making a comparison between his administration and that of the Conservative government for two or three years previously, lie falsified the accounts, shall 1 say ? Not, perhaps, falsified them, but altered them to suit his purpose. The accounts are not the same as the hon. gentleman found them when he came into, power. it in a lump sum against his predecessors for the purpose of justifying an expenditure for the several years, and making a comparison between his government and the Conservative government, on capital account, to the disadvantage of the latter.

Yes ; in 1832 the canal was commenced, and it was finished in 1834. It was built by Act of parliament of Canada. Under that Act the government had power to take it over from the corporation that built it. They took it from the corporation that built it and expended money to finish it. There is the same justification for the expenditure on the Tay canal that I have heard the hon. gentleman give himself. I remember well the support that lie got from Mr. Somerville, the member for Brant. The justification was this : Large sums of money are being expended in different parts .of the country, and it is bard that a section of country which does not benefit by these public works and yet contributes towards them, should not receive a quid pro quo. I well remember the arguments used in support of the minister Who introduced the first item for the purpose of building the Tay canal, and I was gratified to hear the Minister of Finance, speaking in justification of that expenditure in the county of Shelburne using almost the same words. We agree upon that subject, that there should he a quid pro quo in some way or another in regard to expenditures.
But the hon. gentleman surely must be satisfied with the expenditure that is going on now in the maritime provinces. It is about enough to eat up the whole of his surplus since lie got into power,' $21,900,000-if you capitalize the amount that he has given to the Grand Trunk Railway at $4,660,000-'has been expended in betterments on capital on the Intercolonial Railway. He has expended the whole surplus earnings of the Dominion in these prosperous times, not on his little wharfs, or lighthouses, or improvements in the different parts of Ills province, but all expended upon that work which we thought we had finished, and the capital account of which we had closed long ago ; the whole of that expenditure has been wasted on new locomotives and for certain other purposes on the Intercolonial Railway. Do tile people of this country fully understand it ? Do they realize that the whole prosperity of the Dominion of Canada has been pitched in, has disappeared in what I declared 'before to toe a useless expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway ? $22,000,000- who denies the figures ? Who dare contradict them to this House? I will give him Item by item the whole expenditure on capital account, and the deficits on that road, and will show that the people of this country

have expended the whole of their surplus revenue in these prosperous times, for what purpose ? Building up the Intercolonial Railway ? No, for the purpose of disgusting the people of this country with the management of the Intercolonial Railway, so that it may 'become in a short time a property for some company or another to take off our hands, when the country will be so sick of it that it will be glad to get rid of it. The hon. gentleman says : Look at the comparison between the management of that railway now and what it was under the Conservatives ; the management and the deficits in the later years under the Conservative government were as bad as they are under my management. Yes. if the same system of book-keeping is followed he can make a surplus.
The proper way to look at the expenditures and receipts on the Intercolonial Railway is to see what amount of money is expended upon it and what are the receipts. Never mind the capital account, never mind the sidings, never mind the new rails, the new locomotives, or anything of that kind ; ask only : What money do you put into it ? The money you put into that road, as I said before, since the hon. gentleman has been administering it, is $22,000,000, or within $10,000 of that figure, more than the receipts of that road. That money would have given us one of the best systems of transportation in the world, that money would have built the Georgian bay canal ; that money would have put the Canadian people in possession of the best system of transportation in the world. Yet the whole resources of the country must be frittered away for the purpose of enabling these hon. gentlemen to maintain themselves in power by extravagant expenditures. Where is the justification for the 200 or 300 little lighthouses that the hon. gentleman is building down in Nova Scotia, somewhere ? This is not a penitent session. If it were the last session, as the hon. gentleman said, and votes of this kind were perhaps for the purpose of catching the electors without any intention of spending the money it might be different, but two or three years will elapse before an election takes place and it means that this money shall be expended. As I stated before the hon. Minister of Finance and the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals are looking after their provinces well. I cannot congratulate the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Mulock), I cannot congratulate other members of the government when I see the enormous sums of money taken out of the coffers of this country and expended in the useless manner in which they are being expended in the maritime provinces. If confederation is going to exist, we intend to, and we shall have our share of the moneys which are being levied on the people of this country and expended upon works of utility and for the use of the Dominion in other particular 1524
provinces. It is not sufficient, as it is in France and other countries, that the sole and only object of portions of the Dominion should be to see how much they can get out of the Dominion treasury. This must be put an end to ; there must be a fair division of the funds of the people between the different provinces or there will be an end to confederation. This practice was not pursued in the past. We built the Intercolonial Railway. Of course, they contributed, they contributed a sum towards it. We said :	You may have the use of that
railway without the people of the country expecting to receive a cent for it for the purpose of carrying your grain and traffic. It is, to a certain extent, of mutual advantage, but we never contemplated that after the people of this country had been drawn upon to the extent of $02,000,000 or $70,000,000 for the purpose of constructing that road that there should be an additional expenditure taken out of the coffers of the country to the extent of between $3,000,000 and $4,000,000 a year. This is not fair to the rest of the community. If the country is prosperous and growing, the revenue resulting from the growth should be distributed fairly between the people of the country. We have always looked with pride to the growth of the North-west Territories and we have always expected that we would get a return from the development of those territories and from British Columbia. We are willing to make an expenuiture in excess of the amount that is received from that country for the development and building up of that magnificent heritage of ours ; knowing that in the shape of trade and in other ways we will indirectly get a return from the development of that country. Our expectations have been verified and we are getting that return, but, from this expenditure down on the sea coast we are receiving no benefit whatever. Where is the expenditure for the purpose of improving our waterways ? Why cannot we have a magnificent harbour in Montreal V Why have we not terminal facilities provided ? Why has not the St. Lawrence been deepened from Montreal to the sea so as to enable large ships to come to Montreal ? The people in every part of the Dominion are all anxious that this port should be developed. We are anxious to secure a fast Atlantic service and every man in the Dominion would be willing to contribute his share towards that object. What have we done towards that ? Not a single thing. Nothing has been done in the way of improving our transportation, and notwithstanding the abnormal development of our trade, nothing has been done for the purpose of improving our waterways or narbours. The hon. Minister of Finance takes pride in the development of the- country. Can he put his hand on a single work in this country which tends to the development of this country which did

not have its initiation and commencement under the Conservative regime ? He cannot put his hand on a single work, and in that respect, instead of receiving any assistance from the hon. gentlemen who then were on this side of this House we had nothing but opposition to everything we undertook. We can point with pride to the past. We glory in the prosperity of the country at the present time, we hope the country will go on and prosper, but we expect from the administrators of the affairs of this country fair-play at least in the expenditure of the public money. We expect, instead of having the money frittered away in the manner in which it is being done from one end of the country to the other that there shall be some plan of transportation adopted and carried out, some project which will result in the development of our trans-Atlantic service and that there shall be someming done to which the people of this country can point with hope and with pride. We have looked in vain for any such policy in the past from these hon. gentlemen. Their only object seems to be in each of the departments to get as much money as they possibly can to expend for the purpose of purchasing locomotives that cannot run over the road, for the purpose of putting down new rails on the road which was perfectly railed already, for the purpose, as the hon. Minister of Finance says, of taking the Dominion of Canada from a back street and putting it on a front street, so that all the nations can look at us and admire us. This expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway is a useless one. The idea of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals getting from -is colleagues in a country like this tne enormous sums which he has got for the purchase of larger locomotives to carry freight when he has the evidence of his own deputy to the effect that it would be impossible to carry this trade in competition with the roads that are at present in existence. The expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway when the road was first constructed was in the neighbourhood of $27,000,000. Of course, it is a longer roau now, but the means of builumg the road are cheaper now. The hon. gentle-

I have heard over and over again speeches which were pretty
