speechtext: similar to that delivered to-day by the leader of the opposition. I have heard my hon. friends on this side of the House in times past predicting all sorts of disasters because the expenditure was so large. Will my hon. friend the leader of the opposition permit me to say, that he has made to-day what is essentially a party motion, but at the same time he has raised a great national issue. I do not ignore the existence in both political parties of a school which believes that we should not spend much money. I think I know this country as well as any other public man of my years, and I know that there is another school which I believe is in the great majority; a school which has confidence in the future of this country, and which is ready to make all necessax-y expenditure to develop the great national assets we possess. We are spending money. There is no doubt as to that. We are not spending too much money. I see on the opposite benches business men of first rank and standing, and they will not stand before any audience and declare that we must not spend even more money than we have spent in the past. I hope there are enough men in this House to rise above petty party questions on important occasions. We have to face to-day the competition on land and sea of our American friends. Large combinations of capital ai-e monopolizing American railways and English and American steamship lines. Are we going to sit idly by and not do anything ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is what you are doing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I say to the contrary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What have you done ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I will grapple with the question in a moment. We have not been idle. We have before us to-day the motion of the leader of the Conservative party asking us to pause because we are spending too much money, and my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) tells me now that we are remaining idle and not spending enough

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What I say is that you are wasting the money that you are spending.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Oh, that is a mere play on words. When I have taken my seat, I invite my hon. friend to show where we have wasted any money.
I know that my hon. friends on the other side will assail the Intercolonial Railway policy of the government. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways will defend that part of the government policy. I am not . the Minister of Railways and Canals, and it is not my duty to take chai-ge of the department of one of my colleagues, but my hon. friend (Mr. Blair) is quite able to take cai-e of himself. Speaking of the general policy of this government, I ask : Have
we been idle ? We have this year a magnificent crop of over 100,000,000 bushels of grain in the North-west. We have not been able to carry that crop to the seaboard through Canadian channels because we were not sufficiently equipped to do so. We all recognize that. Now, Sir, our duty is to have a strong and progressive policy of equipment by land and by sea. I altogether shai'e the view of my hon. fi'iend the exMinister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Haggart) when he says that the country expects that a fast Atlantic service will soon be established; and in connection with it we must have, as I have said before, a fleet of large carriers to take charge of our crops and trade. But, Sir, there is no government that may take charge of the affairs of this country that will not be obliged to spend more money even than we have spent. Why, Sir, our hon. friends opposite are afraid. The hon. leader of the opposition has invited us to shudder because the debt of this country has been increased during the last 6 years by about $10,000,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Sixteen million dollars.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, a private corporation, have just increased their iudebtedness by $20,000,000. They have asked from parliament the power to increase their stock by $20,000,000, which means an expenditure of that much money and that much additional indebtedness. Why have they done so ? Because they have confidence in the future trade of this country. And why should a great country like this, full of resources, be afraid because we have been obliged in order to carry on large public works, to inci'ease our indebtedness by the small sum of $10,000,000, when there are private corporations which have incurred a larger indebtedness than the Dominion of Canada itself ? One lion, gentleman on the other side of the House, an hon. member for Toronto, said a minute ago that we are wasting our money. I will not discuss the policy of the government with regard to the Intercolonial Railway. My hon. friend and colleague the Minister of Railways will deal with that part of our policy.
Leaving that aside, as it is not my business to take charge of it, of what waste of money are we guilty ? The hon. leader of the opposition has paid me a great compliment this afternoon, and I am very thankful to him for it. After years in this parliament, and after all the inquiries that have taken place in the Public Accounts Committee, lie believes that he has been able to find out that one of my engineers has made a mistake, and that a little pond has emptied itself into the Atlantic ocean. Where is that pond ? I would like to find it. I pray somebody on the other side of the House to find it for me to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It cannot be found.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals has invited me to place on the Table of the House the evidence that there is a pond, and that it has emptied itself ;nto the sea.
I hold in my hand the appropriation Bill of last year, and I invite my hon. friend the leader of the opposition to tell me where that pond is. I tell my hon. friend that there is no pond of that kind. Even if there were, even if one of my engineers had made a mistake, and had spent $500 or $1,000 in trying to build a harbour, we are not infallible in the Public Works Department, and 1 think my hon. friend might have spared me the trouble of looking for the pond. I am very much afraid that the effect of that pond on the Atlantic ocean will be just about as much as the effect of my hon. friend's speech on that point upon the country.
My hon. friend has also alluded to what he called a raid on the exchequer in connection with the construction of the Yukon telegraph' line. There are a great n any business men in this parliament, and I want to know who is the one among them who has never made a mistake in his life, or whose employees have never made a mistake ? I would like to see nis face. I have followed the proceedings of the Public Accounts Committee in regard to this matter, and what has been proven there is this : Mr. Charleson, who had charge of the construction of that line, had with him a gentleman of the name of Rochester. It was understood that he would act as a foreman of the work. After they had been two or three months on the work, Mr. Charleson, rightly or wrongly-imprudently, I grant-let a contract to Mr. Rochester for the supply of poles. After having heard my hon. friend, one would think that millions of dollars had been wasted, thrown into some pond or other. What are the facts ? My department was paying $3 each for poles to a local Yukon company. Mr. Rochester, who was a man of great experience, having been brought up in the lumber trade, made an offer to Mif. Charleson to supply the poles for $2 each. Mr. Charleson accepted his offer, Mr. Rochester supplied the poles, 6,000 of them; these poles were received by a gentleman, a former employee of the Canadian Pacific Railway, Mr. Richardson who in his evidence last year declared that the poles had not cost too much. These are the facts of the case, and this is the famous raid that causes my hon. friend to invite us to shudder. Well, it will require a little more than that to make the country believe that we have administered their affairs in an unworthy manner.
My hon. friend has also referred to the fact that the government have paid the rents of the residences of the judges in the

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Yukon. Rightly or wrongly, when Mr. Justice Dugas and Mr. Justice Craig were invited to take up their residence at Dawson, it was understood and agreed that the government would supply them with residences. We did not erect residences, but we paid the rents of residences for them. .These are the facts, rightly or wrongly; but again the amounts involved are very small. My hon. friend will permit me, I am sure, without my meaning to be in any way offensive, to say that this is peanut politics, and peanut politics has never carried any party into office. I remember very well when on the other side of the House, after the death of the great chieftain, whom I followed as long as he was in public life, when the Conservative party changed their policy and became small and mean-and they became small and mean because there was at their head a man who was not a broadminded man-they started these petty cries all over the country. I speak here in the presence of some of my former companions in arms, and I say that when the Conservative party started a small and narrow policy, they were defeated at the polls, as they will be again defeated if they do not change their ways. The country never takes any stock in reproaches like those levelled at us by the hon. leader of the opposition. I grant immediately that the policy we have adopted in regard to the Intercolonial Railway is worth discussing. It is a large question; we have spent a large amount of money upon it. The question is whether that expenditure was right or wrong. The government have thought it was right. The country will judge. All the other railways are spending to-day large sums of money in order to handle the freight which is increasing in quantity every day. We have followed the same course. We heard all sorts of rumours when the Public Accounts Committee was sitting, but no scandal has been proved. Let me mention that in passing. My 'hon. friends, both of them, reminded us that in former days the leaders on this side of the House promised to reduce the expenditure and debt of this country. My hon. friend from North Victoria (Mr. Ross), alluding to a speech of mine yesterday evening, said that, generally speaking, a minister should not be held responsible for any of his speeches other than those he would make at the Mansion house. No doubt my hon. friends on this side have said in former days that we were spending too much. But times have changed, circumstances have changed. Mr. Justin McCarthy, in his life of Mr. Gladstone, says in so many words that the public man who would attempt to be consistent all bis life would simply be an ass. And I think that Mr. Justin McCarthy is perfectly right. I appeal to all men who have braiins-I do not appeal to itliose who have none for I do not care what they may say- but I appeal to those who have a thinking of their own, and who are able to think.

Where is there amongst us the man who thinks to-day at fifty, fifty-five or forty-five years of age, what he thought when he was twenty or twenty-five years old ? Where is he ? There is not one among us. Our minds have undergone evolution, we have studied, we have learned, we have observed, we have moved in the world. Public men move as well as private individuals. This is a great country, and those who are in office are responsible for its development; and whatever may be the speeches delivered twenty years ago, (this government is in office to administer the affairs of the country and make it prosper, and to make it prosper it is necessary that we should spend money-not waste money, but spend it judiciously. My bon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock) said a moment ago that wo had stood idle. In that my hon. friend was not accurate. He knows better. We have been going along at a high speed developing our waterways. There is no use in denying it. Bet my hon. friend count the number, for instance, of new elevators on the great lakes. Let him count the number of harbours improved. Let him consider the large sums my department has spent in developing harbours and deepening our rivers and waterways. The hon. the ex-Minister of Railways said a moment ago that with the money spent on the Intercolonial Railway, we, could have deepened and widened the St. Lawrence. Well, that work will be completed lin a very short lime. It is going on now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I said it would build the Georgian Bay canal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Let me beg my hon. friend not to call that splendid French river a canal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: A waterway.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Let him say that the French river should have been improved. But public education has to be made as well as private education. Great public works have to be carried out gradually. This country Is spending large sums on its railways and cannot do everything at once. My hon. friends say we are spending too much, and two minutes later they say that wre should have spent more. They tell us that the French river should have been improved, and the Georgian Bay canal should have been built. Well, if the whole system of canalization of tlie Ottawa river were attempted to be carried out liy this government or a private corporation, it would cost in the neighbourhood of $80,000,000. The country is not yet prepared to incur that expenditure, but when tlie country is more advanced, when we have a greater population, perhaps it will then be ready to take hold of tha t undertaking.	>
My hon. friend the ex-Minister of Railways has uttered words which, when he reads them in ' Hansard,' will appear to him
as very imprudent indeed. He has said that unless we take care not to spend so much money in the maritime provinces, something wrong will happen. He has spoken of the disruption of confederation. Mr. Speaker, the people of this country are masters of the situation. Should they find we are spending too much on the Intercolonial Railway, they will say so. They will not destroy that magnificent fabric of confederation. I hope that there is not in this country a public man who would destroy it because an unwise expenditure of money should happen to have been made. Even if we should make an unwise expenditure, let us not speak in such a manner. We are old men. We may not take for granted everything that is said here, but there are in this country people who are not as old as we, and who perhaps might interpret in a serious way words of that character. Let us not speak of destroying confederation. We are a very happy people. We have only to stand by our country and strive to understand each other ns well as we can, and we have a great future before us. There is no reason for destroying anything, but there may be reason for improvement. There is always room for improvement. Let us go on and improve.
I do not see that there is much more to be added by me. A moment ago I alluded to tlie inquiries that have taken place in the Public Accounts Committee. The officers of a great department are no more infallible than are any other employees, either of a bank or a commercial firm. , My own employees may make mistakes. I have made mistakes myself. I know that some of my hon. friends have tried very hard to prove that in the purchase of certain things for the quarantine station, we paid too much. Perhaps we dlid. I do not deny that on certain occasions a public employee may be just as well imposed upon as ifnauy another man. There are able men in this House. Where i.s the one who has never been imposed upon by anybody ? My bon. friend the leader of the opposition, is a very able lawyer indeed. He has argued many cases and he has lost, no doubt, a lot, but that does not prove that he is not an alble man. My hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Brock), who conducted the Inquiry in the Public Accounts Committee, is a very able man and a great manufacturer. I want to ask him whether be has never made a mistake, or whether any of his employees have never made mistakes ? We are all apt to make mistakes, but, speaking for the department over which I have the honour to preside, I challenge the fullest investigation as to any of my employees having ever participated in any dishonest deal. My department is an open book. I have nothing to hide. I may have made mistakes. But there has not been any money stolen, to my knowledge, and outside of my knowledge it has not been proved that any dishonest acts have ever been committed.

In closing, let me repeat what I said In beginning these few remarks. Last year, the appropriation of the department of Public Works, including both main and supplementary estimates, reached the very large amount of $8,454,000. In all those large appropriations the fault has been found only with two or three small items that hare been mentioned here. No greater compliment could be paid to me or to the able officers who administer that department with me. Before I sit down, perhaps the House will permit me to thank hon. members on both sides for the courtesy that has been extended to me not only this year but on other occasions. I have been a sick man for a year or two. On every occasion I have had extended to me on both sides of the House the greatest kindness.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Tarte) seems to be a good judge of human nature. He has thrown himself upon the mercy and charity of the House, so that hon. members may not deal too harshly with the shortcomings of himself or his colleagues. In the course of his remarks the hon. gentleman said : We have spent money lavishly, it is true-

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
No ; I did not say that.
Mr. SPROULE-because the development of the country requires it and the necessity of the country justifies it. Now, so far as that expenditure is needed, so far as it is in the interest of the country, so far as it was properly and economically carried out. we have no complaint to make, but it is because of unwise expenditure, because of improper and extravagant expenditure that we are justified in complaining. The history of this government has been one of great expenditures and extravagances. I make that broad and general statement, and I am sure it is susceptible of proof from the public accounts not only with regard to the government as a whole, but with regard to every department of it. The amounts appi'opriated for the current year were $65,801,000. And yet, when their predecessors proposed to expend over $15,000,000 less they declared that that was far too much for the requirements of this country. How then, can they deny that this last vast expenditure of theirs is a lavish and unnecessarily heavy expenditure ? For next year, that is the year ending June 80th, 1903, we have already voted $65,564,042. And, before the year is out, when we come back next session, no doubt we shall be called upon to vote $4,000,000 or more to cover various shortages that will be found. We are justified in assuming that that will be the case, for it was the case this year and last year and the year before. So, before the next fiscal year is over, we shall have been called upon to vote supplies for

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
the year of about $69,000,000. Yet the Minister of Public Works tells us that while they have been somewhat lavish in their expenditure yet they have spent no more than the demands of the country have required. It is with nations as with individuals in matters of economy. It is very easy to be extravagant, and a nation like an individual can form a habit of extravagance. And, with the nation as with an individual, it is the most difficult thing in the world to curtail extravagance, and, after an era of extravagance, to practice economy. We know how it is with young men commencing life or. with men of any age. Supply them lavishly with money and they will be apt to make their expenditure even more than their incomes. If adversity comes they find it almost impossible to economize. Hlon. gentlemen opposite enjoyed a season of overflowing revenue, but large as has been their revenues, their expenditures have been still greater. When their revenues are less buoyant, when hard times come and the question of economy must be faced, what will be the condition of the country ? It will be a condition of economic disturbance, of curtailed trade, and of sorrow for the people. We are writing a new page in the history of our country, a page which will, for all time to come tell not to the credit but to the discredit of hon. gentlemen who to-day control the affairs of the nation. Because their performance is the very opposite of their promises to the people, the page of history that these hon. gentlemen are writing they are writing to the everlasting disgrace of themselves and of the party to which they belong. They promised us stringent economy, they have given us increased expenditure in every line. Although our revenues have been so large that we had surpluses in a few years amounting to no less than $19,743,537, yet, as the Minister of Finance has admitted, the public debt of Canada has been increased in the same time by $16,000,000. This cannot inure to the credit of hon. gentlemen opposite, but must stand to their disgrace in the history of the country. We are told that the public debt has not increased rapidly. And the Minister of Public Works gave a comparison which he said justified the House and the country in coming to the conclusion that the management of the present government compared favourably in this respect with the management of their predecessors. How did he endeavour to prove that ? By taking a few years of the eighteen years of his predecessors, during which the expenditure was exceptionally heavy, and made so in order to carry out the obligations entered into before confederation, such as building the Canadian Pacific Railway, taking over the debts of the provinces, giving them assistance when they had almost fallen into bankruptcy, taking back 10.000,000 acres of land from the Canadian Pacific Railway and

giving them $10,000,000 in money instead, adding all that to the public debt. During three years of those eighteen the minister said the increase had been $6,000,000 a year, whereas under the present government it has been only $1,900,000 a year. But had the hon. gentleman desired to be fair in that comparison he would have shown a very different state of affairs under the present government. But take these years out of the eighteen years and the public debt increased during the balance of the time on an average at the rate of $3,000,000 a year. Taking the whole three years out and it would show an entirely different condition of things in the interest of the Con-servtive party.
Now, the revenue expected for the present year is $56,800,000, the highest revenue Canada has ever had. When $38,000,000 were taken out of the people under the Conservative administration the Minister of Trade and Commerce said Canada was being bled white by taxation. This year he 'is taking out of the same people $56,800,000, yet he has not a word to say against it. He is perfectly satisfied so long as he is allowed to remain in office and draw his salary. and have the honour of the situation.
The Minister of Finance gave us a very interesting exhibition for a few minutes this forenoon. I watched him carefully, and he reminded me of a certain little fish very common down in his part of the country. Whenever it sees danger approaching it commences to work its tail at an awful rate of speed, mixing up sand and mud and water until it surrounds itself with a cloud that hides it from view. That is exactly what the Minister of Finance did. Or as another hon. gentleman suggested, he reminded us of a badger in the North-west Territories. Whenever you frighten it it makes one race for its hole, and it runs with such rapidity that it raises a cloud of dust around it which conceals it from view until it gets into its hole. So it was with the Minister of Finance. Like that little fish, he worked himself into a state of excitement, and so stirred up the muddy waters around him that he thought he could hide himself from the criticisms directed against him.
He says the country will take no stock in charges of extravagance, because it knows the money is wisely spent. I ask him if the money was wisely spent in the Yukon in connection with the telegraph out there ? I have here some expenditures made by the government in that connection, and I'would ask the people of this country to say whether they have been wisely made. They send a party out there to build a telegraph line, and they think they must treat some of their employees very much like themselves, as if they owned the whole country and aM its resources, and were entitled to live in luxury on the fat of the land. They sent out Mr. Charleson with a party, giving him carte blanche to build that
telegraph. I have looked at the public accounts to see what supplies were furnished these men, and I will give you a few items by which the people will be enabled to judge whether their money is being wisely^ spent. The government are purchasing clothing for their employees, 8 dozen pairs of cashmere socks at $5 a dozen, the very best class of goods they could possibly 'buy. 1 ask the labouring man who is working in the streets of Ottawa if the man who employs him furnishes him with that quality of garment. Then eiderdown quilts at $25 a piece. What farmer in this country would be so extravagant as to furnish even his choice bedrooms with quilts at $25 a piece ? I want the farmers to see the way their money is being spent, and I am sure they will tell the Minister of Finance that they have analysed his statements and that they do not believe them. Caps, 6| dozen at $18 a dozen ; yet the country has nothing to corn-plain of says the hon. Minister of Public Works.

speechtext: Will the minister tell me if he knows of any labourers in the city of Ottawa who are paid that rate of wages, and who purchased goods at those prices ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: There is no comparison between the two because the difference is so great that there can be uo comparisvi. But, the hon. gentleman tells us that these men bought all these things. They bought two cases of Hennessy's B. O. brandy, $16.75.

speechtext: Was it unreasonable that men who went into that wilderness should have their whiskey or their brandy ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: They were supplied with all the luxuries of life and they were given these luxuries because they were enabled to fall back upon the public treasury to pay for them. They were allowed to have all these extravagant luxuries of life because they were employed under the hon. Minister of Public Works. Ten gallons of rum, at $5.25 per gallon, for the poor labouring men up there. How many of the poor labouring men employed on the streets of Ottawa are able to buy rum at $5.25 per gallon ; or how many employees are there who would do it for them ? It is only when men are employed by the hon. Minister of Public Works that they are treated in this fashion. Three thousand Representative cigars, $180. This sum was expended for the choicest cigars that can be produced, to be sent up there to add to the luxuries of these men. Then, there were 1,000 of another brand, Flora Espana cigars, at $45 a thousand. Ask the boys who are going around Ottawa smoking 5-cent cigars, how they would like to be employed by the hon. Minister of Public Works, and be enabled to smoke these expensive cigars. One thousand El Bondoso cigars, at $37 a thousand; 105 pounds of Myrtle Navy tobacco, $73.50 ; 70 pounds of Tuckett & Billings tobacco, $51.80;

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
86 pounds of Prince of 'Wales tobacco, $5S.4S; 1,000 Manual Garcia cigars, $75 a thousand. These men were supplied with the most expensive luxuries and the best cigars that the country could provide when they were sent up there to build that telegraph line by the hon. Minister of Public Works. The hon. gentleman has done this because he is drawing upon the public chest, and yet the hon. Minister of Finance says that the country will take no stock in the statements we have made as to the extravagant expenditure of the country's money. Well, the information is before the country, and it is for the country to say whether it takes any stock in it or not. In my judgment it will take a great deal of stock in it.
Now, I will deal with another point. The hon. Minister of Finance asked us why we did not go before the Public Accounts Committee if we thought there had been anything wrong and prove it. Did we not go before the Public Accounts Committee, and attempt to prove it ? We did. But when the men who could give evidence in regard to this wrongdoing were asked for information they were not allowed to answer the questions. For two years we attempted to get Mr. Charleson before the Committee on Public Accounts, but as soon as the order went out to bring Mr. Charleson before the committee his coat tails were seen flying out of Ottawa, and he was absent for the rest of the session. He was here until the subpoena was issued, but he left immediately for the west and we could not get him back. The excuse was that he was obliged to go away.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the hon. gentleman whether Mr. Charleson has not been here during the whole of the session ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
He has, but owing to the short session we have not had time to get him before the committee. The Public Accounts Committee has not been called once for five times it ought to have been called, and we have been unable on that account to pursue the inquiry in regard to Mr. Charleson to the extent that we would have liked to. We desired to secure the attendance of Mr. Charleson before the committee and we would have done so had the length of the session enabled us to do so. But when we do get people before the committee we cannot get the information out of them. It would have been possible to have proved the charges that we have made but for the impediments that have been thrown in the way by the government of bringing the witnesses before the Public Accounts Committee whom we desired to have. But, we did have a few witnesses before that committee. We had Mr. Rochester, who gave us some information about a contract for the supply of telegraph poles. We endeavoured to ascertain how

much he paid for these poles. We were told that Mr. Rochester bought these poles for 90 cents apiece and sold them to the government for $2 apiece. When that question was asked, who objected to the answer ? I am told that it was the hon. Minister of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: 1 did not do that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It was said that the hon. gentleman instructed him not to answer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I did not do that.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I was not at the meeting, but I am told on reliable authority that it was the hon. Minister of Public Works, and no other. With these impediments thrown in our way we could not prove what otherwise was capable of being proved, if we could have got the evidence which the parties should have been able to give and which should have been taken on oath in regard to these transactions. Something was said in regard to the Intercolonial Railway. We presented allegations of extravagance in connection with that road and we brought before the committee different employees to prove them; or, to speak more correctly, we asked that they should be brought up. They were not brought up. We asked to have Mr. Archibald summoned before the committee. We fought it out in the Public Accounts Committee for a whole day, and we fought it out in this House for a whole afternoon, but the government called upon their majority to vote down our request and we were denied the right of having the evidence of Mr. Archibald before the committee. We were told that the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals bought 1,300,000 ties when an election was going' on when there were not more than 400,000 ties required for that year. The hon. gentleman bought them to help the friends of the party to control the election and when we desired to prove that there was extravagance in the administration of that road the witnesses we required were not allowed to come before that committee. Mr. Archibald was not allowed to come here and we were in this way unable to prove what, under other circumstances, was perfectly capable of being proved, because, when we attempted to bring a witness before the committee, or to elicit information from a witness who did appear, obstacles were placed in our way by hon. gentlemen opposite. The Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) says that the country will not take any stock in our statements about the extravagant expenditures of the government. They have been quite proper, says the hon. Minister of Public Works. How about the expenditure that we will be called upon to vote either to-day or to-morrow for indemnifying Mackenzie & Mann for a contract which ought
not to have been made amounting to $328,000, an item for which appears in the supplementary * estimates ? What will this be after we have voted it ? It will be a monument to the eternal disgrace of the present government, a monument to their folly and incapacity as public men and to their lack of business ability. It will stand as a matter of record against them. They made a contract that should never have been made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that it is not regular to discuss a vote which is to be submitted to the Committee of Supply.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I will say the expenditure which we will be called upon to make in payment of the award of the Exchequer Court, to which the government referred this disputed question. The Exchequer Court has given an award in favour of Mackenzie & Mann that will mean an expenditure of $328,000. Is this wise or otherwise ? Will the people of the country say whether it is wrong or right 7 I will leave it to the people and I have no doubt what they will say about the payment to Mackenzie & Mann for the loss of that contract. But, we are told that the expenditure has not been extravagant and that it has always been wise. What about taking the census ? Let us give the House and the country a little information about that. Has the expenditure for taking the census been extravagant or economical ? That work has been done before and we have a fair opportunity of making a comparison. The predecessors of the present government twice performed work of taking the census of the country. Let me make a comparison of the cost of taking the census so that the people of the country may know whether the present government have been spending money extravagantly or economically.
The census of 1891, taken under the Conservative government, cost the country $548,000 all told, but the census of 1901, taken by the present Liberal government has up to date cost $980,000, and we are told it will cost $170,000 more, making in round numbers a total cost of $1,150,000. It is true that the population has slightly increased, and no doubt there was a little more work to be done, but the last census cost $602,000 more than the census taken by the Conservative government, and that enormous increase in cost can be pointed to by any honest man as a sample of gross extravagance on the part of this government. Every act of this government proves that there is a system of extravagance reigning which is not compatible with econ-. omy and wise judgment. The Minister of Finance told us that our expenditure on consolidated revenue account in 1895 was equal to 15 per cent, while last year it was only 12 per cent, thereby trying to prove that the present expenditure was compnr-

atively less. Well, it is easy to prove the fallacy of that comparison. The revenue of 1895 was only $33,000,000, whereas last year It was $52,000,000, and 12 per cent on $52,000,000 is proportionately larger than 15 per cent on $33,000,000. We cannot turn our face to any quarter without seeing evidences of this extravagance. Look at the Galops rapids. The Minister of Railways was obliged to admit the other night that he had a company of contractors dredging these rapids all last year, and he did not know it, and yet the country will have to pay for it.

speechtext: Why does the hon. member state that I had them there, when they were distinctly instructed that they should not go on, and that there was no appropriation?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am justified in saying that the minister had them there in view of the fact that his own engineers were on the boats all the time directing the work. And yet the minister did not know it, and his chief engineer did not know it. But the company has rolled up an aggregate claim for $50,000, while the minister did not know that this work was going on. There is no doubt in the world but that this amount will be paid. The minister says he notified them there was no vote, but he let the contractors go on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Why do you say I let them go on ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
So far as ministerial responsibility can be brought to bear the minister did that, because his subordinate officers were superintending the work and keeping the accounts which were presented to the minister when the time came to pay them. Is that proper management of the affairs of the country ? I leave the people to judge. I have given a few samples of extravagance and waste on the part of this government, and I could give many more.
I could speak of the Yukon railway, the Drummond Railway, the Yukon telegraph lines, the purchase of ties and rails on the Intercolonial Railway, the Mackenzie and Mann contract, the census expenditure. I could speak of all these and I can submit them to the unbiased judgment of the people of Canada, feeling sure that the verdict would be that this government is spending the money of the country extravagantly, unwisely, improperly, dishonestly and corruptly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I know that any person who attempts to speak during this debate at such a late period of the session, incurs a serious responsibility, but some sentiments were expressed this afternoon by a veteran politician on the other side which I think require reply from a member representing a constituency in the Mr. SPROtTLB.
lower provinces. One would think from the style and quality of the remarks of that hon. gentleman, that there might be a provincial election pending in one of the western provinces, because the attack was made under the guise of a criticism on the expenditure for great public works, whereas, divested of that adventitious envelope it was nothing more than an unjust attack on the maritime provinces. The gentleman who made these observations is, and ought to be, perfectly cognizant of the fact that the maritime provinces have given uniformly and without stint their support to every expenditure that was for the'benefit of the country, and was a wise and legitimate expenditure. Whether that expenditure was made in Quebec, or whether in Ontario, or whether in the North-west, the votes of the lower province members have been in favour of such expenditure for wise public works. We regard it as a very unreasonable and a sectional cry, when the lower provinces are held up as a butt, and represented as partaking in the expenditure of public money for electioneering purposes, and from which no adequate return comes. I allude to the remarks of my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart). He has had a good deal of experience in this House; he occupied for a considerable time the responsible and honourable office of Minister of Railways, and he ought to know better than he speaks. Let me point out to the hon. gentleman that the money spent on lighthouses and wharfs and other works in the lower provinces is a very insignificant sum indeed when compared with the very large amounts which have been voted for public works in the other parts of the Dominion. We, from the maritime provinces have not quarrelled with this expenditure in the other provinces. We have not regarded it, that every dollar expended in Ontario and the North-west and on the St. Lawrence was so much taken from the lower provinces. We have no such narrow or limited or sectional feeling.
Now, Sir, I know the generosity of my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Haggart) ;
1 know his disposition and I know that his heart is perhaps capable of responding to any just appeal. I would like him to take a trip down to the lower provinces, especially around the shores of Nova Scotia, aud enter into the lives of the fishermen and others there. He would observe at once that he was among an entirely different population from those with whom he was familiar, the farmers and others of the province of Ontario. If he did so, wie would not again hear him complain that so much money was taken from the coffers of the country to be expended in aiding those poor fishermen in their precarious avocation. It is important to the business of these men that these public grants should be made for the construction of public works in their vicinity. They have no railroads, and they do not partake of the benefits of many of

tlie expenditures in other parts of the country. Their whole interest is in the sea. Suppose that for the want of a paltry grant of $100 for some lighthouse, all the inhabitants of one of those fishing districts should be swept away In consequence of not being able to make a port in a gale of wind. Again, in regard to the expenditure of $4,000 on the breakwater of Herring Cove, which is one of the subjects of discussion to-day, last year an Atlantic gale swept over that unhappy village, and carried away all the possessions of the fishermen of the place. It swept away their boats, their nets, their fishing houses, and all the means itthey had of getting a living. One of these Atlantic gales is sufficient sometimes to dam up the mouths of these little harbours, and destroy a whole year's living for the fishermen. It may be a most serious matter for them, because the fishing business is not a steady business like farming in the Northwest, but is a most precarious business. Sometimes two or three years will go by without the fishermen being able to obtain enough to pay for one year's living. Suppose the welfare of a community depends on the trifling expenditure of $100 for a lighthouse, what man in this House would rise up and give his vote to the proposition of my hon. friend from Lanark to withhold an appropriation of that kind, when so trifling an expenditure would be attended with such beneficial results ? Then there are people along the shores who have no means of communication, who have to carry their goods to and from vessels in their boats. What man who has any understanding of the difficult business of these men, and the very small amount of money that passes through their hands., would withhold a grant of say $1,000 for a wharf .at some place where there is no man with sufficient money to build a wharf for the accommodation of the people ? And so, when the hon. gentleman rises and in his grandiloquent way inveighs against the waste of public money in the maritime provinces, I think I can see the poor fishermen in those localities reading that speech-and I will take care that it is read by a good many of them. When the hon. leader of the opposition goes among them to solicit their votes-'and he has obtained a good many of them-I do not think he will promise that when his government comes into power, he will withhold the expenditure on wharfs, harbours, breakwaters and lighthouses in the maritime provinces, and especially in the county of Halifax. My hon. friend from Lanark dealt with the expenditure in a department wiith which he is supposed to be more familiar than he is with lighthouses, breakwaters and wharfs; and I would answer him, as other gentlemen have been answered on other occasions, and he knows it very well, that the maritime provinces were not disposed to enter into the union with Canada except on the express stipulation that the Intercolonial Railway should be built to connect the provinces, and that it should be efficiently maintained. The maritime provinces were not disposed to enter into the union with Canada, and that was held out to them as an inducemeut. Now, Sir, it has been a favourite subject in Ontario and perhaps elsewhere to describe all the expenditures on the Intercolonial Railway as expenditures for the exclusive benefit of the maritime provinces, and as matter of indifference to the other provinces-as a matter in which they have no pecuniary interest, but as a sort of boon to pacify the maritime provinces. It is no such thing. A large portion of the province of Nova Scotia has no direct connection with the Intercolonial Railway, and a great many of the inhabitants derive no benefit from it whatever. The province of Nova Scotia, in common with the other provinces, enjoys the benefit of transport over the Intercolonial Railway, but it enjoys no special benefit. It is true, some of the productions of the maritime provinces, a very limited number, are carried over the Intercolonial Railway; but the large bulk of the products carried over that railway have their origin in the province of Ontario, and that province derives very much more benefit from the Intercolonial Railway than the province of New Brunswick or the province of Nova Scotia; and any hon. gentleman who rises in this House and describes that railway as being maintained for the benefit of the maritime provinces simply errs in judgment and mistakes the fact. The great bulk of the benefit is derived by the province of Ontario in the transport of its productions to the markets of the maritime provinces, which take almost every production that originates there, and welcome it gladly as the production of one of the sister provinces of the Dominion. We make no complaints on that score, nor on the score of the expenditures lavished on the canals or on other projects In the western part of the country; but we hear it with ill grace from a mature and veteran statesman like the hon. member for Lanark, when he rises in his place, and, perhaps for the purpose of securing some votes or some eclat in the province of Ontario, denounces the expenditure on these public works which run through the maritime provinces, but which are not for their exclusive benefit. I warn the hon. gentleman that if he expects liis party ever to return to power, he should not place before the eyes and ears of the inhabitants of the lower provinces these denunciations of expenditures which are identified with the daily life and avocations of the working people in those obscure localities and, which they could not carry on successfully without these necessary public expenditures made by the Department of Public Works.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
So, the agreement was made eight or nine days before the opening of parliament. Of course, so far as those contractors are concerned, I think it was recognized, to some extent at least by some members of the House, that, inasmuch as the contractors had proceeded at the instigation of the government before parliament had sanctioned the contract,
there might be some claim on their part to be reimbursed for their actual outlay. Therefore, in any remarks I make, I direct attention to the government who are responsible for the loss to the country and not to the contractors themselves. It seems to me a new phase of parliamentary government that this contract should have been made, signed and sealed just eight days before the meeting of parliament and made subject to the approval of parliament, and yet the contractors should have been directed by the government to proceed with the work immediately. I do not recollect that there were any circumstances which would justify the government in taking the course they did in this matter. Subsequent events in that country have not shown that there was any cause for the very extreme haste with which the government insisted upon these gentlemen incurring liabilities at the expense of the country before parliament had any voice in the expenditure. I have had my attention directed, not during the present session, but during last session to the English practice in regard to such matters, and I think the government departed from the principles of constitutional government, and the due administration of public affairs in taking the course they did, and that they are reprehensible for causing this loss of public money by acting without the sauc-tion of parliament and by urging the contractors as this Order in Council shows they did, to proceed with the construction of this work before parliament had an opportunity to pass upon it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister if the correspondence-I suppose there was some correspondence calling upon the contractors to proceed with the work pending the decision of parliament-has been laid before the House. I presume that there must have been written instructions, because under the terms of the contract, strictly there would be no claim for damages. But, presumably because the executive saw fit to order them to proceed with the work we are called upon to pay this large amount. What explanation does the minister give as to the instructions given by the government before the decision of parliament ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: All the correspondance exchanged between the contractors and the government or any department of the government has been laid on the Table. I know of no verbal instructions having been given. Perhaps the Minister of the Interior might be able to throw some light upon that, if there was any verbal instruction given. As I recollect the circumstances, our action was necessitated by the extreme urgency of the case at that time. We had a very grave problem pending before us with which we had to deal, and, according to the view we took of the question of urgency we could not allow any time to be lost.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I think that when we are called upon to vote such a large item as this, we are entitled to have from some member of the government a statement of the negotiations which led these contractors against whose claim I have nothing to say, if they received instructions to proceed at any rate and under any circumstances-taking the course they did, what instructions were given at the time, and who gave them those instructions. Having such a judgement I think some member of the government ought to be able to tell us how it came about that, although there were only eight days intervening, even less I think, between the signing of this contract and the meeting of parliament-three days, my hon. friend from Montmorency (Mr. Casgrain) says- still we are called upon to-day to pay an immense amount when parliament itself is not at fault. I think somebody ought to explain how such a very large bill was run up against the country. If it was a judgment,
1 would have nothing to say. From the little I know of the circumstances, I think the contractors were entitled to a petnion of right. But this is merely a reference establishing the quantum of damages.

I would like the government also to give this explanation:	Is
this a judgment by the Exchequer Court, or did the government admit its liability, and only go to the Exchequer Court judge to have the amount settled which would be paid to these contractors ? speechtext: There was undoubtedly a hearing before the courts. It took several days and witnesses were examined.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: At the same time there is something very singular about this. This is a large amount of money. Was there a petition of right filed ? Was a fiat given ? Was there a case made out before the Exchequer Court ? Was the Crown heard ? And if the Crown was heard, and judgment was rendered, how is that no appeal has been lodged from this judgment ? If it is a judgment, it seems to me a most extraordinary one. That a court should deliver judgment against the government on a claim of this kind, when it was stated in the contract in so many words that it would be subject to the decision of the House-the whole thing seems very strange. Then if that is true, the contractors took this contract and began work subject to this condition, and the government and the House

I think the award and reference, not to the Exchequer Court, but to the judge of that court acting as commissioner, have been placed upon the Table of the House. At all events, .the Minister of Justice was to produce them, under my instructions. I do not see them on the Table, therefore I will have to give the reference toy memory. The circumstances out of which this whole matter arose are familiar to the House. But though they may toe familiar, in order to make the thing more intelligible, and the present appropriation better understood, perhaps it is just as well that I should give a history of the circumstances from the beginning. The House remembers that iu 1898 the government introduced a Bill to construct a line of railway from Telegraph Creek up to Teslin Lake, which was to be the means of communication between the eastern world and the Yukon. The matter was brought, I admit, hastily to .the attention: of the House. The contract was made in the month of February, if, I remember right, and our intention was that the contractors should proceed immediately with the work, that they should put themselves at once in motion, and have everything ready so that at the opening of the season they would be able to go on at once with the work. AVhat was the reason of this haste V Why did we instruct the contractors to proceed at once without any delay in order to begin work with the opening of the season ? The reason was that in the previous session, that of 1897, the parliament of Canada passed an Act authorizing the construction of a railway from Skagway, on the Lynn canal, to the waters of Lake Bennett, that is to say to the source of the waters of the Yukon. ' This Bill was passed, as a good many Bills have been passed every year, without the government or parliament having any knowledge of the conditions of that country. The Yukon at that moment was a terra incognite. Nobody knew that it contained the vast wealth which events have subsequently shown it to contain. Undoubtedly if, when this charter was granted in 1897, parliament had been informed of the existence of this vast wealth, as it was later on informed in the summer of 1891, when the great discovery of gold was made, this charter would not have been granted. For my part I would have opposed it with all my might; and I am sure the same sentiments which would have actuated me to oppose it, would have actuated every other member of this House. This charter was granted from the waters of the Lynn canal towards the Canadian portion of Lake Bennett that is to say, from a point which is now and was then, in possession of the United States, from Skagway up to Lake

Bennett, which is undoubtedly in Canadian territory. The parties who had that charter had also a charter from the American Congress to build a railway from the waters of the Lynn canal through Canadian territory. I say Canadian territory, because the boundaries had not then been settled, we did not know where the true line was. We knew it w,as somewhere between the waters of the Lynn canal and the waters of Lake Bennett. It has since been established that the boundary is some fifty miles from Skagway. But we were in ignorance of the country then.

speechtext: But that point is not accepted as the boundary.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I meant to say the provisional boundary. It has not been accepted, but it has been recognized to be the boundary, at .all events, it cannot be worse for us than it Is at the present time. The boundary can be extended from the summit between the waters of the Pacific and the waters of the Arctic ocean. But in the summer of 1897 this gold discovery was made. There was a rush, we had to provide at once for a system of communication between the eastern world and the Yukon. We then made the contract with Mackenzie & Mann for the construction of that railway. The great object we had in mind was to have a railway, not from Skagway, but from Telegraph Creek, from one point in Canadian territory to another point in Canadian territory. Under that contract we intended to provide at once for the construction of a railway which would be altogether under our control. I may say it was only a provisional contract, because the Stikine river, though we have the right to navigate It, empties into American territory. But if our contract had been carried out we would have realized our intention to bring this railway to the waters of Observatory Inlet. We made haste to complete that contract for this reason, that if we did not take advantage of the time which was at our disposal, then the other chanter which was given a year before would be proceeded with, and a railway would be constructed from the waters of the Lynn canal, at Skagway, up to the waters of Lake Bennett, and of course this railway being built, it would be a great detriment to our national railway. If our idea had . been carried out, if the Bill which passed in this House had not been rejected by the Senate, then this railway would have been constructed, the railway between Skagway and Lake Bennett would not have been constructed, and we would have to-day an all-Canadian route in the Yukon, instead of having a hybrid route such as we have at the present time. That was the justification in our judgment. That is why there was such haste to have this railway built. The White Pass Yukon Railway people had been watching and were ready to proceed with the construction of their railway, and our own contractors were 153
also ready to proceed. They made haste, there was a great deal of work to do, they sent provisions into the country, they purchased materials, they proceeded to carry on the work in the hope and expectation that their efforts would be approved by the Canadian parliament, that the contract would be ratified, and that as soon as spring was opened they would be ready to proceed and have the railway built during the season of 1898. They spent a large amount of money with that object in view. Unfortunately, the Bill, after having passed this House, was rejected by the Canadian parliament. These contractors made a claim upon us to be recouped for the expenditure which they had made. We asked them to furnish us with a detailed account which they did, but, before we proceeded to have the account settled, we asked them to dispose of all the material they could dispose of, which they did. Lastly, we had the account audited by judicial authority. We referred the matter to Mr. Justice Burbidge, who audited the account and examined it carefully. Mr. Justice Burbidge made a report to the government that Mackenzie & Mann had honestly expended the sum that is established now to be in the neighbourhood of $300,000. Of course, I am bound to say at once that there is no legal recourse against the Canadian government which can be enforced in a court of law, but we admit that Mackenzie & Mann have a moral claim against the honour of the Canadian people, against the honour of the Canadian government, and against the honour of the Canadian parliament, for the money which they then expended in an enterprise which was national in its character and which in my opinion, though, perhaps my opinion is not shared by all the members of this House, in an enterprise, which, if it had been carried out, would have been of the greatest advantage to the Canadian people at large. For these reasons we submit to the Canadian parliament that these men should not be subjected to the heavy loss which would be entailed on them, but as this is a loss which must be borne by somebody, it should be borne by the country and not by the contractors. We may be told that they were hasty, that they should have waited until the contract had been ratified. The excuse and the reason for this haste, and in my estimation it is an ample reason, is that there was not a minute to be lost, that time had to be taken by the forelock, that they had to proceed immediately to collect the materials and to take the measurements necessary in order that as soon as the spring was opened they might be enabled to go on with the work of construction. Of course, if it had not been for the charter which parliament had granted-I will not say improvidently or imprudently granted- but granted in ignorance of the conditions existing in that country, there would not

lave been any necessity for such haste. But, this haste is justifiable by the events which have taken place since. As soon as the contract which we made with Mackenzie & Mann had been rejected by the Canadian Senate, the charter which had been granted by this parliament and by Congress to the White Pass and Yukon Railway Company was availed of, and in the spring the company proceeded with the construction of the railway between Skagway and the Yukon. This makes it a task 'of great difficulty for us now to have a national railway on Canadian soil. Under the circumstances, we say, and it is the only ground upon which we put it before the committee, that Mackenzie & Mann have against the Canadian people a moral claim which ought to be satisfied. The country can bear the loss, but individuals could not bear such a loss as that. The money was expended honestly and in good faith, the money was expended for a good purpose, the money was expended for a purpose, which, if it had been carried out, would have been of untold advantage to the country, and for these reasons I appeal strongly to hon. members on both sides of the House. As to the amount, as I have said, we thought we should not deal with the matter ourselves, but that we should refer it to a person most competent to deal with a matter of this kind, that is to say, to a judge of the land, who has carefully investigated and audited the account. We believe that on moral grounds Mackenzie & Mann should be repaid the amount they have expended, and for these reasons we have asked for this appropriation.

speechtext: I find no fault with the position laid down toy my hon. friend (Mr. Ha-ggart) as to -the status of parliamentary government. He says that the government should not enter into a contract unless they have previous parliamentary authority or unless ;it is provided -that the contract shall be ratified by parliament. That is exactly What was done in this case. The contract which was entered into by the government with Messrs Mackenzie & Mann provided that it should be ratified by parliament, and it failed of Its ratification. My hon. friend asks why the contractors engaged in the work of the contract before it was ratified. Of -course, if it had been like the case mentioned by my hon. friend a moment ago, simply for the adornment of a public building, they would not have been so hasty to do so. But he understands that from the very nature of the work, and from the fact that It was to be carried out in a part of the continent very difficult of access, they could not wait, but were obliged to have their_ materials on the spot so as to be in a position to go on with the construction as soon as the season opened. There was . not an hour to be lost, and they proceeded on the expectation and the presumption that the contract would toe ratified by parliament. I repeat that we do not pretend that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann have a legal claim against the government.

They had the presumption and the necessity of the case, which would have made their efforts absolutely fruitless unless they had taken advantage of the winter season to send their

materials to Telegraph Creek. When the accounts were presented to the government they were carefully inspected and audited by an officer of the Department of Railways. But we were not satisfied to have that audit alone. We thought that a judicial audit of the accounts should be made, and we appointed Mr. Justice Burbidge to make that judicial audit; and I call the attention of the House to the very terms of the reference under which Mr. Justice Burbidge proceeded :
The minister, therefore, recommends that the said claims he referred, under the statute, ir. that behalf, to the Exchequer Court of Canada, for investigation, adjustment, and judgment, but that no claims which do not come within those mentioned in paragraph 4 of this minutes of council and the sum' total of which is given in paragraph 5, be inquired into.
Paragraph 4 says :
The minister considers that the claims which should be recognized are for time and services and money losses actually sustained and' money expenditure actually made or liabilities therefore incurred in good faith in connection with said agreement, and in preparing to carry out the same, and in procuring and transporting men, materials, plant and supplies therefore, and in carrying on the works so far as they may have been proceeded with, and the interest paid on the moneys expended.
This was the nature of the claim which was referred to the judicial audit of Mr. Burbidge. He investigated the claims and made his report, and accordingly, this appropriation is now asked for. I have only to repeat what I said: we cannot present the claim as a legal one ; we present it simply as an equitable one which ought to appeal to the sense of fairness and equity of hon. members on both sides of the House.

When the right hon. gentleman interrupted me I was going on to argue that the Grown has no power to enter into a contract unless the money is voted by parliament or unless the Crown makes it a condition of the contract that it shall not come into force until the money is voted. But here is an expenditure which fell upon us the very moment the contract was entered into. There is no provision in our constitution for anything of that kind. If there is a necessity for any extraordinary expenditure, or if any emergency arises which justifies an expenditure, the only other method by which it can be incurred is by a Governor General's warrant. But no government has a right to enter into a contract by which any expenditure of money can be made before the money is voted by parliament. It is an attack on the privileges of parliament to enter into any such contract. The contract may be made subject to the approval of parliament, but no expenditure under it is justified until parliament votes the money.

stated in a general way and applicable to ordinary circumstances; but the British constitution recognizes that in a case of great urgency, such as the purchase of the Suez canal shares by the British government-a case in which the government considers the matter is of such supreme importance it will be warranted in taking upon itself the risk of getting the approval of parliament in acting without previous parliamentary authority. This has been done more than once, and is regarded as being within the purview of the constitution, although no constitutional sanction is granted to it.

I invite him to distinguish between the case of the half a million or four hundred thousand dollar contract which he gave to Mr. M. P. Davis for the building of Sheik's Island dam and the case of the Murray Harbour Railway work, which he condemns so unhesitatingly.

My hon. friend can do so if there is any possibility of distinguishing between them, but I think he will find it more difficult than he seems to think. It is an interesting question. I could furnish my hon. friend with a number of similar instances which would occupy his consideration, and he might probably be able to tell us wherein the contracts were perfectly legal in the one case and absolutely null in the other. It is germane to this subject, because my hon. friend has dragged in this Murray harbour affair for the purpose of pointing the argument against us in connection with the Mackenzie & Mann contract, to show that the Mackenzie & Mann arrangement was in line with the policy we were in the habit of pursuing. While I am upon this point,
I wish to say a word with regard to the general question of inviting tenders for public works. I do not think there has been any department of the government, either under the present administration or under the former administration, in which there has been fewer cases of contracts being given without public competition than in the Department of Railways and Canals during the past five or six years. But cases will occur, and may properly occur, in which that may be done. If the people and parliament have confidence that the government and the minister will only take that course when the case justifies it, and when the contract is a proper one for such treatment, why should not the public interest be furthered, as it often may be, by placing the contract for work of this character in the hands of a responsible man ? Some people fall down and worship the idea of publicly inviting tenders for every contract, as though that alone would secure the best results for the country and for all concerned. But that is not my view. I do not think that is a position which one who has had any experience in public affairs would feel called upon to adhere to. I think if it were the ideal and the only proper way in which contracts could be given by the government, it would have been followed .in that country to which we all look for what Is wisest and best in the administration of government. But they do not follow this course in England. They very rarely, so far as I can learn, publicly invite tenders. If they want competition among men for any particular service, they privately notify chosen parties by sending circulars to them, and from the tenders received they chose the man. who shall receive the contract. But they do not by any means bind themselves to give the contract to the lowest tenderer even then. Nor are the oases infrequent, as anybody who has followed the subject must know", in which tenders are not invited at all. I believe that it is often the best and wisest course, where you have a man who is already carrying on a work who is responsible, and is doing his work satisfactorily, and at prices which are just and reasonable, to give the Hon. Mr. BLAIR.	'
contract for any extension of the work decided on. It is better that such a contractor should be permitted to continue -better for the government and for all concerned. I think that one of the last things that any man who has had experience in these matters would wish is that a contract which he has to let should fall into the hands of incompetent people, people who know nothing about how to do the business, but who are ready to jump at every opportunity of getting a contract and who, very often, when they have a contract, do not know what to do with it. It is not at all. the best thing for the government always to get the work done at (the lowest possible prices. On the contrary, it is the best thing for the government that its contracts should be let at prices which are fair and reasonable and will allow a fair-not an exorbitant, but a fair-return to the contractors for the investment they make and the work they do. These are the conditions under which contracts should be let. Whatever the nature of the work may be, whether the construction of a railway or the putting up of a public building or other works of that character, the very greatest difficulty arises if the contracts get into the hands of men who are really undertaking to do the work for less than, will give them a fair return for their labour, or is being done at a loss. With such people, you encounter trouble at every turn. You cannot have staff enough to see that such people do not evade you. They have every motive to do so, and sometimes even the motive of saving themselves from ruin; and they resort to all sorts of expedients for the purpose of evasion. If we were not opposed to one another here, some on one side of politics and some on the other, if we were not discussing this question from two sides of the House, there is no hon. gentleman who would not admit that the public interests will be best served by having contracts placed in the hands of responsible people and at prices that will give the contractor a fair return while being also satisfactory to the government. So, I say, I do not admit at all that cases may not properly arise in which the action should be taken which was taken. I do not criticise the action taken by the hon. gentleman-I have no doubt he has good reasons for recommending it to his colleagues. But cases will arise in Which it is necessary for the government to take this course in "the public interest. Now my hon. friend has not given to this committee, it appears to me, by any of the arguments he has presented, any reasons why this item should not pass. He has admitted that it would be a great hardship for these people to be called upon to bear this loss, and that parliament would not be willing under the circumstances, that these people should bear the loss. With the best intentions and with the fullest confidence that parliament would ratify the arrangements made, and yielding

to the strong opinion which was entertained in the country that something must be done immediately for the Yukon, this work was proceeded with. People were rushing in there, and predictions were freely made that fifty thousand people would go in during that season. These people had no means of carrying with them sufficient food to maintain them for any lengthened period. So, it was necessary that, as speedily as possible, easy means of transport should be provided toy which the needed supplies could be carried into that country. The government were aware of that necessity. Not because they wanted to act hastily, or because they felt they were acting hastily, but because they felt the responsibility resting upon them, and that failure to do what was best would lay them open to criticism and condemnation, they took this means to insure, to the utmost extent of their power, the providing of the best means of communication at the earliest possible moment. The contractors guaranteed us that by the end of September there would be a railway to Lake Bennett, and that at the earliest possible moment we should be able to get through that otherwise impassable barrier the supplies that were needed toy the people who were rushing into that country.	;	.
