Yes. But first I want to refer to the question which the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has brought up. I desire to say to my hon. friend that he seems to be very anxious that the constitution should be observed in all respects. I think it is very creditable to the hon. gentleman that about once a day he points out the necessity of sticking to the constitution. There need, not, however, be any haziness upon the constitutional question involved in this contract. Every member of parliament, I apprehend, without being a lawyer, understands exactly what the position is in that respect. The government have no power to make a contract which binds the country, nor have they any power to expend any money, nor have they any power to incur a liability which the country is bound to pay without the sanction of parliament. That is sufficiently evident, even in the circumstance with which we are dealing at the present time; because the government could not pay the amount without a special appropriation of parliament.
But while the rule is abundantly clear and not to be disputed by any person, that contracts cannot be made without the sanction of parliament or without parliamentary authority in the shape of an appropriation, yet that rule is subject to exceptions. While I am not desirous of going over the ground which was gone over at such wearisome length when this contract was under discussion in parliament, I may simply refer to the fact that it is well recognized that in some cases the government does, in the exercise of its functions as a government responsible to parliament, decide that it will take the responsibility of departing from this well recognized rule. If we were a government such as, for instance, there exists in the United States, where they have a President bound by the limitations of a written constitution, such a thing of course could not occur, because the president could have no authority, and could not be justified in taking such responsibility. But inasmuch as our government is differently constituted we have the power of taking that responsibility upon ourselves, being bound to account to the House of Commons, from which we derive our authority, for the exercise of the power that is vested in us, and bound to account for the step which we took in incurring that responsibility. We took the responsibility because we thought that circumstances demanded it. It would be a wearisome waste of time to undertake to go over the circumstances which were discussed in this House, I think more lengthily than any other subject which has been debated since I have been a member of It. But we did take the responsibility of deciding that this action ought to be taken, and we caused this contract to be executed.

Now, for my hon. friend's question. No specific instructions and no general instructions were given to the contractors to proceed; but every member of the government perfectly understood, and the contractors perfectly understood, that they were expected by the government to proceed, because the very terms of the contract-if my hon. friend will take the trouble to look at it again-necessitated the contractors proceeding immediately to expend a large sum of money if they were to fulfil the terms of the contract and the obligations which they had entered into with the government. go the question whether there were or were not any specific instructions given to the contractors, is of no account whatever in endeavouring to arrive at the merits of this question. Undoubtedly, Mr. Chairman, the contractors were perfectly justified, in so far as their relations with the government were concerned, in proceeding with the work. They perfectly understood that the government expected that they would go to work and put themselves in a position to fulfil this contract, and they could not possibly have done that if they had not anticipated the meeting of parliament by taking the action which required the expenditure of a very considerable sum of money.
Now, as to whether it was wise that the government should come to the conclusion that circumstances were so urgent as to require this departure from the regular usage, is a question in regard to which we are quite prepared to take our stand, and to accept the responsibility before this committee, before parliament, and before the people of Canada. My hon. friend will, I think, admit that some of the circumstances, at least, would assist in justifying the government in coming to the conclusion that there were circumstances of peculiar urgency. Suppose that some time about next September or October, some very peculiar set of circumstances should arise, which, in the opinion of the community, seemed to demand special action, and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition should come to a member of the government who was particularly charged with dealing with that special emergency, and urge upon him to take special action in regard to it, to take it immediately, without waiting for a meeting of parliament, then I think that we would be justified in assuming that there were some grounds at least for supposing that a strong case of urgency had been made out. It is within the knowledge of hon. gentlemen, I think, that while that contract was under discussion Sir Charles Tupper, then leader of the opposition, came to my house and urged that the contract should be made; and when I said that the terms were under discussion and that the government had difficulty in agreeing upon the terms, the expression of Sir Charles Tupper was that it was not necessary to stand so much on the question of terms, but Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
that time was the important thing; that the question was one of extreme urgency, and we should act at once; that the contract should be made for the construction of a railway. And by what route ? By the Stikine route, by the very route which we were adopting at that time. And the hon. gentleman, who then occupied the position that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition now occupies, then and there joined hands with the government in the action which they took in that respect. Surely, Mr. Chairman, we had a right to expect that the honour and good faith of the Conservative party were pledged to us in that undertaking, surely we had a right to expect that a man of his years, and experience, and high position, having come voluntarily, of his own motion, to a member of this government for the purpose of suggesting the very action which was taken, would not allow himself to be put in the position of swallowing his own words, dishonouring himself, and going back upon the position he had just taken. I think. Sir, our hon. friends upon the other side of the House have placed themselves in a very invidious position, when, knowing that their lealder had gone so far as to indorse the position which the government had taken, ,they practically took him by the throat and in broad daylight, before the whole people of Canada, compelled him to swallow his own words, to dishonour himself and the Conservative party in this House, as he did upon that occasion. There is at least fair ground, I think, for the suggestion that the case was one of urgency where the responsible leader- of the Conservative party in this House went so far as to pursue the very extraordinary course that he did, in coming and urging "upon the government the very course which the government afterwards pursued.
I am far from undertaking to justify the action of the government by anything" that was said by the then leader of "the opposition. The government does not require to go behind the leader of the Conservative party or any member of the Conservative party for the purpose of justifying its action. The government is prepared to take the responsibility of its action ; and if hon. gentlemen opposite are prepared to take the responsibility before the people of Canada, for the present position of affairs in the Yukon territory, then this government is prepared to take the responsibility of paying $328,000. We will take our share if hon. gentlemen will take their share, which they have placed upon themselves.
Now, after the firm of Mackenzie & Mann had gone on in good faith-and I apprehend from the tone in which this claim has been discussed that our hon. friends on the other side are not disputing the righteousness of paying the claim, or paying whatever may be found to be a proper amount, but after that contract had been executed, and the firm had gone on and expended their money in

good faith, the contract, as the members of the commitee are aware, was thrown out by the Senate at the instance of friends of the Conservative party. After the contract had been drawn up and the operations had been called off, the members of the contracting firm came to the government and explained the position in which they were and asked what redress they were to have and how their claim was to be recognized. The government came to the conclusion, that it was a fair and proper thing that the firm of Mackenzie & Mann should be paid the actual moneys which they were out of pocket, not any profits upon the operation, not any damages for the failure to ratify the contract, but the actual amount of money which the firm were out of pocket in consequence of the operations which they had undertaken for the carrying out of the contract which they had made with the government. I make that statement clearly and definitely' so that this committee might understand exactly' what the government decided to do. We decided, that, under the circumstances of the case which the members of the committee are perfectly familiar with from first to last, it was fair and reasonable and right that the government of Canada should pay to these contractors the actual amount of money which they were out of pocket in connection with the carrying out of the contract insofar as they had gone. Then the question arose as to the adjustment of these moneys, as to the proper ascertainment of the amount which the government should pay. They were told to file their claim with the Railway Department and that their claim would be considered. They filed their claim with the Railway Department and the officers of that department examined and audited the accounts. The government had no other way' of arriving at the amount which should be paid except by referring the claim to the proper department of government where were officers skilled in the examination of such accounts and knowing thoroughly well whether the figures, the items, the prices which had been submitted to them were just, or reasonable, or proper. That is the only' way in which the government could proceed in the adjustment of these accounts. We did proceed in this way and the accounts were sent to the Railway Department and they were audited by' the officers of the department. I am not familiar with the names of the officers who audited these accounts. They were sent there and under the direction of the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Blair) they were placed in the hands of the proper officers and audited. The hon. member [DOT] for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) says that the award of the judge of the Exchequer Court agrees with the amount which had been agreed upon between Mackenzie & Mann and the officers of the Railway Department. This is not a correct statement of the facts. The officers of the
Railway Department made no agreement as to any amount with Mackenzie & Mann, nor did the government make any agreement as to any amount with Mackenzie & Mann. The officers of the Railway Department had no authority to make any agreement. It was the business of the officers of the Railway Department to make a correct audit of the accounts that were placed before them and to report to the minister the result of their examination.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The officers of the Railway Department went out to that country, made an investigation as to the goods, materials and supplies which they had on hand.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I was not aware of that, but I know that the greatest care had been taken, because, at the time, the government took the position that the most careful overhauling of these accounts should be made, because, as hon. gentlemen have said, and as the government quite agree, the amount was very large, much larger even than we had any expectation it would be. What the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) should have said was that the finding of the judge of the Exchequer Court proved that the officers of the Department of Railways had properly audited the accounts. That is what the finding of the judge of the Exchequer Court proved. After the examination had taken place by the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals and after they had reported as to the amount which they found these accounts totalled up to, and which constituted their finding upon the claim which was filed there, we were in this position : Should we bring that claim to parliament, or should we accept the finding of our officers, the officers of the Railway Department, or, should we require some further examination of these accounts? We were quite aware that parliament would required that the utmost care should have been exercised in connection with the auditing of these accounts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Before the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sifton) proceeds from that point was there not an agreement or understanding between Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann and the Department of Railways and Canals as to the prices or the amount ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, there was no arbitration, none whatever.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Not that I ever heard of.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not saying that there was an arbitration. Was there not a settlement between the representatives of Mackenzie & Mann and the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals as to the prices, the amounts, and the reductions ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, not in the Department of Railways and Canals.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
We decided as a government that Mackenzie & Mann should be paid the moneys which they had properly expended in attempting to carry out this contract. They filed a statement of their account, we sent it to the Department of Railways and Canals in order that the officers might decide as to what was the proper amount. My hon. friend (Mr. Haggart) asks : Was it agreed ? If he calls it an agreement that when the contractors filed their accounts in the Department of Railways and Canals the officers decided what they were willing to recommend and allow, then, that was an agreement. That was exactly what the accounts were sent there for, but the officers did not agree that the amount should be paid. The officers were in the position simply of auditors for the purpose of making an audit. As to whether that amount should be paid or not, or whether a smaller amount should be paid, was a matter respecting which they had nothing to do, and the government was in no way bound by the result of the examination which they made. I was going to say that we fully recognized the facts that this House would not take it as reasonable that they should be asked to sanction a payment of this character unless a very full and thorough examination of the accounts had been made. Therefore, after the audit had been made by the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals, in order that there could be no possible question about the amount, in order that there could be no possible suggestion that the accounts were cooked, or that they were padded, or that it was unfair, or unreasonable that any of these accounts should he paid, we sent the accounts to the judge of the Court of Exchequer for the purpose of having his findings upon these accounts.
It is upon the finding of the judge of the Exchequer Court in review of the result of the examination of the officers of the Department of Railways, that we bring this amount before the committee for the purpose of being authorized to pay it to these people. I cannot conceive at this moment of anything more that the government could do for the purpose of getting at a fair adjustment of this account, and I venture to say that hon. gentlemen upon the other side of the House will not in the course of the discussion be able to suggest anything further that the government could have done, or that the government ought to have done for the purpose of adjusting this account, than that which we have done already. We have endeavoured to protect the treasury, we have endeavoured to protect the public, we have endeavoured to protect this House in every way. and in the only way which was open to us. Under Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
these circumstances, so far as the question of the amount is concerned-although It is large upon the face of it; larger perhaps than any of us anticipated-yet we are not in a position to say that it is not a fair and reasonable adjustment.
What is the position therefore in which we are placed as a government in connection with this matter ? It is, that we decided upon a certain line of action at a certain time, and that we took the responsibility of taking that action. We were burked in our endeavour to carry out that project by our hon. friends on the other side of the House, who, not having a majority in the popular Chamber amongst the representatives of the people, sought to prevent us from carrying out our wishes; sought to prevent the majority in this House from having its own way in regard to the handling of the public property of this country, by having the Bill thrown out in another place. So far as we are concerned we are prepared to accept the responsibility of our action. I venture to say that hon. gentlemen upon the other side will not find as time goes on, tha^ their position in connection with this transaction will be regarded by the people of Canada as flattering to them. If this transaction had been allowed to be consummated as it was intended it should be, we should have had a Canadian railway to the Yukon Territory; we should have had a railway; which we would have reached in the first instance by means of a stream over which we have the right of navigation, and we should have been able to reach our own territory by a Canadian route. The scheme of that railway contemplated an extension to a port in British Columbia, and if the first section of the road had been built, undoubtedly the second section would have quickly followed, and long before this we should have been enjoying the benefit of an ocean port in British Columbia, from which we would have running a railway over Canadian soil which would have enabled us to reach the Yukon Territory without crossing American territory. That would have been the position in which the country would have been placed to-day. It would not have cost the exchequer of this country a single copper, and as to the importance of it, I may say that during that very session or the next session of parliament.' we had the admission of the responsible leader of the Conservative party, when he stood upon the floor of this House and actually suggested that this government should propose legislation under which we should provide that that very same railway sho ild be built out of the public funds of this country at an enormous cost. That is the position which the Conservative party committed itself in parliament at that time.
But what are the conditions at the present time ? Instead of a Canadian railway and a Canadian sea port, and a Canadian trade,

what have we got ? If our friends opposite think that the present position is a satisfactory one and that it flatters them, I wish them all possible joy of it. We have at the present time a territory rapidly developing, in which there is a great and growing trade; a territory which we absolutely cannot reach, speaking in a commercial or economic sense, except over territory which is occupied by the American people. We are absolutely in the hands of the American people in regard to our dealings with our own territory there. At the present time the steamboats which run from the ports upon the Puget Sound to Alaska are making it almost impossible for the Canadian boats to carry on business, and this government has an application before it from the Canadian Pacific Railway Company asking for assistance to enable them to maintain their line-the only Canadian line upon the route -because they are subjected to such unfair competition from the Americans. That is the position in which we are in respect to shipping. So far as trade is concerned, if hon. gentlemen opposite will look at the returns they will find that a vast proportion of the trade is done by the Americans. Upon the upper Yukon it is altogether in the hands of the Americans. The large commercial companies are American companies, and by reason of the fact that we have to pass through American territory, and that we are handicapped in every respect in connection with that trade, it is almost impossible for Canadian merchants to compete upon fair terms with their rivals there.
Lastly, Mr. Chairman, leaving out of sight for the moment the question of trade, we are in this unfortunate and humiliating position, that we cannot send a policeman or a soldier into our own territory without that policeman or soldier taking off his uniform and asking leave of the American government to cross American territory. That is the humiliating position in which we are placed in the Yukon Territory by reason of the action of our friends on the other side of the House. More than that, we cannot take a prisoner from Dawson city to a penitentiary in the older portion of Canada, because we would have to take him through American territory, and we would be liable to be called upon to surrender that prisoner, and would be called upon to surrender that prisoner if we attempted to take such action.
Now, Sir, in connection with that country we are placed in a most ridiculous and humiliating position, and we are placed in that position by reason of the action of hon. gentlemen opposite who have forced us to it, or else to incur the enormous expenditure of the building of an allCanadian road out of the public funds. But further, the action which was taken at that particular time had this effect. As the right hon. the Prime Minister has said, there has been a railway
charter to run from the town of Skagway, known as the British Yukon Railway, but now popularly known as the White Pass Railway. It is a fact which is well known to many members of this House, that the promoters of that railway were in the city of Ottawa waiting to learn whether the Mackenzie & Mann Railway Bill would pass or not before they should ask their friends to subscribe a dollar for the purpose of constructing the White Pass Road. They waited in this city until they found out that the Senate had determined to throw out that Bill, and so soon as that action was taken, they went to work and got the money to build the road. And if that Bill had not been thrown out; if the Mackenzie & Mann charter had gone through, then the White Pass Railway could never have been built, because its promoters would never have risked a dollar of investment in that road. What is the result to-day ? By the throwing out of the Mackenzie & Mann charter the construction of the White Pass Railway has been made possible, and the existence of that road makes it an economic impossibility almost to get any money upon a commercial basis for the purpose of getting another railway constructed over Canadian soil. We are therefore in the unfortunate position, that unless and until the trade of that country would justify the government of Canada in making enormous sacrifices for the purpose of getting a railway in there, we shall not have a Canadian railway, and we shall be in the unfortunate and humiliating position of doing everything practically by the leave of eur American friends. I am bound to say that so far, our relations with the American government in respect to the right of way and passage across the strip of territory at Skagway, have been of a reasonable and satisfactory character. But there is no member of this House who reflects for a; moment who cannot see the difficulty of the position in which the Dominion of Canada is placed, by having access to its own territory only by permission of a foreign power. I have only to say in conclusion on this point that so far as the government are concerned, they regret that they are called upon to ask the committee to pay this sum of money; but they have no reason to doubt that the position they took at the time in connection with this enterprise was correctly taken, and we adhere to the opinion more strongly even than then that the Bill which we placed before parliament at that time was in the public interest and should have been passed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What is the estimated cost of a railway such as was proposed by this contract ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I have not an engineer's estimate by me or I would be happy to give it to the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not propose to discuss the question of the constitutionality of this payment, or whether it should be made in the way proposed. But, considering it on ordinary business principles, I thoroughly approve of the payment to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, the contractors, of whatever amount is found to be fairly due to them, they having expended money under a contract that was entered into by them in good faith with a government having a very large majority at their back. I think that any contractors are justified under these circumstances in immediately making a large expenditure of money, and I think that the government and this House should pay them whatever is properly due to them for that expenditure. It may be that the government are not going about the matter in the right way. It may be that the amount settled upon is not the right amount. IThat, I should gather from what I have heard of this discussion, is quite open to question. It is evident that the amount which the Exchequer Court awarded was an amount that had been arrived at between the government and Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann before the accounts were submitted to the Exchequer Court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Necessarily that is the only inference that can be drawn, because the amount fixed by the Exchequer Court is practically the precise amount that the government had agreed to before submitting the case. It.is quite evident further that there was very little if any investigation into the accounts by the Exchequer Court. There was practically no evidence whatever taken in regard to those accounts. That is quite plain from the fact that the total amount asked from this House in connection with fees and disbursements is only a [DOT]little over $800. I do not pretend to be able to say from the discussion whether the amount awarded was right or was not right, but I for one am of opinion that the principle of paying what these contractors expended in good faith under such a contract is one that ought to be approved of by the House and carried out. As regards the contract itself which the hon. Minister of the Interior has attempted to defend, I think it was a very vicious one. The statement which the hon. Minister of the Interior makes in reference to Sir Charles Tupper has, so far as I am aware, been heard for the first time in this House to-night. That statement, I venture to say, would not have been made if Sir Charles Tupper had been present, but would have been contradicted by him flatly and emphatically. It is a statement that was never made when that gentleman was in this House. It is quite true, Sir Charles Tupper said at that time that it was a wise thing to build that railway, but the terms of the contract were denounced by Sir Charles Tupper, as they Hon. Mr. SIFTON.
were by every other member on this side of the House, and as they were denounced by every man in the country who looked into them. But let us go further. It is the duty of those who assume the responsibility of government, if they meet with difficulties, to find a way out of those difficulties. But what steps did the government take when the Bill which they introduced was defeated by the Senate ? Did they do what men would have done if they were in earnest-at once set to work to carry out the object which they had in view and which they said they approved of ? No, they dropped that Bill and they shirked all attempts to re-enact the measure, knowing that their own followers and the country would not for one moment have endorsed the carrying out of another contract. If the condition of affairs is as humiliating to-day as the hon. Minister of the Interior says it is, what is to prevent the government bringing in a Bill for building another railway on somewhat similar terms ? I do not suppose it will be denied for one moment that much more favourable terms could be obtained to-day than the terms which were then given.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: We could not get as favourable terms to-day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
You could get a contract to-day on terms so much more favourable to the government and the country that there would be no comparison between the two. If that contract at that time was worth the enormous grants of land and privileges given to Mackenzie & Mann, it is worth very much more to-day. The terms of that contract were such as outraged the sense of justice and fairness of this country and the government dropped as quickly as possible all further reference to the Yukon Bill. What have we seen this session ? We have seen a contract, less in value to the extent of its being less in scope and volume, but similar in its terms, made with the private firm of Messrs. Treadgold & Barwiek-a contract quite as outrageous in its terms as the Yukon contract; and what happened in regard to it ? As soon as the governor of the Yukon came down here and remonstrated with the government, and advised them that there would be a revolution in the Yukon if it were carried out, the objectionable terms were cancelled immediately. Why were those terms given ? They were given either without any knowledge of what was being given away, or for some purpose, because the moment the outrageous terms of the contract were brought to the attention of the government those terms were withdrawn. I say that if the railway which the action of the Senate prevented the construction of, was as important as some members of the government now assert, the government could now have that railway built on much more

favourable terms than those of the Mackenzie & Mann contract.
They have a Senate which is practically favourable to them now, and they need not fear that it will throw out their Bill. I have not been long enough in the House to make the statement with authority, but I venture to say that, if there ever has been a case, it is extremely rare, when the Senate has thrown out a Bill twice. Why did not the government re-enact the Yukon Railway Bill ? Because the Bill was so vicious, because the contract was so inadvisable, and so much against the interests of the country, that they dared not reenact it. I did not intend to discuss any subject beyond the actual policy and principle of paying this money, and would not have done so had it not been for the defence made by the hon. Minister of the Interior. As regards the payment of money to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, if the amount has been arrived at fairly, and is fairly known to be what was expended, I believe that the government should pay it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) has talked to us about the humiliating condition in which this country finds itself on account of the action of the Senate in rejecting this contract. He does not seem to understand in what a humiliating position he has placed himself and his colleagues by the statement he has just made. He says that the Canadian trade has been lost to that country and that a great many evils have befallen the Yukon on account of the action of the Senate in throwing out this Bill. I asked him, how much it would take to build the railway, and he did not know. What was there to prevent the government from building the railway itself that same year if it had desired ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It would have cost a great deal of money.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
They were deterred by the expense. They were willing to place this country in the humiliating position in which he says it is, because they were afraid of spending the money. Well,. I have no doubt that it would have been a great deal cheaper for us to have built that road ourselves than to have had it built by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, under the proposed contract. But whether the sum required to build it as a government road be great or small, this government had the responsibility cast upon it of dealing with the matter; and if the facts are as the hon. the Minister of the Interior has stated them, this government has failed in its duty in not having brought down an appropriation for that purpose. These hon. gentlemen are on the horn of a dilemma. Enther we are not to trust the statement of the hon. the Minister of the Interior, or if we do, this government has been recreant in its duty in not having provided for the
building of that railway by a public grant and appropriation and in not having done the work itself if necessary. I would like to know how the hon. gentleman is going to get out of the difficulty. The government did not seem to want a railway into the country. I recollect myself that when a company asked for a charter, the government laid down the policy distinctly, in rejecting the measure proposed, which did not call for the expenditure of a dollar of public money, that while they were considering the whole subject they would not give any charter to parties to build a railway, and they had that charter voted down. They adopted that policy because they said they were considering the subject. They took a whole year to consider it. Why did they not come down the next year with a proposition to build a railway if its construction was of so much importance ? Why did they allow four years to pass and a condition of things continue to exist such as has been described by the hon. Minister of the Interior to-night ? The hon. gentleman, instead of placing in a humiliating position hon. gentlemen on this side, who have no power to deal with the subject, has placed himself and his colleagues in a most humiliating and extradordinary position by the statement he has just made.
I agree with my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier) that, so far as this claim is concerned, it ought to be paid. It is the government we are censuring for their conduct in connection with this contract, and we are not objecting to the payment of the claim of Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann.
There is another thing I would like to say to the hon. the Minister of the Interior, and it is this, that when Sir Charles Tupper was face to face with him in this House in 1S98, when this matter was discussed for a month, and when Sir Charles Tupper was face to face with him in the session of 1898, and in the session of 1900, it is most remarkable that the hon. Minister did not take occasion, in any one of these sessions, to make the statement he has seen fit to make to-night about Sir Charles Tupper going to his house. These hon. gentlemen are very sensitive sometimes about statements concerning people who are absent. This matter was discussed, as the hon. gentleman has said, in wearisome detail in 1898, and I heard no such statement from him then as that which he has seen fit to make to-night. He has waited until Sir Charles Tupper was absent, to charge him with dishonour, to cast imputations on him, but he never saw fit to make any such charge when Sir Charles Tupper was present to defend himself.
There is just one more circumstance I would like to mention. The hon. gentleman said that the Conservative party threw out that measure in the Senate. Well, if all rumours be true-and we heard a good many on the subject at the time-there

were a great many Liberal members here, who voted for that measure, under the stress of party discipline, who were as much opposed to it as gentlemen on this side. And if- we are to believe what is told us by gentlemen in the Upper Chamber, some of those members exercised influence on the senators to have the measure thrown out, because although they felt compelled to support the government in this House, they felt that the passage of the measure was not in the true interests of the country.
It is not worth while for me at this day to go into a great many of the matters dealt with by the hon. Minister of the Interior, for the purpose of malting party capital. So far as I am concerned, I think that these men should be paid, but at the same time I think that the government are to be censured for having entered into this contract in the way they did, and for not having waited until parliament could pass upon this measure before committing the country to the expenditure we are now called on to vote and pay over to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I have just a word to say in reply to some observations made by my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier). I do not know how my hon. friends on the other side can entertain the opinion, and repeat ft in this House that the account which parliament is called on to pay is one which had been settled between Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann and the Department of Railways. Nothing of the kind has ever taken place, and such an assertion is purely imaginative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Was there a report made to the government or the Railway Department by the officers of the department who investigated the accounts ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Here are the accounts themselves, presented by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, and which have been audited again and again by the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals, and audited with great care.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What is the amount of the account ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Practically the same amount as the award.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not know what mysterious feature there can be in the fact that the accounts, which were audited by the officers of the Department of Railways and Canals, were found to be accurate, or about as accurate, by the official auditor. The claim was handed in by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann to the government. It was audited again and again by Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
the officers of the Railway Department. Items were eliminated, all the profits claimed by Mackenzie & Maun were eliminated, and after it had been audited, by the officers of the department, a judicial audit was ordered by the government. The judicial auditor went through it no doubt with great care, and I am surprised that any doubt should be passed on the auditor, Mr. Justice Burbidge, and that he should be supposed not to have done his work with accuracy.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. Minister of the Interior has just stated that the judicial auditor sat upon the reference, and that the reference was the papers audited by the officials of the department.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend find fault with that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The auditor simply dealt with those figures.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: If the judicial auditor was satisfied, if he had sufficient evidence in the record to dispense him from calling for other evidence, will my hon. friend insinuate that Mr. Justice Burbidge had not acted properly ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: No.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: My hon. friend says that because Mr. Justice Burbidge did not seek other extraneous evidence, therefore some doubt must be cast on his audit. I do not know what evidence he should have sought. I am content with believing that since Mr. Justice Burbidge has reported that a certain sum was due, he must have found evidence in the record to justify such a conclusion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The right hon. gentleman said, in the course of his speech, that the judge of the Exchequer Court acted simply as an auditor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Certainly.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Therefore he dealt with no other documents than those presented here. AVas there any interest included in the award ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: If you add a reasonable amount of interest to the $300,000 you will come pretty close to his award.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
What fault does the hon. gentleman find, then, if Mr. Justice Burbidge finds that the claim presented to him was correct in amount that he should say so ? If he found that th<? amount claimed was the amount due, what fault does the hon. geutlemanl find that he should so declare it ? AVhy, he could not do anything else. And I presume that the character of Mr. Justice Burbidge will satisfy every lion, member that the work was
properly done; and, since lie lias reported that the claim is correct In amount, every lion, member of this House ought to be satisfied so far as that is concerned. Now,
I come to the statement of the leader of the opposition a moment ago. He found fault with the government for refusing to allow the passage of another charter for a railway to communicate with the Yukon. So we did. But why ? Because this charter if we had granted it would have been the means of establishing communication with the Yukon through American waters, and we should have no relief, so far as having a national railway is concerned, from the position of having to communicate with the Yukon through American territory. The reason was that we would not again complicate the settlement of the boundary question which we have enough difficulty in settling already. The toon, gentleman says also that we did not bring in a new measure for a railway after this one had been defeated. Sir, there was all the difference in the world between building a railway to tliat part of tlie country in 1898 and building .it afterwards. When we asked parliament to sanction tbe contract whicto we toad made with Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann for tbe building of a railway from Telegraph Creek to Teslin Lake, there was no railway between Calgary and Lake Bennett. It is a matter of fact, unfortunately, that the best line of railway to communicate with the Yukon country is by way of Skagway. That is the shortest line. Before 1898, contractors could have been induced to put money into tbe enterprise, because there was no rival to compete with them. But after a shorter railway to the Yukon has been built, as it was in tbe summer of 1898, everybody realizes that to build and run a line of railway from Telegraph Creek to Teslin Lake would involve a very much larger expense. My hon. friend said that tbe terms we offered to Mackenzie & Mann were extravagant. On tbe contrary, I venture to say we might offer tbe same terms to-day, and there is not a firm of contractors who would accept them and build tbe road. In 1898, we were told on the floor of this House that we were giving to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann an enormous area of gold-bearing territory. Tbe fact is that over that whole space of country not a single discovery of gold has been made ever since, outside of Klondyke Creek, except that last winter there was a discovery on Stewart river. But in the parts where we gave Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann the option to locate their claims, not a single discovery has been made. And I venture to repeat what I have just said, that no firm of contractors would to-day accept the contract on the same terms as those given Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann. Had the contract gone through at that time they would have had a monopoly, whereas now they would have to compete with the American railway which has
a monopoly. These are the reasons which have prevented us up to this time froimask-ing parliament to sanction the building of that railway. I venture to say that we may have to propose a project of that kind at a future time. We cannot remain very long as we are, dependent as we are upon the good-will of the American people to give us access to our otvn country. The _ position is not only humiliating, but, as stated by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, it is dangerous and dangerous in the extreme. Why, last year, we were told that there was a conspiracy about Skagway on the part of some American desperadoes to ' rush ' the country and take possession of it. There was such a conspiracy. It did not amount to much, I am glad to say. But, with the character of the population there we do not know when attempts may be made to ' rush ' the country and take possession of it. And we are absolutely helpless. If we are to send men to that section, as was stated by the Minister of the Interior, we have to send them as civilians, they cannot go through as a military force. We have almost to smuggle them into the country. This is a most alarming position, and one which we must ask parliament to remedy. And when that proposal comes before parliament, then parliament will realize what an egregious mistake they made in 189S.

speechtext:
The hon. leader of the opposition was exercised toy two things. The first was that I should put myself in such a humiliating position as to say that the country Is suffering from tlie lack of a railway, and yet that the government should not bring down a Bill to construct that railway. I venture to say to my hon. friend that if he should have the good fortune to sit upon this side of the House, he will find that there will be a great many things that would be of service to the country and for the want of which the country might be said to be suffering, and yet he will not be able to bring down an appropriation to parliament to furnish them. That is the position we are in with respect to many things in the Dominion of Canada. We know that the Dominion of Canada is suffering to a very considerable extent by reason of the fact that there is not an all-Canadian railway to the Yukon district. Yet, we are not prepared to take the responsibility of recommending to parliament a sufficient appropriation for the construction of that railway. That is a very plain and reasonable and intelligible position, and I am quite unable to agree with my hon. friend that, in any respect whatever, the statement of that position places me or any member of this government in a humiliating position. My hon. friend is further exercised by the fact, as'he believes it to he, that I would not have made the statement -with regard to Sir Charles Tupper calling upon me or saying

what he did to me upon this matter, if Sir Charles Tupper had been here. I did not hear what my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) said, being unfortunately, unable to hear him very well when he addresses the House, but an hon. friend beside me tells me that the hon. member for West Toronto took the same view as his leader upon this subject. My hon. friends * are forgetful in this debate of many circumstances, and they are particularly forgetful of tlhe debate which took place on this very question. Members of the House will remember what I said to Sir Charles Tupper who then led the opposition, when he made liis famous somersault upon this question and, at the dictation of the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean), allowed himself to be compelled to swallow his own words and to do what was directly contrary to his own judgment, because the hon. member for East York and those who were with him thought they could gain a small party advantage over this government by that course. It is not necessary that l should have Sir Charles Tupper here to refer to a fact which he has admitted himself. If the hon. leader of the opposition will take ' Hansard ' of 1898, and refer to the report of my remarks wihen the subject of this Yukon Railway Bill was under debate, he will find in the first place, that I called attention to the fact that Sir Charles T.upper had taken this somersault on this question and I said he hadi done it not in accordance with his own judgment, but because he had been dragooned into taking it by hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. Then I went on to quote an interview with Sir Charles Tupper himself in the ' Mail and Empire ' newspaper, and hon. gentlemen wall find it on page 572 of the ' Hansard ' of 1898. I said :
The authenticity of this interview is vouched for by my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean), the gentleman who, in the Conservative party, fills the role of private detective and regulator of the party leader.
I do not know whether he fills that position in regard to my hon. friend who leads the opposition at present.
It appears that Sir Charles Tupper was asked by the correspondent of the ' Mail and Empire ' to state his views regarding the arrangements the government had made. This is what he said :
He stated that the route chosen is the best that comld have been selected. ' When I was in the west,' he said, * I made inquiries, and I reached the conclusion that Canada ought at th'e earliest possible moment to have communication with the Yukon. I impressed it upon the British Columbia government that it should co-operate with the Dominion government to secure the construction of a link between the Stikine river and Tesliu lake. At Winnipeg I declared that the undertaking was a necessity, and when I returned to Ottawa I went immediately to Mr. Sifton. I impressed upon him the absolute necessity of opening up the route to secure Canadian trade.

speechtext: There is an imputation throughout this debate that the Senate of Canada did a wrong thing in throwing out that Bill. Sir, if the Senate of Canada ever justified its existence it did so in throwing out that Bill. Hon. gentlemen have an idea and they are always formulating it, that because they control the majority of this chamber therefore what they say ought to go in parliament. But the parliament of Canada is made up of this chamber associated with the other chamber, having equal authority, and associated with it also is the Governor General. What rules in this country is, not a brute majority of one party in this House, hut it is ultimately public opinion that rules ; and the public opinion of this country on that occasion was voiced by the Senate who threw out that infamous proposition.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Where was public opinion in 1900 ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Where will public opinion be on the 29th of the present month, iu the province of Ontario ? But the Minister of the Interior, who has just left his seat, has never got over the soreness he felt because his pet project was thrown out of this parliament and was condemned by public opinion. He could not get public opinion to endorse it to-day, and therefore he cannot bring it in. It still remains a sore point with him that in some way the Conservative party, through its leader, was committed to that proposition, and because he didn't get the support he expected, he could not put it through. The government of this country has come to this, that they cannot bring forward any measure without its being iu some way endorsed by the Conservative party before hand. If they want to undertake any great railway project they first try to get the endorsation of the opposition, and then they bring it forward. Now, that has come to an end. The government, or at least certain members of it, have a great proposition in connection with the Georgian Bay ship canal, and in an insidious way a petition was circulated on this side of the House, and they tried to dragoon this side of the House first to give support to the proposition. Now, we are not here to do business in that way. I resent the doctrine that is laid down here to-night, and a great cry is made over it, and we hear a lamentation made before the country that the project fell through because they could not count on the support of the leader of the opposition. All that must end. The government must come forward witli their proposition supported by themselves, and they must assume responsibility for it. We hear to-night that their scheme failed because it was not supported by the opposition. Sir, their scheme failed because it was a bad one ; their scheme failed because it meant the giving of an enormous

amount of territory to a private company who proposed then and there to exploit tne London market with a $10,000,000 or a $aj,-000,000 proposition ; and if that agreement had been sanctioned and had been exploited on tlie London market-and it had actually been underwritten-there would have been the greatest Yukon scandal the world had ever heard of. The country would have been disgraced. We never would have got a railway, or if we had, it would have been a railway at the mercy of the Americans, just as lion, gentlemen have said that the present scheme puts us at their mercy. If there was an all-Canadian route independent of American territory, lion, gentlemen never had the courage to bring it forward, because they knew it involved too large an expenditure. I say to-night in face of the whole country that if the Senate of Canada ever gave a reason for its existence, it did on that occasion. There are times when public opinion can only find its expression and its outlet through the Senate, and it did find its outlet there on that particular occasion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I consider this question as one of the most important that ever came before this parliament. It is important because it involves a radical departure from tlie well understood principle of constitutional government, the principle that the executive are responsible to parliament and parliament is responsible to the people. In this particular case the executive incurred a very large and unwise expenditure before parliament was.consulted, and within a few days of the meeting of parliament. The reason given for their justification is that of urgency. The contract was entered into nine days before parliament met because, as they said, the case was an extremely urgent one. What has taken place since then to justify the plea of urgency) Have we seen any of those direful results taking place that we were told would take place if this contract was not sanctioned ? Not by any means. We were told that it was necessary to build this railway immediately because we could not get our soldiers in there, and there was danger of an insurrection. Have there been any signs of an insurrection ? Have not the North-west Mounted Police been able to make life and property just as safe there as in any other part of the Dominion ?
There is no evidence to indicate that there is the slightest trouble, but there is evidence to show that peace and harmony prevail there and that the authority of the Canadian parliament has been maintained the same as it has been maintained in all the other provinces of this Dominion. Therefore, I say, that the argument advanced on that ground lias no force. In the next place, it was said that we would lose the trade of that country and that the trade would go entirely to the United States. I would remind hon. gentlemen that one of their own 154
friends made a statement inside of the last year in regard to the trade of that country, if my memory is correct, in the city of Toronto before a commercial audience, which was something to the effect that of the trade of the Yukon to-day, about 60 per cent is done by Canadians, that the goods which are supplied to the people of that country are Canadian and English to that extent, and not American. Therefore, so far as that argument is concerned, there is nothing in it. It has not been verified. These predictions have not been verified, these forecasts have not come true and these prophesies have been unfulfilled. The next thing was that the people were crowding in there in such large numbers that they would likely die of hunger and starvation, because provisions could not be got into that country. How many people have died of starvation on account of not being able to get provisions into the country ? We have never heard of any difficulty in that regard. After the charter was thrown out by the Senate, people went about their ordinary avocations just as they had done before. They had plenty of provisions, there was no sign of starvation and they continued in the enjoyment of the luxuries of life. This was one of the strong reasons urged why it was desirable that parliament should pass that Bill. As none of these forebodings or prophesies have been verified, and as none of them are likely to be verified, we are justified in saying that when parliament threw that Bill out at that time parliament did right. But, the government are doing a very improper thing, and for another reason. What is it ? I say that they are violating one of the well understood principles of constitutional government in entering into specific contracts, giving orders to go on with these works, and incurring expenditures which undoubtedly the country will be called upon to pay without parliamentary assent having first been sustained. I do not blame the contractors for asking for an indemnification for what they have lost. The government were instructing, either by implication or direct authority and advice, these contractors to go on and make heavy expenditures and in doing so they knew that parliament would be called upon to indemnify them in the event of the contract not being ratified by parliament. It was not ratified, and we find this condition of things that we have here to-day. Our constitution never contemplated it, it never authorized it, it is contrary to free parliamentary government, and it confers no right upon a minister to do what the hon. Minister of the Interior did at that time. Therefore, these hon. gentlemen are violating a well understood principle of constitutional government, which above ail things ought to be sacred, not only in Canada, but in every other colony in the British Empire. But, they are doing more; they are estabiish-



ing a very bad precedent, a precedent tbat no doubt will be taken advantage of in tlie future by designing parties who wish to get claims before the government, by parties who desire to make money and who can find a government weak or servile enough to co-operate with them in entering into a bargain-I will not say that it would be a collusive bargain, but a bargain which they know parliament will not ratify, because, when they see proceedings of this kind taking place, and a precedent of this kind established, they will know that they would be justified in coming before parliament and asking to be indemnified, not only for every dollar they have put into the undertaking, but for the interest on their money, and for the costs which they have paid to the lawyers who have conducted the case for them. Such a precedent is bad on the face of it in Canada or in any part of the British Empire. Yet, we have lived to see the day when the Reform party, the party which above all others have always professed a desire to live up to the well known principles of free constitutional government, will depart from the principles in a most radical way, at the same time establishing a very bad precedent in the country. We are adopting a very bad precedent, a precedent that may work any amount of trouble and injury to the country in the future. To-day, we are asked to go it blind in this matter as to the amount of money to be voted. Hon. gentlemen have said that this question has been submitted to the Exchequer Court, but what information has been given to the House as to the question that was submitted to the Exchequer Court ? If it were the sale of a dog, involving a transaction of $2, as much trouble would have been taken to see that thq transaction was a fair one as has been taken in regard to this transaction involving $328,000. They submitted the accounts to the Exchequer Court that were received from Mackenzie and Mann, they were looked over by an officer of the Department of Railways and Canals, who was instructed, no doubt, to prepare a report on them which would be submitted to the House, and which would be of such a favourable character as to justify whatever action the government took upon the claim, but they gave no opportunity for the opposition to analyse it in such a way as to determine whether we are justified in voting this amount or not. In looking over the accounts carefully, I came to the conclusion that the government have taken no more interest in this account than they would in a transaction involving an expenditure of $100. They submitted the question to the Exchequer Court, and the judge was to report his judgment, but the court was not asked to determine the legal standing of the parties, or how far this country was liable or responsible for this transaction, how far the country was called
upon to indemnify the contractors for the loss they had sustained. That question was not submitted to the Exchequer Court or to any other court in the country. No effort was made to appeal from the decision of that court to a higher tribunal. The government claim that they have taken the ordinary course, but if this had been an ordinary contract, if advertisements had been published and an invitation had been given to contractors to submit tenders, and the contractor who had secured the work had a claim of $200 or $300, or $3,000 for work done under his contract, the government would have submitted the claim to the Exchequer Court, and if an adverse decision had been rendered by the Exchequer Court they would have appealed it to a higher court. Did they do so in this case ? No, they accepted the judgment in silence, and they paid no more attention to the matter than if it had been a claim involving $100 or $200. They did not take it to an independent tribunal with the view of determining the legal rights of the contractors who were applying for this large amount of money, or the legal liability of the country to pay it. They simply submitted the claim to this House and asked this House to ratify it. Then, there is something behind all this yet that seems to be of a very important character. When the Bill was before this House, and when it was considered and forced through the House by the majority that the right hon. leader of the government and his friend^ have at their backs, and it went to the Upper House, and after being carefully looked into, that house decided that the bargain was a very bad one, they decided that the reasons given as a justification for the passing of that Bill were not good, they decided that it was an attempt to exploit the domain of the state unwisely and imprudently, and they decided that a young Napoleon had floated one of his transactions on the country that would not bear the light of day, and the result was that they threw the Bill out. But, now, we are asked to vote the sum of $328,000 to indemnify these contractors. What say have the Senate whether that shall pass or not ? They were the portion of this parliament which prevented the Bill from passing ; they threw it out.
The Senate has no say as to whether this item shall pass or not, because if they reject it they could only do so by rejecting the whole Supply Bill, which they would not do, and so this procedure on the part of the government has wrested from, the Upper Chamber the power to pass judgment upon this matter. I do not blame the company for preferring this claim against the government, but I blame the government for giving them instructions to go on with expenditure under that contract. And although the government have hedged very adroitly upon that question I have no doubt in my mind that they gave instructions to

speechtext: Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann to go on with the work. Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann are too astute to be guilty of the blunder of spending even $100, if they had not a well understood agreement with the government that they would be indemnified if the contract was not ratified by parliament. I oppose this because it is in violation of the well understood principle that no expenditure should be incurred without the assent of parliament. In a matter of extreme urgency the government has power to raise money by Governor's General warrant, but in this case they did not dare resort to that expedient. We are told by the Minister of the Interior that we appealed to the electorate of Canada in 1900 on this question and that as a result we are in opposition. What was the result in the minister's own province ? Were it not for the most bare faced corruption he would have come back here with but a single supporter from Manitoba. What was the result in the great province of Ontario that will be called upon to pay the largest share of this ? The result was a majority of 16 or 18 members against the government, a clear and distinct condemnation of their action and policy. The Minister of the Interior tells us that he cheerfully accepts the responsibility for this action, and he intimates that the majority behind him will carry him through. Well, majorities have done many improper things in the past, and I have no doubt they will repeat it to-night. It is not the first time that the Minister of the Interior has done an improper thing and trusted to-I was going to say his servile majority-to carry him through. He is called the young Napoleon because he was willing to exploit anything which in the judgment of wise people would be regarded as unconstitutional and improper, and he does that because he depends upon his majority. We know that after the election of 1896 he illegally incurred the expenditure of public money in violation of all constitutional principles. He ordered an inquiry at the cost of the public treasury for which he had no legal authority under heaven. He did It because he depended on his majority, and therefore his statement that he accepts responsibility does not mean that his action was either constitutional or proper. He tells us that in this matter he endeavoured to protect the treasury, when as a 'matter of fact it is an act of piracy perpetrated upon the treasury. Why, the men who above all others should protect the trea-su.y are the men who are burglarizing the treasury through their contractors In this scheme. There is nothing to show whether these accounts are correct or not. There is nothing except the statement of the contractors who ask that they shall be paid out of the treasury their claim and their costs and everything else.

speechtext: At first it was not; but ultimately it was to be. Was the road which was proposed to be built from Telegraph Creek to Teslin Lake to be an allCanadian road ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Not a bit of it. One end was to toe in the United States, and you would have been obliged to make use of the navigation which would put you just as much under the power of the United States as if you went over a railway built in the United States territory; and it would not answer the purpose which the Minister of the Interior declared they 'had in building that railway. These hon. gentlemen have given no evidence that they want a railway into that country, or they would make an effort >to get it. They have had companies knocking at the doors of parliament for permission to build a railway there, tout they would not give permission. I have often thought they held it back for the purpose of using as an argument against the Senate the action of the Senate in throwing out that Bill. The Minister of the Interior will have to convince us in a different way that ithe government desire to have a railway built in that country. He went on to tell us of the wonderful bargain they bad made, and the advantages they were to get from it. By that contract they were giving away all the gold land in the country. I beard an Englishman say in the Brunswick hotel at the time that Bill was before the House:	' If Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann
make over to me toy power of attorney the right .to handle that scheme in the British market, I will make a fortune for myself and bring them back $40,000,000 of bard cash.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Did you .believe it ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I did, because I knew the man to stand high in the financial world.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the ,hon. gentleman think the land was worth $40,000,000 ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I can answer the hon. gentleman by telling him that the government would not sell the land for less than $10 an acre. That is the price they asked from the poor miner.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Nobody ever asked $10 an acre.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Why did the government hold the land at $10 an acre and refuse to sell for less ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: They did not.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: They did not offer to sell it at less.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Nobody wants to buy it.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Why then make such a regulation ? Why not have said that you *would sell it at a dollar an acre. I am justified in taking the valuation which the government themselves put on the land, and what does that valuation amount to for the building of the railway. I think it is $37,500,000.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I will stake my word to this fact that the government could not sell that land in any bulk for fifty cents an acre.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is the bon. gentleman a miner ? Has be been out there in the mining business ? Or, is he simply a newspaper editor in Regina. What does he know about it ? He knows no more than I do. What does the government know about it ? What does the Minister of the Interior know about it ? Why did the hon. Minister of the Interior recommend to Council the land should be valued at $10 an acre if it was not worth half a dollar an acre ? On what authority did he make that recommendation ? What, the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Scott) says to-day is the strongest condemnation of the Minister of the Interior and the government. They have not offered for sale or sold a single acre of mineral land in that country since that time at less than $10 an acre. I am therefore justified in taking their own valuation as the consideration they were giving that company. What were they charging the poor man for a royalty ? Ten per cent on the gold he took out, no matter how poor he might have been or bow unable to pay it. And all they were charging this wealthy company was one per cent royalty. Taking all these things into consideration, we would be doing less than our duty if we did not raise our voices in the strongest protest against this transaction. It is a violation of the principles of constitutional government. It establishes a bad precedent, and for my part I enter my protest against it in the strongest possible language I can use.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am sorry that the right hon. leader of the government is out, because I wished to refer again to a statement I made as to an arrangement having been come to between the Department of Railways and Canals and Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann regarding the amount of the latter's claim, which statement my right hon. friend contradicted. I thought I remembered that I had seen in the papers laid on the Table some time ago some correspondence between Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann anld the department regarding their claim. It seemed strauge that the final claim of these gentlemen should amount to $302,239.69 and that the amount recommended by the Railway Department is exactly the same. Mr. Shannon of the Railway De-

partment went over the accounts and found that that was the correct sum due them. There is another thing which appears in the correspondence, and of which we have not heard before. These parties were entitled to the money they had expended on the road with interest. That was the understanding. That was the interpretation of the sub-imission as given to us, but when I look into the account, as arranged between the department and Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, X find that they are allowed, in addition to the money they actually expended, nearly $60,000, or fifteen per cent on the amount they expended on the road. We never heard of that before from the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals nor have we heard it from the right hon. the First Minister. I remembered seeing in the papers some correspondence between the department and Mackenzie & Mann regarding the amount due the latter. And perhaps I had better read the correspondence so as to put it upon record and in order that there may be no doubt about it in the future
Toronto, July 18, 1899. Leonard Shannon, Esq.,
Accountant of the Department of Railways and Canals, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-Re our account and claim for disbursements in connection with the Canadian Yukon railway matter.
