Just the amount the department found was due, just the amount given by Mr. Justice Burbidge in favour of Mackenzie & Mann, and that includes $58,000, or 15 per cent advance upon the claim against the government, besides the interest which was awarded by the Exchequer Court. And I would ask hon. gentlemen to give me reference to the statute under which they referred the question to the Exchequer Court. Nobody seems to be able to answer this. But it is a very important question. We do not want the country to believe that a judgment was rendered by the Exchequer Court to pay this amount to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, because, as I said before, this contract had a saving clause under which the contractors knew they could not oblige the government to carry out the contract unless they had the authority of parliament to enter into it. The contract was with that condition, a condition sine qua non, that it should be approved by parliament. It was submitted to parliament, and, rightly or wrongly, parliament refused to approve it. Therefore, the conditiou under which these gentlemen entered into the contract never arose, and they had no binding legal claim, as was admitted by the right hon. gentleman who leads the House. The only claim they had against the country and against the government, was an equitable claim which they could not enforce in law. That is the reason why I asked whether this was a judgment or whether it was an order, or what it was. It becomes evident now that the only thing that the government did was to refer the question to the judge of the Exchequer Court as a persona designata as to whether the account could be audited in a proper manner and was a proper account to be paid, supposing the government were bound in law to pay it. Moreover, the first thing the government did before submitting this to the judge of the Exchequer Court was to acknowledge its liability that this amount should be paid by the Dominion. Therefore, I object, and I say that the resolution should be amended. This resolution, if I may use the word, bears upon its face a falsehood. For, if there was no judgment, it is not a true representation of the facts to say that there was a judgment of the Exchequer Court. There has simply been a report made by Mr. Burbidge, it may be, by any other person, but not by a court. Therefore, I call the attention of the Committee to the fact that this resolution proposed to us bears upon its face a falsehood when it says ' to pay amount of judgment of Exchequer Court to Messrs. Mackenzie

& Maun.' Why, the Committee cannot pass that resolution; the Committee cannot say that there was a judgment when it was admitted on all sides that there was no judgment and that there could be no judgment. I am in the judgment of hon. members who are of the legal profession when I say that no judgment of this kind could be rendered against the government in connection with this contract. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurler) said himself, and nobody can deny it, that these gentlemen have no legal case against the government. At all events, this resolution must be amended so as not to make it appear that there was a judgment. Otherwise, what would happen ? When hon. gentlemen opposite go upon the hustings to defend their policy in connection with this item, they will say : We were condemned by the judgment of the Exchequer Court to pay the amount. We had no discretion, for if we had not paid it, execution might be issued against us or other means taken to compel the government of the Dominion to pay the amount. But that is not a valid excuse; and it cannot appear in the resolution that there was a judgment when there was no judgment. If the resolution passes, as I think it will, it will have to be amended so as to read otherwise than as a declaration that there was a judgment of the Exchequer Court, when, by the admission of ail the hon. gentlemen who have spoken, there was no judgment either by Judge Burbidge, sitting as a judge, or by the Exchequer Court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cas-grain) is to be congratulated upon making a remarkable discovery at this late period of the debate. He has read the item which goes to show that there was, in point of fact, a recognition of this claim and an acknowledgment that it had to be paid. My hon. friend tries to draw a very large conclusion from very limited premises. There Is not a word in this paper that will justify any man of business, any man who has experience in affairs, in making any such statement as he has made. The claim was handed to the government by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, and by the government referred to the Department of Railways and Canals for audit. The department was not asked to say whether the claim ought to be paid or whether any item of it ought to be paid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: But they objected to some items.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
All the department were asked to do was to ascertain whether or not the items which went to show large disbursements for the purposes stated, had been made by Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann in connection with this business. The question was, whether the disbursements which
these gentlemen claimeu to have made for supplies, for freight, and other proper charges in connection with their preparations for the construction of this railway had, as a matter of fact, been made. Now, how would you go to work Jo ascertain that, preliminary to a decision as to whether or not you are going to pay it or pay any part of it ? Mark you, the government had not declared, it had not come to any decision, as to what would be paid, whether the whole or any portion of the claim. The government simply felt, as several hon. gentlemen on the other side have said they would feel under like circumstances, that Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, having been induced by the government to enter into this contract, ought not to be left to pay the loss which has resulted to them from their endeavour to carry it out. Now, the auditor, taking up the claim item by item, examined it. What are these items 1 They are for material of all kinds, for supplies for wages paid to men, for moneys paid for all the purposes which will occur to the minds of hon. gentlemen as likely to be called for in connection with this undertaking. Now, how would the auditor satisfy himself upon that point 1 What ought he do to satisfy himself as to the correctness of the items ? One thing you will say he ought to do-he ought to go to that portion of the country wherever it was, where the supplies were which had not been used.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What was the finding of the auditor. Tell us. Don't be all night about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman will pardon me, I will take as much time as 1 please, and if he does not like the fullness of the answer I give him, he will have to bear it with such patience and serenity as he can command.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman do this-will he, instead of showing at great length what the auditor ought to do, tell what he did do ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is what we want.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am charmed with the clearness and acuteness displayed by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lennox). It is not often that we have an opportunity of congratulating the hon. gentleman upon the clearness and lucidity with which he puts a point. But, had he been following me, he would not have felt called upon to interrupt me in doing the very thing which, with the clearness and astuteness of his intellect, he sees I ought to do.
Now I was proceeding to say that the auditor went to that country, he went to where these supplies were that had been

purchased for the use of this railway but that were not used on the railway. He makes his inventory, and he compares the inventory which Mackenzie & Mann had given in this bill with the articles themselves on the ground ; and he finds that it either corresponds or does not correspond with their inventory, as the case may be. He found that it did not entirely correspond, although it did to a large extent, and where it did not correspond the items were struck out.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Will the minister tell us in what respects they did correspond and in what respects they failed to correspond 1

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I will read for the information of the hon. gentleman the statement which the auditor himself has made :
Sir, in accordance with your instructions I have personally made an audit of the account presented by Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann & Co., in connection with the Canadian Yukon Railway, and have the honour to make the following report :
I find that the vouchers submitted for the expenditures of each month, with certain exceptions to be hereafter mentioned, represent the amounts charged in the statement and are correct as to amounts, and that the necessary details have been given to enable a proper audit to be made. In nearly every case each voucher contains not only the receipt of the parties to whom money was paid, but also the retired bank cheque, which in itself is sufficient evidence of the money having been paid out. .1 found the following errors which I have altered to the correct amount in the statement, namely:
Then he enumerates a number of errors.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What is the amount of the errors ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Some are small and some are' large. I will read it all to the hon. gentleman, if he would like to hear it:
Voucher No. 46, March, originally charged $816.50, but one account of $61.50 has been withdrawn, making the amount not charged, $755.
Voucher No. 29, Juns, should be $106.80 instead of $116.30.
Voucher No. 45, June, contains items to the extent of $120.30 which are also included in; voucher No. 46. I have, therefore, reduced the, amount to $161.25.
Voucher No. 47, June, returned as $138.50, should be $128.50.
Voucher No. 70, July, returned as $11,642.11 should be $11,632.11.
Voucher No. 10 and 11, December, for $100 and $630 respectively, are not yet paid, so these amounts have been transfered to the list of vouchers approved by Mackenzie, Mann & Co., but unpaid.
I also found in the pay lists submitted several sums amounting to $80. Twelve representing overpayments to men, and have accordingly deducted them, but Mr. Lukes representing Messrs, Mackenzie, Mann & Co., informs me that those items should be considered inasmuch as they were caused in all cases by the store account, and other charges against the men being in Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
excess of the amounts earned, and not due to any clerical error.
After making the aforementioned corrections, I find that the actual amount of vouchers paid and pay rolls, including interest at six per centum per annum up to January 1st last, to be the sum of $317,767.65 which together with accounts approved but not yet paid amounting to $26,800.88, makes a total of $344,568.53, and with 15 per cent added by Messrs. Mackenzie, Mann & Co., $51,685.28, and less proceeds of goods sold as per statement of credits, viz., $34,362.09, makes'a grand total of $361,891.72. In connection with this I would draw attention to the 15 per cent being calculated upon the sums of interest claimed.
In addition to the above, the statement contains accounts and claims in dispute to the extent of $114,890 which with the 15 per cent added makes a total of $131,893.50.
I also beg to draw attention to the nature of the following vouchers :
He enumerates the vouchers which he thinks ought to be brought to the notice of the department.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I presume the miuister, having gone over these figures, can tell us what was the difference made by the auditor. It was a matter of less than $100, was it not ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is really making a desperate effort to be sarcastic.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Not at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Yes, he is making a painful effort, but be has not succeeded.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS :

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It is not painful to me, though it may be to my hon. friend. But can he tell us what was the total difference made; by the auditor as the result of going over these accounts ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The total amount finally settled upon was $302,239. There appears to have been a claim for $510,422. There appears to have been credits which were afterwards brought in to the extent of $208,182. What the auditor did by this finding was to see that the disbursements which the company proved as having been actually made, amounted to $302,239. The very moment that the auditor came to that conclusion. Mackenzie & Mann, recognizing that the audit was fair and just, withdrew any larger claims they had, and preferred a claim for the amount which the auditor had declared to be proper, a very reasonable and proper course for these gentlemen to take. Now the hon. gentleman draws the inference that there must have been some collusion between the government and Mackenzie & Mann because the judge, when he came to examine into this matter and hear witnesses under oath, came to the conclusion that the amount which the auditor had passed upon was a proper amount to allow with the additional interest, whatever it might be. If the audit was properly made, and if the

disbursements were truly shown, and it was proper to allow interest upon the money actually paid out, and something for services given 'by these contractors to the work, then the claim would be that allowed by the audit, and so the judge finally decided. This matter passed into the hands of the Department of Justice, and immediately upon the auditor's report being received, the claims, papers, reports and everything else went over to the Department of Justice. The Department of Justice made a recommendation to Council as to what would be a proper mode in which finally to have this matter determined, and Council was advised by the Department of Justice that a reference should be made-not a petition of right, because a petition of right would have to be founded upon a legal basis, but this was regarded as a claim of an equitable nature, rather as an application to the grace and bounty of the Crown than as the preferment of a legal claim founded upon a legally authorized contract.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
It was not a judgment at all.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAY'S AND CANALS. A reference was made to the judge under the Order in Council.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: There cannot be a judgment except there be a suit. There was r.o suit, there was no petition of right and the hon. gentleman does not say there was. There was really no reference under the law as far as I can see. There was not even an award, and further the right hon. leader of the government said this afteruoon that there was simply an audit of these accounts by Mr. Justice Burbidge. There was no judgment, there was no award, there was no decision.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Was there not a finding ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: No, there was no finding ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Cas-grain) is quite correct in saying there was no judgment of the court. I am prepared here to admit that the hon. gentleman is, absolutely right ; there was no judgment of the court in which that expression can be technically used. There was a reference. No one wants to have the item appear in any other form than according to the fact. This matter was referred to the judge, the judge took evidence under oath, he examined witnesses, he heard what they had to say, and he came to the conclusion that the amount was properly made up, that these disbursements had been actually made and that, under the terms of the reference, $32S,-000 was the proper amount to pay.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The result of what the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals says is that the reading of this resolution is not correct, and the committee cannot decide
that there was a judgment when there was not. The committee cannot say that tins amount is the amount of a judgment rendered by the Exchequer Court. I would suggest that these words be substituted : ' To pay the amount due under the report of Mr. Justice Burbidge to Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: A rose by any other name would smell as sweet. I do not suppose that we need quarrel over the words. As a matter of fact the Order in Council distinctly states that this matter is to be referred to the Exchequer Court, that the judgment of the Exchequer Court is to be accepted, and the Exchequer Court does not appear to have taken any exception to the form of the reference.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am sorry to differ with the hon. gentleman, but I hold in my hand the statute which shows that there can be no judgment of the Exchequer Court because the statute says :
The head of any department in connection with the administration of which any claim arises may, instead of referring such claim to the court for adjudication thereon, refer the same to one of the official referees for examination and report, both as to the matters of fact involved and as to the amount of damages, if any, sustained.
The statement which is made is that a decision has been rendered by the court in a case which has been regularly instituted by these gentlemen, Messrs. Mackenzie & Mann, against the Crown. This is important to this extent that if this question came up for discussion on the hustings, hon. gentlemen on the other side will get up and say that as this was a judgment of the Exchequer Court we had no discretion in the matter, but we had to pay it. I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite, whether, in view of the facts which have been stated by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals and by the right hon. leader of the government, it is fair to put in this resolution that there has been a judgment of the Exchequer Court. I do not care What the reference, or what the Order in Council said. I am very much surprised to see that such an eminent lawyer as the hon. Minister of Justice should have drafted an Order in Council in the terms which have been mentioned by the lion. Minister of Finance because that would not be according to the law at all. This is a simple reference to Mr. Justice Burbidge and in this matter he is hot even acting as a judge of the Exchequer Court but he is merely acting as a persona designata.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
As to the question of the words, we do not attach any importance to them. I do not think the great public of Canada will see as clearly as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Casgrain) does the distinction between a judgment of Mr. Justice Burbidge in the Exchequer Court and the report which Mr. Justice Burbidge

has made in this matter. The fact has not been disputed that the duty of the court was simply to pass the accounts, and I think the great public will not see the distinction between a judgment of Mr. Justice Burbidge and a report of Mr. Justice Bur-bidge, but, that the public will see that this is the opinion of Mr. Justice Burbidge whether you call it a judgment, or a report, or a finding.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am sure that if the hon. Minister of Finance and myself were on the hustings discussing this question, ho would be astute enough to take the position that this was a judgment of the Exchequer Court. I would not have very much to say because I would not be able to deny that, if this were a judgment of the Exchequer Court the government are bound by it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: But, as the Order in Council distinctly declares that the liability is admitted, I would not put myself at the mercy of the hon. gentleman by making any such statement.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think we are getting into greater difficulty by reason of the statement of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding). He tells us that by the Order in Council it was referred to Judge Burbidge of the court of Exchequer to give judgment. If it is the case that no judgment has been given we are not in a position to treat of the matter at all, but I think we may take che statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals as putting the matter in a fairly clear light, and keeping that in mind, 1 think the hon. Minister of Finance does not give the great public credit for the astuteness which it really possesses. I think the public will see a very broad distinction at oiice between a judgment of the Exchequer Court, as it has been pointed out by my hon. friend here (Mr. Casgrain), and the case as put by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals. What I understand is that there had been an audit by the Department of Railways f. -id Canals for the purpose of ascertaining the correctness of the items, that they did go into the matter and did ascertain the correctness of the items and that for the purpose of verifying that further-if I understand the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals correctly, and I hope the hon. minister will not say that I am sarcastic in any degree

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: You are not now.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I am improving- all the time. For the purpose of verifying that and for greater assurance and for the purpose of justifying the government in any action they might subsequently have to take they referred the matter to Judge Burbidge, as a persona designata. It might have been referred to any other well qualified persm. He could corroborate by a report the amount arrived at by the audit that bad Hon. Mr. FIELDING.

I call the attention of the minister to the report of his officer on the condition of the Poonamalie bridge, and I would ask the minister to insert an item in the estimates to put that bridge into proper shape. The government engineer reports :

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is a most extraordinary way to make a contract.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
It was a most peculiar contract. The first time I asked the Minister of Railways whether this work was let by tender, he said yes. I understood then that the whole work was let by tender from Charlottetown to Murray Harbour. On April 9th the question was asked in the Senate by Mr. Ferguson, whether the work had been let by tender, and the answer was that it had, but in the neighbourhood where the work is being done, it was believed that only one portion, 111 miles, had been let by tender, and on the 1st May the Hon. Mr. Ferguson inquired in the Senate :
Whether it is the intention of the government to invite public tenders for the construction of the railway from Chnlottetoivn to Murray harbour other than section 2.
If so, when will the notices for such tenders be issued ?
The Hon. Mr. Scott replied as follows
The answer sent me is as follows :-The department invited tenders by public advertisement for section 2 covering 11J miles from Mutch's Point towards Murray Harbour and the contract was awarded accordingly to a responsible contractor, at prices which the engineers pronounced reasonable. The next section was continued at the prices for the work as Mr. BARKER.
settled under the first tenders, by Order in Council. The contract has been sent for execution by the contractor.
In reply to my question as to whether any work had been done before the Order in Council was passed, the hon. Minister of Railways said no, that the Order in Council was passed before the contractors had begun to do the work on the other sections of the road. But what are the facts ? Here is what Mr. Ferguson said in the Senate :
Hon. Mr. FERGUSON-That is most extraordinary, in the face of the replies that were given across the floor of the House on the authority of the chief engineer of railways, that no work was being done on any section hut No. 2, when now it appears that by an Order in Council the work was prosecuted on other sections of the road on the same terms as No. 2.
Hon. Mr. SCOTT-The hon. gentleman is right except as far as the date is concerned. After my hon. friend made the statement that work was going on, I called the attention of the Minister of Railways to it and he denied it, and I spoke to Mr. Schreiber about it. It appears the contractor went on with the approval, perhaps, of the local engineer. Subsequent to tbe statement made, on a report from tbe local engineer, conarmcd by Mr. Seh-reiber, a continuation of the work was given beyond the 111 miles to this contractor at schedule prices contained in the first contract.
Hon. Mr. FERGUSON-That is ail right, but what becomes of the denials given by my hon. friend on the authority of the department, that work was being done by the government ?
Hon. Mr. SCOTT-Evidently the department did not know the work was going on.
Hon. Mr. FERGUSON-And it was done by Order in Council ?
Hon. Mr. SCOTT-No, he went on1 before the Order in Council. The Order in Council was passed, if my memory is correct, after my attention was called to it by my hon. friend.
What becomes then of the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways that the work was, in the first place, let by tender for the first 11J miles, and then that a contract was given for the other 31 miles, on the schedule prices of the first tender and without inviting any competition. I need not go into the constitutional question, whether the hon. gentleman had the right to do this or not. There are enough sins against the government without charging it with anything more. But the hon. minister did what he had no right to do. By law lie is bound to advertise for tenders for the construction of all these works. But the hon. gentleman does not seem to pay much attention to the law in these matters. However he extended the contract, and he told us that no work was done by the contractor until the Order in Council was passed. It appears now, however, that the contractor was doing the work by some one's authority, without the knowledge seemingly of the minister, and without any Order in Council having been passed. According to the hon. minister's colleague in the other House, he seems not to have

known anything about this. The work, it seems, was going on without his knowledge, and it was only authorized by Order in Council when the attention of the minister's colleague in the Upper House was brought to the fact by Senator Ferguson.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has discovered a mare's nest. Let me tell him that the questions which he has asked and which have been answered, have been truthfully answered. The question he asked me, whether or not the Order in Council authorizing the giving of the second contract to the contractor, on the schedule prices of the first, was made before any work was done, I replied in the affirmative. I still say that it was.	.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Before the work was commenced ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Before any work was done on the extension. I am confident of that because that Order in Council was passed long enough ago, and I do not think that the contractors could possibly have begun the work before it was passed. Let me make a suggestion to my hon. friend. He has been during last summer with his hon. friend beside him (Mr. Barker) travelling over the Intercolonial Railway. The attention of these two gentleman has been given during the recess almost exclusively to the subject of the Intercolonial Railway. They travel- j led over the line, listening to all the stories they could hear, and they were convinced that when parliament was called together and when the Public Accounts Committee went into all these transactions, they were going to make a great exposure of wrongdoing. The minister was to be proved guilty of all sorts of transactions next to criminal. The air was blue with the predictions they made. They took a certain amount of comfort out of that. They were buoyed up during the recess by the confident expectation that something was going to happen disastrous to the government, as the result of their labour. Well, I would suggest to them now that they should proceed at once to Prince Edward Island and gather all the reports and information they can regarding the Prince Edward Island Railway, and let them buoy themselves up until next session with the expectation that they are going to prove any quantity of misdeeds. Let them go into the Murray Harbour transaction, sift it to the bottom, and make a great exposure of it. That is something to which they can devote their attention during the recess with great benefit, no doubt, and from their point of view, to the country . But it is rather late now to go into an inquiry of that kind. It is a thing which will keep. If^ everything is in such a deplorable condition, no doubt they will have abundant opportunity a year hence to make a reputation for themselves
even exceeding what they have succeeded in establishing this session.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Did the hon. minister contemplate, when he began building the railway from Mutch's Point, 11* miles south, to continue it to Murray Harbour 1 If so, why did he not, when letting that part of the contract, let also the whole line ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It was not intended then to carry it on so soon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: You only intended building 114 miles then.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It was very largely in the discretion of the minister on the island then, and he recommended that 114 miles be taken up.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: As a business proposition, I should think that you would have intended building the whole section.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: There was a very serious question about the route, as to the direction we would continue. And that matter had to be looked into, as the hon. gentleman knows. That was the reason why only 11* miles were taken.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would say with regard to the building of these lines on the island

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Which one ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Take the whole enterprise. It should not be dealt with las a number of small sections. If the hon. gentleman is going to build fifty miles he should call for tenders for that work. But I can understand why tenders were first called for this 11* miles from Mutch's Point. It appears the hon. gentleman contemplated *building only 114 miles, but. since then, lie has changed his mind and is building 45 or DO miles, and is giving these parties an opportunity to build through the level section the grading of the railway, the ballasting and track laying, on the basis of a tender for 114 miles. I think 'that is very unfair to the contractors in that part of the country that they should not be afforded an opportunity to tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: But they had an opportunity.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: On the 114 miles, but not on this.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The small contractor could handle 114 miles easier than he could 30 or 40 miles.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: They had an opportunity 'to tender for the work in the most hilly part of the country-

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Which is the most profitable for the contractor.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: We know Which is the most profitable. And if the hon. minister will consult his deputy and chief engineer, who built the railway in Prince Edward Island, he will learn how it was bu Lit around the hills in every direction, and it has cost the country over $17,000 within the last few years to strighten out those curves. Now, the ihon. gentleman is building this railway through the country south of Hillsborough, the hilliest part of Prince Edward Island.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) object to the location of the railway in this section ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am not objecting to the portion of the country the railway traverses. But I am objecting to the bou. minister giving the contract for building 111 miles through the most hilly part, and then continuing the contract to the contractor for 311 miles through a level section without giving others an opportunity to tender.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) say that it is easier to build the 311 miles than to build the 111 miles ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: On what authority does he make that statement ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: On his own.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I asked the hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I make the statement on this authority, that, in building the Prince Edward Island Railway, the line was run around the hills, and it has cost this country, as I say, almost $20,000 within the last few years to straighten out the curves. The hon. gentleman will understand that it is more difficult to make a straight line through hills and levelling up the valleys than to build it in a level country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: But it ,is much more profitable to the contractor. So, the hon. gentleman is not making out a very strong case.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: As the straightening out of these curves has cost the country so much one would suppose that the minister in laying this track for 114 miles would lay it in a straight line through that section of the country, ,so that trains could be run without difficulty. If you gave a contract for this 114 miles for a straight line through the hills levelling up the valleys, then It would be a different matter to get contracts for 314 miles where you have a level surface.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Starting at Mutch's Point where would the 114 miles bring you to ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
About to the ten-mile house.
Mr. HUGHES (King's;. About to O'Neils. It does not pass the ten-mile house at all, but passes 'beyond it. The hon. gentleman does not know the location of the road. Has the hon. gentleman ever been over that road that he says lit is a more level road from Mutch's Point to O'Neils than over the other part of the road ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That is the very opposite of what he said.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman understand that, in going from Mutch's Point to O'Neil's you go over Tea Hill ?

speechtext: No, you go east of Tea Hill. Has the hon. gentleman ever been over that road ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I have been over it, I can assure the hon. gentleman, and I was down to Vernon river last summer.
Mr. HUGflES (King's). How far did the hon. gentleman go ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: To Murray harbour. And let me say that I think the hon. gentleman's interruption on this occasion has been quite impertinent.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Now I make this statement, and I venture to say I shall be borne out by the engineers, that the latter portion of the road is more difficult to build than the former. The hon. gentleman stated that the first of the road was over a more level country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes, King's) is making a worse case for his friends.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I mean, that the ihon. gentleman said it was through a hillier country. But that was not in accordance with the facts. speechtext: And the hon. minister says that is where you can do the cheapest work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am making my statement in contradiction of the hon. gentleman from West Prinice (Mr. Hackett). He says that the 114 miles was the hilliest section of the road and that the rest was a very level country, and I must say that that is not in accordance with the facts.

road to ask for tenders, and to receive them from four or five different contractors. But now that lie is constructing 314 miles he does not think it is necessary to call for tenders, thougti the statute under which he exercises his authority requires him to do it.

I may as well take occasion of this item to refer to a question asked by the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Richardson) with regard to the dismissal of the postmaster at Holstein. I have in my hand a copy of the information given to the hon. minister as to why he was dismissed.
Memorandum for the Post Master General in reference to the removal of the Postmaster at Holstein.
The Postmaster General is informed that complaint was made that the postmaster was
conducting a public library in the room where the Post Office was located, and that looking after his duties as librarian conflicted with his duties as postmaster, causing thereby both delay and inconvenience to the public. It was further complained that the postmaster was not exercising proper care over mail matter, and that the public in going to the library had more or less access thereto.
This complaint having been referred to the inspector, he reported on the 11th of March, 1902, that the Postmaster was acting as librarian and also attending the public telephone, that he was also engaged in the grain trade, to which he devoted the greater part of his time, and that he found considerable dissatisfaction at Holstein on account of the public library being kept in the Post Office. In his opinion the Post Office is not a suitable place for such library. He also stated that during the time he was examining the accounts of the office a person called and asked for twelve books, that the person in charge left the Post Office work to look over the library to see if such books were in stock ; that at the same time the telephone was ringing, which also had to be attended to by the same person, causing thereby considerable confusion in the office. The Postmaster himself was absent from the office that day.
The inspector further states his opinion that the office was of sufficient importance to be separated distinct from the public library aud telephone business, and that sufficient privacy for those depositing money in the savings bank and seeking money orders, could not exist under existing conditions.
Under the circumstances the Postmaster was removed ou the 12th of March, 1902.
Now, I have here a copy of a petition sent to the Postmaster General with reference to that. I may mention the fact that this petition is signed by 151 parties who use the office, and I am told represents about leighty per cent of all those who use the office. It reads as follows
We the undersigned who are served by the Holstein Post Office have learned with most profund regret 'that our present Postmaster, W. T. Petrie, has been notified that the postmastership is about to be changed. We are thoroughly satisfied with 'the equipment and arrangement of the public library and telephone being in the post office building, and also that the service and accommodation are entirely satisfactory. And your petitioners do humbly pray that you reconsider your decision and leave the office and service in its present form.
The postmaster, writing a letter regarding this question, draws attention to the fact that in Dromore the library Is in the post office as at Holstein, and no complaint appears to be raised. In several other post offices the same thing is done. I have personally known Mr. Petrie for many years. He is a most enterprising man in the community, enjoying the respect and good will of almost the entire community. He is a business man of many years standing and has done everything that could be reasonably expected to benefit the place and serve the

492S
public. I do not wonder that it is regretted, as this petition expresses it, that a change should be made in respect to a man who has served the interests of the public so long and so faithfully.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) expects me to make any observations as to the report of the inspector to which he has referred as a justification for the action taken. It is quite clear that the convenience of the public was not being sufficiently regarded in the management of the office. In the course of carrying on the department complaints were made, the matter was referred to the inspector and he made his report. I do not think the department could have done less than change the postmaster under the circumstances.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The office seekers seem to be satisfied that their interests are being very well served.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I know this oflice, I know the postmaster, and I know personally the service he has given to the community in that place. It is a pretty well known fact that a simple matter of keeping a village library in the post office is a convenience to the public. It is something to which there is no emolument attached, it is a gratuitous service to the public which is very much appreciated, I am sure, in this case. There is one tiling in the inspector's report that carries with it great improbability, and it is the statement that somebody comes into that village library and asks for twelve books. It seems to me to be incredible unless it was arranged specially when the inspector was there that something of the kind should be done. Usually only one book is allowed out at a time, or two at the outside. I know how the library is kept and it does not require any one to go out of the office to see whether the books are in their places or not. I know Mr. Petrie is very highly esteemed by the community there and that the petition is, I am credibly informed, signed by 90 per cent of the people who are served by the office, irrespective of political lines altogether. It does seem somewhat strange, with a petition of that character presented, that no further inquiries seem to have been made, but that on this flimsy pretext, the postmaster is simply dismissed in order that a place may be made for a man who has been a very active politician and supporter of the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

speechtext: This is simply another of those cases in which the Postmaster General has seen fit to dismiss men without giving them auy opportunity whatever to reply to the charges made against them, and has acted upon ex parte statements without giving the officers of his department an opportunity to make a defence. I have a similar letter from Mr. David Mitchell, of Jeddore, who states that as far as political partisanship is concerned, he canvassed no man for or against the government, he was on no committee and had nothing to do with the elections.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is the statement of the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) there ? I do not remember the case. I sent the hon. gentleman (Mr. Borden, Halifax) the particulars.

speechtext: The documents that were handed to me in Mr. Kaulbach's case were two so-called affidavits of a very indefinite character, taken before a justice, not giving any dates or particulars, but making a general charge of political partisanship against Mr. Kaulbach, which he has denied.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: In what constituency is that ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It is in my own constituency.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Does Mr. Roche represent that too ?

speechtext: I think there is some communication from him.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Nothing from the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) was brought down by the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
What I submit to the hon. gentleman is that it does not seem to be a very fair way of dealing with these men to dismiss them without even letting them know anything about the charges against them, and upon ex parte statements of this character, to dismiss them from their positions with a certain imputation upon their character without giving them an opportunity of making their own defence. I have put that forward in this House a good many times without any effect. I think it is absolutely unfair to the officers of the department to dismiss them for alleged political partisanship without giving them an opportunity of making their defence against these charges. I know that notwithstanding the pledge which was given by the right hon. gentleman who leads the government, the practice has been defended from the other side of the House of dismissing these men upon the statement of a member of parliament purporting to speak from actual knowledge. I do not think that the hon. member from Halifax (Mr. Roche) would pretend to have any personal knowledge of the alleged partisanship of these' men, because they live a long distance from Halifax, where he resides, and he must, in any statements he has made, have had information given to him by other persons, so that the cases do not even come within those that I have mentioned. There is another difficulty in regard to the Jeddore postmaster, and it is that the people of that community are to be deprived of any opportunity to communicate to the outside world by telegram, because the only person who is capable of taking charge of the telegraph office there is Miss Mitchell, daughter of the postmaster, and it would not be worth her while to devote her attention to that work, as her father has been deprived of the post office. I have had a communication from a strong supporter of the Liberal party living in the vicinity, who has complained to me very bitterly in regard to this matter, and I think the hon. gentleman had better look into that and see whether the public are not likely to be inconvenienced very greatly by the dismissal of this man without any opportunity being given him of saying anything in his own defence.
There is another matter I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. gentleman, and that is that 21 petitions of right were tiled three years ago and the fiat asked for, which has not been granted in regard to any of them up to the present time. We have had at least two cases this session where people have been offered fiats and have declined to receive them, and their claims have been submitted to the Exchequer Court, not on the question of legal liability, but on the question of what is 155
fair and right apart from legal liability, and very substantial claims have been voted by this parliament upon the reports made under references of that kind. If the government see fit to grant references with respect to claims where there is no liability; on what ground does the Postmaster General persist in refusing petitions of right to these men who simply ask that claims against the Crown shall be adjudicated on in the Exchequer Court. Under a statute passed this session, the Crown has the right to exact security for costs from all these men, and whatever justification there might have been before-and I think there was none-there certainly is no possible justification now for refusing these men the right to have their claims decided on before a properly constituted tribunal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
In cases where the claimants have any substantial claims ; claims in good conscience as well as legal claims, I would agree with my hon. friend that a fiat should issue as a matter of course. But you have to look at these cases in order to see whether it is in the interest of right that they should be facilitated in proceedings against the Crown. It is rather late at night to take up the whole subject, but speaking generally what are the facts ? My hon. friend has not perhaps studied all the facts. Permit me to tell him that in the year 1895-9(5, the government-probably because they expected an early election or for whatever reason-proceeded (to disregard the statute which governs the Postmaster General, and right and left they issued contracts for the carrying of mails in contravention of that statute which says that tenders shall be invited for mail service and the contract awarded to the lowest tenderer; but, that in special cases the contract may be renewed. The cases that my hon. friend refers to are renewals of contracts. Now, not in one instance is there a special circumstance so far as appears in the department to warrant entering into these renewal contracts. They were renewed not only without justification under the statute but against the interests of the public. I do not know whether the observations I am about to make apply in detail to each one of the twenty-one cases, but I am sure that an analysis of the facts will show that many of the cases fall within the class I am about to describe. Tenders had been invited in many instances by the late government and after their receipt sometimes opened and the amounts ascertained, and then disregarded, the contracts were let to the old tenderers at prices in some instances enormously in excess of the general average of prices for which the new tenderers were prepared to perform the contracts. In some instances tenders were not even opened and scores and scores of new contracts were let for services which had been advertised and for which there



were tenders by the score in the department. In some instances contracts were let-and I believe one or more of the contracts referred to by my hon. friend-were let to the tenderers at higher prices than their tender. There are instances-and I think there are one or more among the twenty-one cases speaking from memory- where the old contractor put in his tender in the ordinary course for the new contract, and yet the government of the day chose to ignore his tender and let to him the contract at the original contract price, which may have been 50 per cent in excess of the amount of his new tender. These contracts, I submit, are not worth the paper on which they are written. There is no equity in their claims. If the contracts are good in law; if the statute does not mean what it seems to say, then it will be on the barest technicality they could recover. If they choose to disregard the right, and by their understanding with the government of the day or for whatever reason obtained improper contracts from the government, they have no claim upon the government to aid them, because they did not enjoy the full fruits of these improper contracts. Rather, they should be compelled to account for the portion of the excess they received during the currency of these contracts. It is incredible to suppose that in hundreds and hundreds of the simplest service that Canada affords, there were special circumstances that warrant the abandonment of the principle of inviting tenders, and yet that is what took place wholesale, and these cases are of that class. Under the circumstances there is no merit in good conscience in these claims, and the claimants have nothing to claim, but rather they should congratulate themselves that the government proposed to have the contracts treated ns null in the first instance, and did not call upon them to make good to the Crown the excess of money which during the time they purported to render service, they received.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The doctrine laid down by the Postmaster General is absolutely subversive of the principle upon which petitions of right have been granted in the past. The Postmaster General in effect says : Because my predecessor was guilty of laxity in the public service, I will annul these contracts whether I have the legal right to do so or not, and I will refuse these men a fiat which will enable them to substantiate their claims in court.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The other party is just as guilty.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What other party ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The petitioner is a party to the wrong.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: If the petitioner is a party to the wrong; if this contract is

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: not worth the paper it is written on, it is perfectly competent for the Crown to go into Court and say that. If the argument of the Postmaster General means anything it means that there was a conspiracy between these men and his predecessor in office to defraud the government. If that can be established in court, then not one of these men can recover. But the Postmaster General sees fit to judge these men behind their backs. He refuses these men the right to urge their claims in court, just as he refused the two postmasters the right to be heard in their own defence before he dismissed them. That is the position which the Postmaster General takes. I would be willing to leave it to the House and to the country as to whether that is a position which can be fairly maintained by any man who is desirous of doing right. If what the Postmaster General says, is true, then the government has nothing to fear because these men cannot substantiate their claims in court. If on the other hand these men are able to prove that what they say is correct, they have a valid claim against the government and they should have the privilege before the court of seeing whether they are right or whether the Postmaster General is right. But that right the Postmaster General denies them. He judges their cases himself and he deprives these men of that which every man in this country is supposed to have : The right to have his claim determined in a court of law by a proper tribunal, and after hearing both sides of the case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I desire to bring to the notice of the hon. the Postmaster General a case which I brought before the House last session when he was away in Australia, and the acting Postmaster General ;could make no reply. It is the case of a man named Kelioe who had the contract for carrying the mails between Tignish and Mail Point. Mr. Kelioe was requested by the inspector of post offices in Prince Edward Island, Mr. Brecken, at the expiration of his term of three years or so, whether he would renew his contract on the same terms, namely, $30 a year. Mr. Kelioe said he would, and signed the bond in my presence, and entered into a new contract in accordance with the request of the inspector. A few days afterwards an order came from Ottawa that the mails were to be delivered to another man, Thomas Nelligan, that Mr. Kelioe was not the contractor. Mr. Nelligan has been carrying the mails for the last two years and has been receiving $50 a year for the same work that Mr. Kehoe did for $30 a year. I would ask the horn Postmaster General if he has any knowledge of this matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

speechtext: occasion. If my lion, friend had intimated to me that he was going to bring it up I would have been prepared with a statement of the facts. maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to say with regard to the post office at Holstein, that if inadvertently an injustice has been done to the late postmaster and also to the public who by petition have expressed their satisfaction with the service and their desire to have the post office conducted by the same man, in view of the fact that no irregularity has been found in the office conducted by him for many years, and that he had no opportunity of hearing the charges made against him or making any defence. I think the Postmaster General should at least make some further inquiry into the matter. This is a case in which a gentleman who has rendered good service to the public for many years has been suspended on short notice without any opportunity to defend himself, ad the position given to a very active political partisan.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know what my hon. friend would suggest could have been done. It was a question of the proper management of the office, and the course pursued seems to me to have been a reasonable one. Charges were made, the proper officer was instructed to investigate he did investigate, and he ascertained that the public were not receiving fair consideration. The officer was conducting a telegraph or telephone business and a public library and was also engaged in the grain trade, so that the public were not receiving reasonable service. If the public are to be considered, it seems to me that it was a case calling for a change of postmaster. The inspector was at the office and saw for himself what was going on there. The postmaster, or his assistant, or his people were there. A new officer has been appointed, and I suppose the transfer has taken place, so that new rights have arisen. I see by the papers that the report was made early in March last. If so, the new officer has entered on his duties. He has his rights now, and it will be quite impossible to undo what has taken place.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I understand that it is a very common thing to have a telegraph or telephone system conducted in a post office. The emoluments are so very small in these offices that these businesses have to be combined for the convenience of the public. As to the other little matter of keeping the village library there, only five miles away a village library is kept in the post office and no complaint is made, and I do not believe there would have been any com-155J
plaint in this case if it had not been got up by a few people who were opposed to the postmaster. I know that he is a popular man. I believe that this petition asking that he be continued in the office has been signed by from eighty to ninety per cent of the people served by the office. It certainly seems to have been a case in which there might have been an investigation and opportunity given to comply with requirements of the department with regard to keeping library or telephone office.
The POSTMASTER GENERAL There was an investigation and the inspector made a report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That was the only investigation. He had no opportunity of making a defence.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: He had every opportunity.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
There was a postmaster in my county who was dismissed last fall. The other day I put a question on the Order paper about the dismissal and the Postmaster General replied that he was dismissed because Mr. Talbot had asked that he should be, as he had taken an active part in the election of 1900. Mr. Talbot was at that time, like myself, busy at home, and ho knew nothing about what was going on in my county. All he could say was that some one told him so. Well, the hon. Postmaster General should not listen to what he hears in that way, especially from politicians. He cannot expect to hear anything else, whether it is so or not. I remember very well in 1896 that question came up in the House, though not with regard to my county, and the Prime Minister said that people employed by the government would have the right to vote for whom they pleased and they would not be deprived of talking politics if they wanted to, but he said that a man employed by the government had no right to make speeches nor to publish articles in the newspapers. He said it made no difference whether the parties were Conservatives or Liberals, they would be dismissed. Now, to show you that this promise has not been carried out at all, I know a man perfectly well-he is a friend of mine if he is a Grit, and I do not like to mention his name-who last January spent some eleven days in the county of Beauce. On his return home he and I rode on the train together, and he was telling me how muck money he had spent in the county and how many days he had been there. He was also in the company of the Minister of Justice. Some time ago this question was brought up in the House by the hon. member for Laval (Mr. Leonard), and the Minister of Justice replied that he knew nothing of it. In this case it would not do to say that he knew nothing of it.
The hon. member for Bellechasse and the hon. Minister of Justice were in the county

of Beauce doing electioneering work. I do not ask that this man,' be dismissed, but I say it is rather strange to find one man treated in one way and another man treated altogether differently. If a Conservative works, or even if he does not work, but is reported to have been working in an election, he is dismissed. But a Grit is allowed to work right along, right and left in election time, and he is not interfered with. Is that treating citizens of this country on an equality ? I say it is mot. Let me draw the attention of the Postmaster General to another case. In 1890, there was a man in my county who got a contract for carrying the mails and he got it by tender. In 1895 that contract was renewed without public tender. In 1896, the present Postmaster General dismissed that man and gave the contract to somebody else. I have no fault to find with that, but what took place in 1897, right in the very town where I live ? I know all about the contract and the man. The contract expired and was given to another man, after public tenders were asked, for ?55 a year to carry the mails from the station to the post office. That contract expired some time last fall. The contractor wrote the department asking that his contract be renewed, but he got a reply that it was given to another man without any tender having been called for at all. Why is it that the Postmaster General condemns men and contracts just when it suits him and in any way he likes? If it was not right in 1895 to give a contract without public tender, why was it right to give it without public tender last fall ? If the hon. minister can explain that, I will be very grateful to him.

dent that occurred five years ago, and which has reference to one out of ten thousand contracts. I will, however, look the matter up and find out all about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would like to call attention to the change made in the post office at Keith. A post office existed between the two villages of Robinson and Gould, and that has recently been removed. A post office had been established many years at a point supposed to be the most central, marked out in former days, by the joint actiou of tlie mayors of the two towns. It is about 12 miles from Robinson to Gould, and the point that had been selected by the community, in which the office has existed many years, is supposed to be the most central and most accommodating to that district. By the change, the office has been removed many miles nearer Gould. To-day there are four farmers and their families living between the location of the present post office and the village of Gould. Naturally those farmers would be served at Gould which is the natural place for them to transact their business. The result has been to compel the people living for many miles in that vicinity to travel all this distance in order to get their mail. To meet these conditions I understand that an open bag of some sort is carried by the mail carrier and a sort of distribution takes place between Robinson and the present location of the post office known as Keith. I know no good reason why this change should be made. There is a large petition, I presume almost a unanimous petition, which was forwarded to the bon. gentleman from that section asking that this change be not made.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: When was it made ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Perhaps sixty days ago. Perhaps thirty days ago. 1 understand that the postmaster who previously handled the mail there was a Conservative, which, I suppose, is no great crime in the estimation of the Postmaster General. The present occupant, I presume, is a Liberal. I do not know. It is sometimes difficult to ascertain in my constituency those who are Conservatives and those who are Liberals. The Postmaster General has been asked on more than one occasion to make changes in my constituency. None of these changes have been favourable to the public. Some of them have been moved back again to the section in which they first were-not to the same parties, I admit. But I am perfectly willing to have the hon. Postmaster General appoint his own friends, provided he serves the public well. But I must say that in my constituency he has been particularly unfortunate in the advice he has received in the past. If he has no better source of advice in the future, I would ask him to come to me-not that I could give him any particular advantage, but I wrould at least
give him the prestige of serving the public well, and I am sure he will estimate it at its proper value such an advantage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: There is a way by which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Pope) can get the patronage.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That would be to expensive to principle. Ambitious as I may be, that would be too expensive, I am sure the hon. gentleman will see that. I feel somewhat interested in the post office at Keith, because it is an inconvenience to a lot of people as the mail has to be carried along this entire route, nine or ten miles until it gets to the post office as now located. I would ask the hon. Postmaster General, in the interest of these people, to open a way office that might possibly be more convenient and very little more expensive to the country. We have been told that this is a growing time, and I trust that the Postmaster General will regard this district as growing with the rest of the country and will hold it entitled to better service than it has ever received. I would ask him to open, somewhere, between the present post office, Keith and Robinson, a way office that can serve the farming community. There is not a village, but a straight road, and farmers located as they usually are in a district of that kind. I am pleased to see the Deputy Postmaster General on the floor. He has always treated me with great courtesy, and I trust that my words to the Postmaster General will strike the pan of his ear somewhat favourably, and that the people of that section will be given the accommodation to which they are entitled.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I will promise that the application of my hon. friend (Mr. Pope) will receive careful consideration. The general practice-I do not think it is ever departed from-is to change the location of a post office only on the report of the inspector.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I believe that in this instance the Postmaster General is more or less correct. From my Information, the inspector did recommend the change. But that does not alter the fact that the present arrangement is an inconvenience to the people. The cost of putting in a way office would be small and it would be a great accommodation to the people. Therefore, I ask it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I would ask the Postmaster General to inform me why the change at Alberton has taken place, and Sir. Thomas Keith, who was postmaster for nearly twenty years has been retired and somebody else appointed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: 1 will make a note of it and will let the hon. gentleman know to-morrow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
These notes are very well. But we have no difficulty in under-

standing that Mr. Keith was dismissed because he was a Conservative.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I will give the information to-morrow.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am glad to learn that it is the intention of the Postmaster General to transfer the mail carrying service in the county of Inverness from the present carrier to the Inverness and Richmond Railway. As this is an important portion of the county which I represent, I would like to know how it is intended to carry the mails on the trains. Does the hon. Postmaster General intend to have them sorted by mail clerk, and delivered as is ordinarily done, or merely as baggage in the baggage car ? I can tell the hon. gentleman that this is a most important part of the community, that there are three very thriving mining towns springing up in the county of Inverness along this very route. I hope that the delivery will not be made in such a fashion that the change will be regarded by the people as a retrograde step. For the last thirty-five or forty years, the mail has been delivered twice in every twenty-four- hours along this route. I am sure that anything short of a delivery by mail clerk from the train would be considered by the community over this long distance, fifty-eight miles, as a step of a retrograde character. I did not have an opportunity within the last week or two to discuss this with the Postmaster General. 1 did talk it over with the gentleman in charge of the railway mail service, but he was not very clear then as to the manner in which the mail service in this connection was going to be canned out. And I would like to learn what is intended ? _

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
That reminds me of the fact that the mails going west of Summer-side are delayed at Summerside for twenty hours. There is no connection between the steamboat arriving at Summerside and the train going west. I would ask the hon. gentleman in the interest of the public living west of Summerside that close connection should be made between the boat arriving and the trains going west. There are several towns, two of them 70 miles west of Summerside, and I hope that the Postmaster General will see to it that the mails shall not be delayed at Summerside for twenty hours, where you have only to run trains four or five hours to reach the homes of the people and convey the news that they are expecting from all parts of the world. I trust the Postmaster General will consider this matter. At present we have a steam-Mr. HACKETT
boat running between Pointe de Chene and Summerside, and when mails go to Charlottetown there is no connection to carry them west. Supposing I left here to-morrow morning, I would reach Summerside on the evening of the next day, and there I will be delayed until the following day. For just 60 miles, there is no connection between the mail and steamboat service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I will say to my hon. friend from Inverness (Mr. McLennan) that the matter he has brought to my attention is a very important one, and it will receive the careful consideration of the department. I will say to my hon. friend from Prince (Mr. Hackett) that I think the mails are despatched on all trains between Summerside and Charlottetown, and Georgetown and Charlottetown. Probably if there is any interruption it is because of there being no railway communication.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

speechtext:
I did not say that.

speechtext:
Assistant postmasters are paid a salary based upon the revenue of the office.
