To provide for increases of salary for employees in the outside service, not provided for in the main estimates, $2,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: When the fiscal year closes, the officers, as in the case of the inside service, will go through the staff and report to the deputy and the deputy will report such as are entitled to the increase. If they should all be reported for an increase it would exceed the sum of $2,500.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is the hon. gentleman able to give the names of the employees who salaries are to be increased ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: When the fiscal year closes then the officers make a report as to who are and who are not entitled to the increase. At present we are assuming they will all be entitled to it. I trust such may be the case. The report is made to me by the deputy. He, I presume, gets his advice from the officers immediately under him. In the inside service there are heads of branches, and I presume that he bases his judgment largely upon the recommendation of those heads of branches. In the outside service, I presume, he would have the report of the postmaster. It is the duty of the postmaster to inform himself of the efficiency of his staff and report. In the case of inspector's offices he would have the report of the inspector ; and in the case of the railway mail clerks, the report of the controller, I suppose. He in turn will get the advice of the local superintendents of the railway mail service.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is this the usual way in which the vote is passed, waiting for a report to be made at a subsequent date ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: That has always been the practice, I am informed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Pass the vote in general form without stating how many persons are entitled to it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The usual practice has been to provide for everybody and then get reports.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It may be the practice in the bon. gentleman's department, but it certainly is not the practice in other departments. The minister usually comes down with his estimates and says : I propose to recommend an increase to certain persons whose names are given, and if necessary I will ask the House to appropriate a sum of money for that purpose. I do not see why a different principle should prevail in the Post Office Department, and I do not see any reason why the officers of the hon. gentleman's department cannot make up their report.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: We cannot do that until the years' services has expired.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not see that that has anything to do with it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know about other departments.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Well, if a method of this kind is not necessary in other departments why is it necessary in the hon. gentleman's department ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: These estimates were prepared before Christmas.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: They may have been prepared two years ago, but they are presented to the House now, and we are asked to deal with them now. When the hon. gentleman comes down with his estimates he should be prepared with the report of his officers as to those whom he proposes to recommend for increases. I do not think it is a very good practice to ask parliament to vote a general sum in this way subject to a further recommendation. We can have nothing to say about it at present. We do not know what is going to happen in the future. If the hon. gentleman would name a particular individual we would know from him as to what the report was, and we would know something as to the length of the officer's service. AVe cannot know that very well when we have an appropriation in this general form.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not know what the practice is in the other departments, but I cannot myself understand how an officer could give a report as to a person entitled to an increase until the year of his service had expired. When, as a result of the year's service you can tell from his efficiency and fidelity whether or not he is deserving of the increase. To-day, no officer can report whether A B of this department would be entitled to an increase in July. There is a month and a half's time yet to expire. He might disqualify himself in the meantime and therefore the report for the whole period can only be made after the lapse of this time. We cannot anticipate how the service will be performed before the end of the fiscal year. This seems to be the common sense system. If there is a different system I think it ought to give way to one like this because we cannot give a certificate until we come to the conclusion that the officer is entitled to promotion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General an instance in the North-west Territories, where I think there is fair ground for asking for increased postal facilities. The Pasqua branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which runs from Aloose Jaw to North Portal on the boundary line, is a part of the Soo railway line, the greater portion of which is in the United States. There is a first class daily train service each way on that line and has been for eight or nine years past, but up to tlie present time there has never been a mail car put on the trains running on that line of railway, tint ft within perhaps a couple of years this has not caused

any grievance, because, on the Canadian part of the line, there was not a very large population, but within the past three years, and within the past two years particularly, a very considerable immigration has been coming into that particular district chiefly from the United States, and there are now some eight or nine considerable towns between Moose Jaw and North Portal. The hon. Postmaster General will remember that some time during the past winter an application came into the department from Milestone, asking the privilege of a daily mail from tlie train each way ; that is to say a double daily mail. The application came from the representatives of a very large American Land and Immigration Company which had established offices at the town of Milestone, and this company found that it was put to considerable inconvenience owing to the lack of the facilities which it asked. For instance, a letter posted at Milestone, addressed to the company's general offices in the United States, had to go first west of Moosejaw and then back towards its destination. I think there is good reason for asking now that additional facilities be furnished to the people of these towns by placing a mail car and a regular mail clerk on that branch railway.
Mi'. ICENDREY. Before that item is passed. I would like to bring to the attention of the hon. Postmaster General a matter in reference to the post office in the town of Peterborough. The Postmaster, I understand, from the 1st of July is to be reduced in salary from .$2,000 to $1,750. I also understand the salaries of the assistant postmaster and some of the subordinates are to be increased. The revenue of the post office in Peterborough has increased at the rate of about $1,000 a year, the work has increased with this increase in revenue and I would like to ask the hon. Postmaster General on what principle he makes this reduction in the salary of the postmaster at Peterborough.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
Whilst there is no absolute equality in the salaries of postmasters there is an effort as nearly as possible to bring post offices of this character under the same conditions. The postmaster of Peterborough, I have noticed, has a salary which is exceptionally high, as compared with the salaries of postmasters in other offices of the same character. I think that as a rule postmasters in offices of that importance do not receive $2,000 a year. Speaking from memory, I think I wrould be safe in saying that the postmaster at Owen Sound, which is a town perhaps almost equal in importance to Peterborough, but probably the responsibilities of the office are equally great, the postmaster at Berlin, which is another town of that character and of Brantford do not get as much as the postmaster at Peterborough. I do not think the postmaster at Brantford Mr. SCOTT.
gets $2,000 a year. In fact, the salary of the present postmaster at Peterborough is exceptionally high as compared with the salaries of postmasters in similar towns. I think there is one other town where the postmaster has a salary equal to that of the postmaster at Peterborough, but perhaps that will have to be 'looked into. It is not finally decided to carry out that arrangement. Mr. Edwards, of Peterborough, has brought the matter to my attention and has written a very lengthy memorial on the subject. I propose to look into it carefully and to endeavour to prevent any injustice, but you will find that it is a little difficult to defend giving a postmaster $2,000 a year and not much more to half a dozen others. Of course, the postmaster occupies a more responsible position, but at the same time there should be some reasonable relation between the salaries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: The reason that I bring this matter up is that in the office in Peterborough the work has been increasing from year to year and the hon. Postmaster General knows that the revenue from that office is increasing at the rate of about $1,000 a year. It does seem to me that so far as the postmaster at Peterborough is concerned, the responsibilities of the office are greater than those in many other cities and that it would be unfair to reduce the salary of the postmaster in order to raise the salary of the assistant postmaster and the subordinates on account of the work which has to be done there. It seems to be unreasonable because I can compare Peterborough with Belleville. Our revenue was very large and I wish to call the hon. gentleman's attention to the fact that while the revenue has been increasing the work has been increasing. I understood some time ago that the salary of the postmaster was to remain at $2,000. I do not think that the Postmaster General intends to do anything that is unreasonable, and I hope he will not do an injustice in this case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think the hon. gentleman will find that the salary of the Belleville postmaster is a good deal less than $1,750.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I understand that the postmaster of Belleville pays his own subordinates and that in Peterborough the subordinates are paid by the government.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think the same principle applies in each case. There is a sum of money set apart to meet the salaries of all the staff, and instead of the postmaster hiring his staff and paying them as formerly, he is limited to a certain amount in regard to his own salary, and the remainder must be apportioned amongst the staff.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I understand that the postmaster in Peterborough has a salary of $2,000, and the staff are paid by the gov-

eminent, while in Bellevilie the postmaster has a lump sum and he hires the help in the offices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think the arrangement is precisely the same in the two places. When there is a vacancy in the post office the postmaster reports it to Ottawa and then the department calls upon our friends in the district to recommend a suitable person, and that name is submitted to the postmaster for his approval. No person is forced upon the postmaster, and he can veto the recommendation. The money set apart for the maintenance of each office is divided by the government and a certain amount is fixed for the postmaster and the amount assigned to the members of the staff goes to them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Do I understand that the Postmaster General has recommended that the salary of the postmaster of Peterborough shall be reduced from $2,000 a year to $1,750, and that the $250 taken off his salary shall be distributed amongst the employees.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Nothing has been done in that way. The postmaster's salary is one thing and the salaries of the staff another. There may be an increase in the salaries of the staff, and there may be a reduction in the salary of the postmaster.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Has the postmaster of Peterborough been notified that on the 1st July his salary will be reduced to $1,750 7

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It was in contemplation and he may have been so notified. Mr. E. B. Edwards, of Peterborough. called upon me and asked me to reconsider the matter, and I requested him to put his views in writing. My secretary, I think, told me that a lengthy communication covering a good many pages of foolscap has come from Mr. Edwards, and I have deferred the pleasure of reading it until after prorogation.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Has the notification been sent to the postmaster ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Probably he has been notified, but I have told Mr. Edwards that I will reconsider it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: All right.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I wish to say a few words in defence of the Postmaster General who has evidently been wronged by some of his friends. The hon. gentleman stated a few moments ago that he was endeavouring to regulate the post offices throughout the Dominion on some principle. I am perfectly prepared to accept the hon. gentleman's word, but I would point out to him that so far, the Belleville post office has not 'been treated by his department on any principle. Before the advent of the Postmaster General to power, Belleville was a city post
office and had a postmaster under the Civil Service Act. Envious people, without any grounds whatever tried to get that postmaster removed from his position. Attack after attack was made on him and in fact he almost lost his position on the ground that he had driven a voter to the polls during my last election, but on inquiry it was found that the voter he had driven was a warm supporter of the Liberal party. When it was impossible to secure his removal with the consent of His Excellency, Belleville was reduced to the status of a country post office for the sole purpose, it is said, of getting rid of the postmaster. It is now announced by the Postmaster General that he desires to apply the principle, and desires to act fairly. Every one will be pleased to hear that, because the fact remains that of all the cities in Canada, Belleville is the only one reduced, while other offices with less revenue and greater expenditure are not interfered with. The fact remains that there are men in the States drawing superannuation allowances while others are filling their places at the salaries the gentlemen who were superannuated were willing to work for. I am sure that the Postmaster General must intend to apply the principle to which he has just referred, or otherwise he would not have spoken of it. I would call his attention in all humility to the Belleville post office and ask him to apply precisely the same principle to that office that he has expressed his intention of applying to every other post office in this country. If the hon. gentleman keeps his word he will restore Belleville to the list of city post offices, and see that the country is not burdended by having to pay to some persons superannuation allowances while others are drawing salaries for doing the same work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
The changes in ithe Belleville posit office were deliberately made on my own judgment without advice from any one else. Belleville was on a city basis, as it is called, and if it had remained on that basis, the expenditure on the staff would to-day probably have attained to $10,000 a year. I do not wish to be held bound by the figures I now mention, because they may be slightly incorrect; but my recollection is that up to the time it was moved .from a city basis the salaries had attained to $8,000 or $0,000 a year. The expenses of that office were out of all proportion to the revenue. With the exception of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, I think there was no city office in Canada having so small a revenue ns Belleville. Therefore, I removed Belleville from the city basis for the purposes of economy and to prevent an abuse. My hon. friend is wholly in error in suggesting that the public is under anything like as great expense now, even including -the superannuations, as it would have been had Belleville been left on the city basis. I think

the reduction in the expense of the office was not less than $4,000. With regard to the question of my hon. friend from Western. Assiniiboia (Mr. Scott), with reference to an increased mail service on a branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I can only say that the matter will toe carefully looked into.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I accept with pleasure the statement made toy the hon. Postmaster General, and X presume that if I can show him that there are other cities ini this country whose returns are less satisfactory compared with the expenditure than those of Belleville, he will either reduce those offices to a basis of country post offices, or restore Belleville to the list of city offices.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I do not wish to enter into any controversy with my hon. friend. I said that at the time Belleville was reduced, it made a worse showing than any other city in^Canada, except Charlottetown; but the latter, being a seat of government, I felt wTas entitled to a little different treatment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: It is not a question ot controversy with me. I am merely asking the hon. Postmaster General to apply the principle which he himself- stated in this House a short time ago it was his intention to apply, not only to Belleville, but to other places ; and as he gives certain reasons why Belleville has been reduced, 1 take for granted that if those reasons are proven to be erroneous, he will do justice, and restore Belleville to the list oif city offices. That is all I ask.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I wish to call the attention of the hon. the Postmaster General to the fact that the town of Peterborough, though it has only a town post office, has a revenue of $21,000 as against $14,000 of revenue in Belleville.

speechtext: If the session were not so far advanced and the hour not so late, I would like to say something about the terms of the concession granted by this government, known as the Treadgold concession. The terms were not submitted to this House at the opening of the session as they should have been. Whether or not they were required to be so submitted by any statute or regulation, the interests dealt with were so large that I think the government should have brought the papers down and have had them printed earlier in the session, for the purpose of informing the House as to the nature of that concession. That was not done. We did not get them until a date at which the government, in consequence of representations made to them from the Yukon, had themselves come to the conclusion that the terms on which that concession was granted in the first instance were not such as should be continued. But it does seem to me that that contract must have been entered into by the government in a very hurried way and without much consideration. To illustrate, I might mention the fact that the miners were to be charged at the rate of $1 per inch for the water supply and this was afterwards reduced to 25 cents an inch. I do not know the provisions of the later Order in Council with regard to this. Lookiug over it to-day, I could not see any provision on the subject at all. Some communications which I have had from the Yukon Territory indicate that the dissatisfaction with the conditions of the contract as at first framed was very strong, and was not confined to those who are opposed to this government, but was widespread and was felt as strongly and deeply among gentlemen who otherwise approved the policy of this government, as among their opponents. It seems to me, so far as I have been able to consider it, to give a monopoly in the Yukon which will be very valuable to the gentlemen who receive it, and will probably-if we may rely upon statements made by the press of the Yukon and by a great many men interested in that country-prove very detrimental to the miners there for a long time to come. In addition to this monopoly, the men who have obtained the concession have rights which are very much more valuable, so far as I can understand the situation, than those which can be obtained by ordinary miners in the district. For example, what is called the necessity of representation or something of that kind was dispensed with in the first concession so far as these men were concerned. I do not know whether or not that still continues. The effect, as I understand it, was that persons who obtained that concession were not obliged to perform the work of development or pay the annual sum which was necessary on the part of other miners. But these are only a few of the circumstances to which my attention has been directed with regard to this concession. I think it would have been better if the government had submitted a proposition of that kind to parliament before entering into the contract. But putting that aside, there can be no doubt that the terms should have been brought down to the House in the early part of the session so that discussion could be held for which opportunity up to the present time has not offered.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I admit that my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Hali-ax) has some ground for finding fault because the Order in Council was not laid before parliament sooner. But, as my hon. friend knows, I was away, being in ill health, and even when I returned, I was not able to give attention to the House for some days. The papers were prepared as soon as the motion was made for them and they were brought down. I can assure the hon. gentleman that whatever questions may have arisen, whatever difference of opinion there may have been as to the government's action, that action was not taken in haste. The whole subject has given the government a great deal of consideration, and anxious consideration, in order to bring about the best results. A question which has not yet been realized in regard to the development of the mining ground of the Yukon Territory as completely as it will be realized is the question of the water supply. So long as the rich pockets upon the creeks now well known continue to be worked, the effects of the lack of a proper * water supply are not likely to be seriously felt. But as soon as these beds begin to be exhausted-and we are getting pretty near to that now-the difficulty about the water supply will press for attention. There is an enormous quantity of gravel of a much lower grade than the miners have been heretofore operating upon which it will be necessary to work if that portion of the country which is producing the largest quantity of gold is to be kept up to its present position. It was the desire of the government to secure the inauguration of some scheme whereby water would be brought in on a large scale, and, to do that we felt that it would be justifiable and proper in the interest of the country that pretty liberal privileges and concessions should be given to those who engaged in that enterprise. If the scheme as originally contemplated had been carried out, the expenditure involved

would have been $7,000,000 or $8,000,000. It was thought that all the water would have to be pumped from the Yukon river. But subsequently the promoters came to the conclusion that water could be got from a stream called Kock creek and brought by gravitation, reducing the cost of operating considerably, though, perhaps not the cost of putting in the plant. Under that arrangement, the corporations were bound to introduce certain quantities of water under certain conditions and supply it to the miners. The dissatisfaction which arose, I think arose owing to the changed conditions as time went on and the matter was further considered. If, when the contract was first entertained, the proposition had been promulgated I do not think there would have been any opposition. But the condition of affairs had changed. Gold in paying quantities was found in some of the abandoned claims though not to the same extent that the newspapers would lead us to believe, and there was a disposition on the part of those who had no mining claims to take these* abandoned claims. My own opinion is that the abandoned claims were probably of no great value, but it is hard to tell with certainty. The change was of such a character as to demand consideration. Mr. Ross, the commisssioner of the Yukon, was here on other business, and Mr. Treadgold, representing the promoters, was here and we endeavored to remove the objections. Under the second Order in Council the plan was passed so that, while many of the privileges given to the promoters are surrendered, the obligation on the part of the promoters to deliver water is removed and it is left practically in the shape of a voluntary enterprise. I still have strong hopes that this arrangement will be successfully carried out and that it will result in the production of an enormous amount of gold from places where at present it cannot be produced at all.

I want to refer to a statement made in the House by the Minister of Justice while I was absent the other night. In connection with this settlement of the Noble Bros, claim, the Minister of Justice made the following statement :
I have not. looked into the matter very fully. According to the report, the whole proceedings were the result of a conspiracy started by this man Elliott. I say so, and I am in a better position to know than the hon. minister or the hon. gentleman who interrupts me. I was here in the department at the very time and heard Mr. Noble declare to the minister that they were not violating the law in any way; and within five minutes of the time that statement was made a telegram was laid down on the Table giving the information that the fishery inspector had seized those boats, because they were fishing illegally. I have this to say with regard to the fishery inspector. I have known him since childhood, I believe him to be an intelligent, respectable truthful and honourable man, who would be above entering into a conspiracy to injure any one carrying on work up there; and I think I know the source from whence that statement comes; and it comes with very bad grace from the parties who gave that information to the hon. Minister of Justice. If he knew the parties and the facts as well as he should, he would never have made the statement he did in the House of Commons against the fishery overseer who was doing what the department instructed him to do, and what any overseer ought to do. He reported the result to the department, and the department handled the case after that. Therefore it was out of his hands. If any injustice was done to the Nobles, it was done by the minister in charge of the department, and not by the overseer; and a statement of this kind in the House of Commons, traducing a respectable man's character, does not come with very good
grace from the hon. Minister of Justice, unless he makes sure that the statement is absolutely correct. When the overseer endeavoured to stop that illegal fishing, he was dealing with a crew who had been practically outlaws on the Georgian Bay for years; and he did what he was instructed to do by the minister, and reported the result, after which it was out of his hands. To say that it vwis a conspiracy is to do a great injustice to the overseer, and it is not waranted by the facts.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: Is it the intention to introduce the metric system generally ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I suppose we shall have to follow the example of England and the United States, 'and. we are preparing .to do so by distributing these metric systems throughout the schools of our country. At present the system is optional, but perhaps within a year or two we will have to make it the legal standard for the whole country. So We are affording the means of teaching our inspectors throughout the Dominion how to inspect these measures of weight and length. We have already been requested by some people in the trade to inspect measures of the metric system. We must therefore have a standard of the same nature, and we need at least one, or two, or three of our officers to be competent and ready to inspect these measures. The system being optional now, every merchant or trader can use the metric system if he chooses. We recognise the fact that within a short time we shall have to adopt the metric system There are already, if I am not mistaken! two or three Bills before the American Congress to adopt this system, bringing it into force gradually.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I think it is a mistake to have two systems of weights and measures in the country. It is not many years ago since we spent over $20,000 to purchase standard weights and measures for general use. I understand the minister to say that this system is an optional one. I think it would be wise for the government to decide whether they intend to introduce it in the future or not.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: There are not two systems at present in use, for while one is only permissive, the other is a compulsory and legal one. I am not in a position now to state what I shall do with regard to the adoption of the metric system.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: What is the opinion of the government ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext:
I do not think the government has formed any idea with regard to that subject, except that we shall be compelled to follow the example of other nations. If we wish to trade either with England, or France, or Belgium, or the United States, or Ger-lmany, we will have to use the same system of weights and measures that those 'countries use. I appreciate the difficulty we would have if we had in use at the same time the metric system and our present system. To introduce the metric system and make it universal would be a revolutionary measure in that branch of business. We cannot expect our people 'who have been long accustomed to the old system, readily to adopt the new system. Therefore we are commencing to educate 'them to the use of the metric system, by distributing the sets of weights and measures throughout the various educational institutions of the country. Last year we purchased fifty sets. I am receiving quite a number of requests for them, even from members of parliament, who wish to distribute them among the schools in their constituencies.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
subtopic: THE CASE OF J. M. HURLEY.
speechtext:
With the permission of the House, I desire to mention this one matter briefly. When the estimates of the Marine and Fisheries Department were under consideration, the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr.' Porter) stated that he had some information with regard to one of the fish-

eries inspectors taking part in an election. The hon. leader of the opposition also made some remarks, and I gave my promise that I would write to the officer referred to. I wrote inclosing him a copy of the remarks of the kon. member for West Hastings, and have received his reply and also the affidavit of the party who was alleged to have been influenced by this officer to sign the protest against the hon. member. The hon. member for West Hastings has spoken about it once or twice, and if he had been present when the estimates were up I would have been pleased to lay the information before the committee. I believe this should be done, and I think every one will recognize that it is only due to the officer whose conduct has been called in question that his letter should be given. This is the letter :
Belleville, Ont., March 6, 1902. The Hon. James Sutherland,
Minister of Marine and Fisheries,
Ottawa.
Hon. Sir,-I have the honour to acknowledge receipt of your letter, dated Ottawa, March 3rd, respecting the statements made by Mr. Porter, M.P. for West Hastings, that X took an active part in the recent by-election in that riding, and that I solicited the petitioner to sign the petition against him.
In reply to the first statement, I beg to say that I took no part, directly or indirectly, in the recent election contest in West Hastings, nor did I ask any man to vote or not to vote. I may say further that I did not attend any meeting, either public or private.
With regard to the second statement made by Mr. Porter, I beg to say that I dil not solicit the petitioner to sign the petition against him, nor did I ask any one else to sign it nor did any one consult me about signing the petition.
I have the honour to he, sir,
Your obedient servant,
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE A.ND FISHERIES (Hon. James Sutherland).

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

speechtext:
Fishery Officer.
The following is the affidavit of the party referred to :
In the matter of the West Hastings Dominion by-election.
I,	Comellius Mullins, of the city of Belleville, in the county of Hastings, sailor, make oath and say :-
1.	That I, am the person whose name is signed to the petition filed herein against the return of Mr. E. Guss Porter, as member for the West riding of Hastings.
2.	That I have been advised and believe that certain charges have been made against Mr. J. M. Hurley, Inspector of Fisheries, to the effect that it was by his inducement and representations, I was prevailed upon to sign the said petition.
3.	That the said J. M. Hurley did in no wise try, procure or endeavour to procure my signature to the said petition, nor did he have anything to do therewith, nor was the question of election of, or protest against the return of the said candidate ever spoken of by him to me.
And it was not on his inducement or procurement, or by ai^y request on his part that the said petition was so signed by me.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.

speechtext:
Sworn before me at the city of Belleville, in the county of Hastings, this 6th day of March, A.D. 1902.

I am sure hon. members will be pleased to know the state of affairs, and no person, 1 am sure, will be more ready than the hon. member for West Hastings to accept the facts with regard to the case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-THE CHARLES A. BULL PRODUCE COMPANY.
speechtext: I am sure that every one will be glad to know that this officer did not take part in election contests. But there is just one observation I would like to make, and that is, that a great many officers of the government have been prepared with evidence equally cogent of their freedom from political partisanship so far as taking part in elections is concerned, but who, nevertheless, have been dismissed without being given an opportunity of making their defence before an impartial or indeed any tribunal.
